APIRequestContext.summary: APIRequestContext sends HTTP requests for API testing and test setup. It can share cookies with a browser context or use isolated cookie storage.
APIRequestContext.explanation: APIRequestContext sends HTTP requests for API tests and service setup. You can get one from a browser context or create an isolated one. Requests update the context cookie store, and browser-linked contexts share cookies with the browser context.

parameters.name: url_or_request
parameters.description: Target URL, or a Request object for `fetch()`.

parameters.name: data
parameters.description: Request data. Objects are serialized as JSON unless another body option is used.

parameters.name: headers
parameters.description: HTTP headers to send.

parameters.name: params
parameters.description: Query parameters added to the URL.

parameters.name: timeout
parameters.description: Request timeout in milliseconds. The default is 30000; 0 disables it.

APIRequestContext.returns: Request methods return APIResponse. Cookie methods and dispose return NoneType.

example.title: Send an API request
example.code:
import asyncio
from playwright.async_api import async_playwright

async def main():
    async with async_playwright() as p:
        request = await p.request.new_context(base_url="https://example.com")
        response = await request.get("/")
        print(response.status)
        await request.dispose()

asyncio.run(main())
example.explanation: This creates an isolated request context, sends a GET request, prints the status, and releases the context.

useCases.title: Prepare test data
useCases.scenario: Call REST endpoints to create, update, or remove test data before a browser test.

useCases.title: Test web APIs
useCases.scenario: Check API responses without opening a browser page.

useCases.title: Reuse browser authentication
useCases.scenario: Use browser-linked cookies for authenticated API calls.

useCases.title: Isolate sessions
useCases.scenario: Create independent API sessions for tests that must not share cookies.

interview.question: How do browser-linked and standalone request contexts differ?
interview.answer: Use `browser_context.request` or `page.request` when API calls should use the browser context's cookies. Use `api_request.new_context()` when the API calls need separate cookie storage.
interview.followUp: How can you verify the stored cookies? Call `request.cookies()` with no URLs for all cookies, or pass URLs to filter them.

interview.question: What does `APIRequestContext.fetch()` do?
interview.answer: `fetch()` sends an HTTP request and returns an `APIResponse`. It accepts a target URL or an existing request and can send JSON data, form data, or multipart data.
interview.followUp: How would you upload files? Build multipart form data and pass it through the `multipart` option.

interview.question: How are response errors and redirects handled?
interview.answer: The request methods return responses for all status codes by default. Set `fail_on_status_code` to make a request fail when the response code is outside the 2xx and 3xx ranges.
interview.followUp: What happens with redirects? Request methods follow redirects automatically; configure `max_redirects` to change the limit or set it to 0 to disable following.

keyPoints: Use the class to call API endpoints during tests or to prepare a service before browser tests.
A browser context provides a request object through `browser_context.request`; `page.request` is a shortcut to the same object.
Create a separate request context when browser access is not needed or cookie isolation is required.
Requests read cookies before sending and store cookies received in responses.
HTTP request methods follow redirects without extra code.
Responses stay in memory so their body can be read later; dispose the context to release those resources.
gotchas: A standalone request context does not share cookies with the browser context.
Dispose the context only after all requests and response reads are complete.
Requests time out after 30 seconds unless you set another timeout or use 0.

Browser.summary: A Browser is a running Playwright browser. Use it to create isolated browser contexts and pages, check connection state, and close browser resources.
Browser.explanation: A Browser represents a running Playwright browser. Create isolated BrowserContext objects with newContext(), then create pages inside them. Close contexts before closing the browser so pages close cleanly and recorded files are saved.
Browser.syntax:
browser.newContext(options?)
browser.newPage(options?)
browser.close(options?)
browser.contexts()
browser.isConnected()
browser.browserType()
browser.newBrowserCDPSession()
browser.bind(title, options?)

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Browser options object. close() accepts an optional reason string; bind() accepts host, port, metadata, and workspace directory options. newContext() and newPage() accept browser configuration options.

parameters.name: title
parameters.description: Name used to identify the browser server.

Browser.returns: Methods return BrowserType, boolean, arrays of BrowserContext objects, Promise<void>, Promise<BrowserContext>, Promise<Page>, or Promise<CDPSession>, depending on the method.

example.title: Create a page and close resources
example.explanation: Launches Firefox, creates an isolated context and page, visits a URL, then closes both resources.

useCases.title: Isolate test users
useCases.scenario: Create separate test sessions with independent cookies and cache.

useCases.title: Run a small browser task
useCases.scenario: Create a page quickly for a short script.

useCases.title: Expose a browser server
useCases.scenario: Share a browser with another client through a named pipe or web socket.

interview.question: What is a BrowserContext used for?
interview.answer: newContext() creates an isolated browser context. It does not share cookies or cache with other contexts, so it is useful for separate sessions.
interview.followUp: How should a test clean up? Close each context first, then call browser.close() so artifacts such as videos and HAR files finish saving.

interview.question: What does browser.close() do?
interview.answer: browser.close() closes a launched browser and its pages. For a connected browser, it clears contexts created by the connection and disconnects from the server.
interview.followUp: Why close contexts explicitly? It lets pages close gracefully and flushes artifacts before the browser is closed.

interview.question: When should you use browser.newPage()?
interview.answer: browser.newPage() creates a page in a new browser context. It is a convenience method for short, single-page scenarios; production code should create a context explicitly.
interview.followUp: What happens when that page closes? The context created by newPage() closes too.

keyPoints: contexts() lists the BrowserContext objects currently open in the browser.
isConnected() returns a boolean that shows whether the Browser is still connected.
browserType() returns the BrowserType associated with the Browser.
newContext() creates an isolated context with separate cookies and cache.
bind() can expose the browser through a web socket on an operating-system-selected port.
gotchas: Use newPage() only for short, single-page code. Closing its page also closes the context created for it.
newBrowserCDPSession() cannot be used with Firefox or WebKit.
Do not call Browser methods after close().

BrowserContext.summary: A BrowserContext is an independent browser session. Create contexts to isolate pages, cookies, permissions, and other browser state between tests or users.
BrowserContext.explanation: A BrowserContext is an independent browser session. Create one with browser.new_context(), then create pages inside it. Pages opened from a page, such as popups, stay in the same context. Close the context when finished; this closes its pages too.

parameters.name: cookies
parameters.description: List of cookie dictionaries. Each cookie needs a URL, or both a domain and a path.

parameters.name: urls
parameters.description: Optional list of URLs used to limit returned cookies.

parameters.name: page
parameters.description: A page or frame targeted for a new CDP session.

parameters.name: url
parameters.description: A glob, regular expression, or predicate used to match request URLs.

parameters.name: handler
parameters.description: The function that handles each matched request.

BrowserContext.returns: BrowserContext methods return values documented per method. new_page() returns Page; cookies() returns a list of cookie dictionaries; expect_page() returns an event context manager; new_cdp_session() returns CDPSession; methods such as close(), add_cookies(), and route_from_har() return None.

example.title: Create and close a browser context
example.code:
from playwright.sync_api import sync_playwright

with sync_playwright() as p:
    browser = p.chromium.launch()
    context = browser.new_context()
    page = context.new_page()
    page.goto("https://example.com")
    print(page.title())
    context.close()
    browser.close()
example.explanation: This creates an isolated context, opens a page in it, visits a URL, and closes the context.

useCases.title: Isolate test sessions
useCases.scenario: Run tests with separate cookies, permissions, and pages.

useCases.title: Group related pages
useCases.scenario: Open several pages that share one session.

useCases.title: Control context network traffic
useCases.scenario: Mock or block requests for every page in a session.

interview.question: What is a BrowserContext?
interview.answer: A BrowserContext is an isolated browser session. It can contain multiple pages, and a popup opened by one of those pages belongs to the same context.
interview.followUp: How would you isolate two users in one browser process? Create two contexts with browser.new_context(), then create each user's pages inside its own context.

interview.question: How do you manage a context's lifetime?
interview.answer: Use browser.new_context() to create the context and context.new_page() to create a page. Close the context after the test; its pages are closed with it.
interview.followUp: Why close the context instead of only the page? Closing the context releases the whole session and closes every page that belongs to it.

interview.question: How does context-level request routing work?
interview.answer: context.route() can match requests with a glob, regular expression, or predicate. The handler can inspect or change the request, and routing applies to pages in the context.
interview.followUp: What limitation should you check when routing? Service Worker requests are not intercepted, so disable Service Workers when request interception is needed.

keyPoints: Use separate contexts when tests or users need independent browser sessions.
A popup opened by a page remains in that page's context.
Call context.new_page() to add a page to an existing context.
context.add_cookies() installs the supplied cookies in every page in the context.
context.clear_permissions() removes permission overrides for the whole context.
Use context.expect_event() when an action should produce a context event.
gotchas: A context made with browser.new_context() is non-persistent, so it does not save browsing data to disk.
Do not call close() on the default browser context.
new_cdp_session() works only with Chromium-based browsers.
A matching routed request must be continued, fulfilled, or aborted.

chromium.summary: Playwright needs matching browser binaries for each version. Install them with the CLI, select browsers with projects or channels, and manage their dependencies and storage with the documented options.
chromium.explanation: Playwright uses browser binaries that match the installed Playwright version. Install the browsers with the CLI, choose browsers with projects, and use channels when you need Chrome or Edge. Playwright can also install system dependencies and store browsers in a shared directory.
chromium.syntax:
npx playwright install [browser]
npx playwright install-deps [browser]
npx playwright install --with-deps [browser]
npx playwright test --project=<project>

parameters.name: install arguments
parameters.description: Optional browser name or installation option, such as chromium, webkit, --with-deps, or --only-shell.

parameters.name: --project
parameters.description: Optional project name used to select a configured browser project.

chromium.returns: The CLI returns an exit status; a nonzero status indicates failure when invoked through the .NET API.

example.title: Install and run Chromium tests
example.code:
npx playwright install chromium
npx playwright install-deps chromium
npx playwright test --project=chromium
example.explanation: This installs Chromium and its system dependencies, then runs the Chromium project.

useCases.title: Set up browsers
useCases.scenario: Install the browsers needed by a local project or CI job.

useCases.title: Cross-browser testing
useCases.scenario: Run the same tests against Chromium, Firefox, WebKit, or device profiles.

useCases.title: Test branded browsers
useCases.scenario: Use official Chrome or Edge channels for regression or codec testing.

useCases.title: Control browser storage and downloads
useCases.scenario: Share browser binaries between jobs or use a custom download host.

interview.question: How do you install Playwright browsers?
interview.answer: Run the Playwright install command after installing or updating the package. Without a browser argument, it installs the default browsers; a browser name installs only that browser.
interview.followUp: How would you reduce a headless CI download? Use the --only-shell option when the Chromium channel is not used, or --no-shell with the new chromium channel.

interview.question: How do you run tests on several browsers?
interview.answer: Use browser projects in the Playwright configuration. Each project can select a browser or device, and --project runs one selected project.
interview.followUp: How would you test a branded browser? Set a Chromium project channel such as chrome or msedge.

interview.question: Where are browser binaries stored and how can you share them?
interview.answer: Playwright downloads Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit to an operating-system cache. Set PLAYWRIGHT_BROWSERS_PATH during installation and test execution to use a shared directory.
interview.followUp: How can unused browser versions be retained? Set PLAYWRIGHT_SKIP_BROWSER_GC=1 or pass --no-remove during installation.

keyPoints: The browser binaries must match the Playwright version.
Run the install command without a browser name to install the defaults.
Use install-deps for operating-system packages, or combine it with browser installation using --with-deps.
The supported main browser engines are Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit.
Use browser channels to launch installed Chrome or Edge release variants.
Browser files use an operating-system-specific cache unless you configure another path.
gotchas: Updating Playwright can require another browser installation.
Use Playwright's Firefox build instead of the branded Firefox application.
Use WebKit instead of the installed Safari browser.
Chrome and Edge headless behavior can differ from Playwright's default Chromium headless shell.

Clock.summary: Playwright's Clock lets tests control browser time. It can install fake timers, advance or pause time, resume it, or set a fixed or system time.
Clock.explanation: The Clock API controls time for every page and iframe in a BrowserContext. Install fake timers to control time-dependent APIs, then advance, pause, resume, or set time as the test requires.
Clock.syntax:
page.clock.install(time=...)
page.clock.fast_forward(ticks)
page.clock.run_for(ticks)
page.clock.pause_at(time)
page.clock.resume()
page.clock.set_fixed_time(time)
page.clock.set_system_time(time)

parameters.name: ticks
parameters.description: Milliseconds to advance, or a readable duration such as "01:00".

parameters.name: time
parameters.description: Initial time; defaults to the current system time. Numbers are Unix seconds.

parameters.name: time
parameters.description: Time at which the clock should pause. Numbers are Unix seconds.

example.title: Control page time in a test
example.code:
from datetime import datetime
from playwright.sync_api import sync_playwright

with sync_playwright() as p:
    browser = p.chromium.launch()
    context = browser.new_context()
    page = context.new_page()
    page.clock.install(time=datetime(2024, 12, 10, 8, 0, 0))
    page.goto("http://localhost:3333")
    page.clock.pause_at(datetime(2024, 12, 10, 10, 0, 0))
    page.clock.run_for(1000)
    browser.close()
example.explanation: This installs a fake clock before navigation, pauses it at a chosen time, and then advances it while running due callbacks.

useCases.title: Control timer-driven behavior
useCases.scenario: Test countdowns, polling, retries, or scheduled UI updates without real delays.

useCases.title: Test a fixed date
useCases.scenario: Check date and time rendering for a known moment.

useCases.title: Simulate a system-time shift
useCases.scenario: Verify behavior after a clock or time-zone change without firing scheduled callbacks.

interview.question: What does clock.install() control?
interview.answer: Install fake timers with clock.install(). It controls Date, Temporal.Now, timer functions, animation callbacks, idle callbacks, and performance APIs.
interview.followUp: When should set_fixed_time be preferred? Use it for a simple fixed-time test where timers should keep running; use install for more advanced control.

interview.question: How do run_for() and fast_forward() differ?
interview.answer: run_for advances the clock and fires all time-related callbacks. fast_forward also advances time, but each due timer fires at most once.
interview.followUp: Which method models a suspended device returning later? fast_forward, because it represents closing and reopening the laptop after a period.

interview.question: How should pause_at() be used during page setup?
interview.answer: pause_at moves the clock to a specified time and pauses it. While paused, timers do not fire unless a clock-advancing method or resume is called.
interview.followUp: Why install before page.goto()? Page-loading timers need to run normally; pausing too early can leave the page stuck.

keyPoints: Use fake timers when a test must control time instead of waiting in real time.
Time advances accept milliseconds or readable strings for seconds, minutes, and hours.
resume returns the clock to normal time flow and timer behavior.
set_fixed_time freezes date values while leaving timers active.
gotchas: Installing the clock affects every page and iframe in the BrowserContext.
Install the clock before navigation and start slightly before the target time so page loading timers can run normally.
set_system_time changes the reported time without firing timers.

Coverage.summary: Playwright Coverage records which JavaScript and CSS parts a page uses. It works only with Chromium-based browsers.
Coverage.explanation: Coverage records which parts of JavaScript and CSS a page uses. Start the needed coverage type before navigation or other actions, then stop it to receive reports with used ranges and related script or stylesheet data.

parameters.name: options.resetOnNavigation
parameters.description: Whether to reset coverage on every navigation. Defaults to true.

parameters.name: options.reportAnonymousScripts
parameters.description: Whether anonymous scripts generated by the page should be reported. Defaults to false.

parameters.name: options.resetOnNavigation
parameters.description: Whether to reset coverage on every navigation. Defaults to true.

Coverage.returns: startCSSCoverage and startJSCoverage return Promise<void>. stopCSSCoverage returns Promise<Array<Object>> containing stylesheet URL, optional text, and used ranges. stopJSCoverage returns Promise<Array<Object>> containing script URL, script ID, optional source, and function coverage.

example.title: Collect JavaScript coverage
example.explanation: This starts JavaScript coverage, loads a page, collects the reports, and closes the browser.

useCases.title: JavaScript coverage
useCases.scenario: Measure JavaScript used during page load to create a coverage report.

useCases.title: CSS coverage
useCases.scenario: Find which stylesheet ranges were used by a page.

useCases.title: Usage analysis
useCases.scenario: Inspect script and stylesheet usage during automated browser flows.

interview.question: Which browsers support Playwright Coverage?
interview.answer: Coverage APIs collect usage data for JavaScript and CSS on a page. They are supported only by Chromium-based browsers.
interview.followUp: What should you do when a test must collect coverage in Firefox? Use another coverage approach, because Playwright's Coverage APIs do not support Firefox.

interview.question: How do you collect JavaScript coverage?
interview.answer: Call startJSCoverage before the page activity you want to measure. Call stopJSCoverage afterward; it returns reports for scripts, including their URLs, optional source, and function coverage ranges.
interview.followUp: How are anonymous scripts handled? They are excluded by default, but reportAnonymousScripts can include them with an empty URL.

interview.question: What does CSS coverage contain?
interview.answer: stopCSSCoverage returns reports for stylesheets. Each report can include a URL, stylesheet text, and sorted, non-overlapping ranges that were used.
interview.followUp: What CSS content is missing? Dynamically added style tags without sourceURLs are not included.

keyPoints: Coverage measures used parts of page JavaScript and CSS.
Both coverage start methods reset data on each navigation by default.
JavaScript coverage can optionally report scripts created without a URL.
stopJSCoverage returns one report for each measured script.
stopCSSCoverage returns reports for measured stylesheets.
CSS usage ranges are ordered and do not overlap.
gotchas: Coverage does not work in Firefox or WebKit.
Scripts made with eval or new Function are omitted unless anonymous-script reporting is enabled.
Injected style elements without a source URL are not included in CSS reports.
Disabling navigation resets may still fail to preserve coverage because of browser architecture limits.

defineConfig.summary: Playwright's `use` configuration sets browser and context options for tests. It supports navigation, authentication state, emulation, network behavior, recording, and other test settings.
defineConfig.explanation: The `use` object sets browser and context options for tests. You can configure it globally, override it for a project, or change it for a test file with `test.use()`. Common settings include navigation, authentication state, emulation, recording, and action timeouts.

parameters.name: baseURL
parameters.description: Base URL used for pages and relative navigation paths.

parameters.name: storageState
parameters.description: Saved browser storage state loaded into the context.

parameters.name: actionTimeout
parameters.description: Maximum time for each Playwright action, in milliseconds.

parameters.name: browserName
parameters.description: Browser engine used to run tests: chromium, firefox, or webkit.

parameters.name: trace
parameters.description: Trace recording mode.

example.title: Configure test use options
example.explanation: This sets a base URL for relative navigation and records a trace on the first retry.

useCases.title: Relative navigation
useCases.scenario: Use a local application URL without repeating the full address.

useCases.title: Authenticated tests
useCases.scenario: Start tests with saved cookies and authentication data.

useCases.title: Cross-browser and device testing
useCases.scenario: Run the same tests with different browsers, devices, or locales.

useCases.title: Test recording
useCases.scenario: Collect traces, screenshots, or videos for debugging failures.

interview.question: What is the purpose of the `use` section?
interview.answer: The `use` object contains options inherited by browser contexts created during a test. It can define values such as `baseURL`, `storageState`, viewport, locale, and trace behavior.
interview.followUp: How can one test use a different locale? Use `test.use({ locale: 'fr-FR' })` in the test file or describe block.

interview.question: How do `baseURL` and `storageState` help tests?
interview.answer: `baseURL` lets a test navigate with a path such as `page.goto('/settings')`. `storageState` loads saved browser state into the context, which is useful for authentication.
interview.followUp: What should be used for separate browser or environment configurations? Define projects with different `use` values.

interview.question: How do trace modes differ?
interview.answer: Trace modes control when traces are recorded and which traces are kept. For example, `on-first-retry` records only the first retry, while `retain-on-failure` records every run but keeps traces only for failed runs.
interview.followUp: What happens with `on-all-retries`? It records every retry and keeps those retry traces.

keyPoints: `baseURL` supplies the starting URL for pages and allows relative paths in navigation calls.
`storageState` loads saved cookies and related browser state into the test context.
Set `locale` to test behavior for a particular user language and regional format.
`permissions` grants selected browser permissions to every page in the context.
The `screenshot` option controls whether Playwright captures screenshots, including only after failures.
Projects group tests that share configuration, such as browser, device, timeout, or retry settings.
gotchas: Runner settings such as retries, workers, timeout, and reporter belong at the top level, not inside `use`.
Options passed directly when creating a context override the inherited options from `use`.
Screenshots, videos, and traces are disabled unless their options are enabled.

devices.summary: Playwright can emulate devices and browser conditions for tests. It supports device profiles, viewport, locale, time zone, permissions, geolocation, color scheme, user agent, offline mode, and JavaScript settings.
devices.explanation: Playwright applies emulation settings when it creates a browser context. You can use a built-in device profile or set individual options such as viewport, locale, time zone, permissions, geolocation, color scheme, user agent, offline mode, and JavaScript support. Settings can apply to all tests, a group, one test, or a manually created context.

parameters.description: Named settings from Playwright's device registry, such as a mobile or desktop profile.

parameters.name: viewport
parameters.description: Browser viewport width and height.

parameters.name: locale
parameters.description: Browser locale.

parameters.name: timezoneId
parameters.description: Browser time zone identifier.

parameters.name: javaScriptEnabled
parameters.description: Whether JavaScript runs in the browser context.

useCases.title: Regional behavior

useCases.title: No-JavaScript behavior
useCases.scenario: Test fallback pages when scripts are unavailable.

useCases.title: Environment-dependent features
useCases.scenario: Check browser features that depend on location, permissions, or display preferences.

interview.question: How do you emulate a mobile device?
interview.answer: Use a device entry from Playwright's device registry and pass its settings when creating a context. With the test runner, spread the device settings into a project's use configuration; with the library, pass them to newContext.
interview.followUp: How would you avoid a platform-specific user agent? Unset the userAgent after applying the device settings.

interview.question: How do you control the viewport?
interview.answer: Set viewport to a width and height in test configuration or when creating a context. For one page, page.setViewportSize can resize the viewport during the test.
interview.followUp: How can you simulate a high-DPI display? Set deviceScaleFactor together with the viewport when creating the context.

interview.question: Which browser settings can Playwright emulate?
interview.answer: Set locale and timezoneId in the test configuration or in browserContext options. These settings affect the browser, but not the test runner's own time zone.
interview.followUp: How can you test a page without client-side scripts? Set javaScriptEnabled to false for the test or context.

keyPoints: A device profile can set the user agent, screen size, viewport, and touch behavior together.
Use the device registry to select named desktop, tablet, or mobile profiles.
A test can replace the viewport from a selected device.
The isMobile setting controls meta viewport handling and touch events.
Set locale and timezoneId to test browser behavior for another region.
Set javaScriptEnabled to false to test pages with JavaScript turned off.
gotchas: Built-in device profiles include a platform-specific user agent. Remove or unset the user agent when the test should use the host platform's user agent.
Browser locale and time zone settings do not change the test runner's time zone.

Dialog.summary: A Dialog represents a browser alert, confirmation, prompt, or beforeunload dialog. Handle it from the page's dialog event, then accept or dismiss it.
Dialog.explanation: A Dialog represents a browser dialog opened by a page. Handle it through the page's dialog event, then accept or dismiss it. You can inspect its type, message, default prompt value, and source page.
Dialog.syntax:
dialog.accept(prompt_text=None)
dialog.dismiss()
dialog.default_value
dialog.message
dialog.page
dialog.type

parameters.name: prompt_text
parameters.description: Text to enter in a prompt. It has no effect for other dialog types.

Dialog.returns: accept() and dismiss() return None. The properties default_value, message, and type return str; page returns NoneType | Page.

example.title: Dismiss a browser dialog
example.code:
import asyncio
from playwright.async_api import async_playwright

async def main():
    async with async_playwright() as p:
        browser = await p.chromium.launch()
        page = await browser.new_page()

        async def handle_dialog(dialog):
            print(dialog.type, dialog.message)
            await dialog.dismiss()

        page.on("dialog", handle_dialog)
        await page.evaluate("alert('Hello')")
        await browser.close()

asyncio.run(main())
example.explanation: This listens for a dialog, prints its type and message, then closes it.

useCases.title: Read and close a dialog
useCases.scenario: Test an alert or confirmation

useCases.title: Enter prompt text
useCases.scenario: Submit form-like browser prompts

useCases.title: Inspect dialog details
useCases.scenario: Debug unexpected browser dialogs

interview.question: How do you handle a browser dialog?
interview.answer: A Dialog is delivered through the page's dialog event. The handler must call accept or dismiss; otherwise the page can remain blocked.
interview.followUp: What happens if no listener is registered? Playwright dismisses the dialog automatically.

interview.question: How do you inspect a dialog?
interview.answer: Use the dialog's type property to identify alert, beforeunload, confirm, or prompt. Use message to read the displayed text.
interview.followUp: How can you process a prompt? Pass the text to accept(prompt_text).

interview.question: How do accept and dismiss differ?
interview.answer: Call accept with optional prompt text to approve the dialog, or call dismiss to close it. The prompt text has no effect for non-prompt dialogs.
interview.followUp: What value can you read before accepting a prompt? Use default_value to get its default prompt value.

keyPoints: Register a handler on the page's dialog event to receive Dialog objects.
accept() approves the dialog and can optionally enter text in a prompt.
The optional prompt_text argument only matters when the dialog is a prompt.
default_value gives a prompt's initial value and an empty string for other dialog types.
message contains the text shown to the user.
type identifies whether the dialog is an alert, beforeunload, confirm, or prompt.
page identifies the source page when Playwright has that page available.
gotchas: After adding a dialog listener, always accept or dismiss the dialog. Otherwise the page can wait forever, and actions such as clicks may not finish.
Without a dialog listener, Playwright dismisses dialogs automatically.

Download.summary: A Download object represents a file download started by a page. Capture the download event, then save or inspect the file with its methods.
Download.explanation: A Download represents a file transfer started by a page. Wait for the download event, then use its methods to save, inspect, cancel, or delete the file. The browser context removes its downloaded files when it closes.

parameters.name: path
parameters.description: Destination path where the download is copied.

Download.returns: A Download object is produced by the download event. Individual methods return the values documented for each operation.

example.title: Save a downloaded file
example.explanation: Wait for the download event before starting the action, then save the completed download with its suggested name.

useCases.title: Save test downloads
useCases.scenario: A test clicks a link that starts a file transfer and needs to store the result at a known location.

useCases.title: Check download results
useCases.scenario: A test needs to verify that a download succeeded or inspect its suggested name.

useCases.title: Cancel or delete downloads
useCases.scenario: A test must stop a large or unwanted transfer and remove its temporary file.

interview.question: How do you reliably capture a download?
interview.answer: Start waiting for the download before clicking the control that triggers it. Then await the event result and call saveAs() to copy the file to a chosen location.
interview.followUp: Why must waiting begin first? The click can emit the download event immediately, so setting up the wait afterward can miss it.

interview.question: What does saveAs() do?
interview.answer: saveAs() copies the download to a user-selected path and can be called while the transfer is still running. It waits for the transfer when needed.
interview.followUp: How can you choose a useful name? Use suggestedFilename(), which is commonly derived from the response header or the download attribute.

interview.question: How can download completion or failure be checked?
interview.answer: failure() waits for the transfer if needed and returns an error string, or null when there is no error. cancel() requests cancellation and does not fail if the transfer already ended or was canceled.
interview.followUp: What result indicates a successful cancellation? failure() resolves to the string canceled.

keyPoints: A page emits a download event when a download starts.
Files owned by the browser context are removed when that context closes.
suggestedFilename() gives the browser-computed name to use when saving.
delete() removes the downloaded file and waits for an unfinished transfer.
createReadStream() provides a stream only for a successful download.
page() identifies the page that started the download.
gotchas: The file path is not ready when the download starts. Wait for completion before using path().
Do not use path() when the browser is connected remotely; save the file to a chosen path instead.
path() returns a temporary file whose name is not the suggested download name.

ElementHandle.summary: ElementHandle represents one DOM element in a page. Playwright discourages it for most tests; use Locator objects and web-first assertions instead.
ElementHandle.explanation: An ElementHandle refers to one specific DOM element. It can become stale when a framework replaces that element, while a Locator stores how to find the element again. ElementHandle supports actions, DOM evaluation, frame access, bounds, and state waits, but the documentation discourages it for most tests.

parameters.name: state
parameters.description: Element state: visible, hidden, stable, enabled, disabled, or editable.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Optional AbortSignal and timeout settings for waiting.

ElementHandle.returns: ElementHandle methods return values that depend on the method. For example, boundingBox returns an object or null, contentFrame and ownerFrame return a Frame or null, and waitForElementState returns void.

example.title: Prefer a Locator
example.code:
const button = page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Save' });
await button.click();
example.explanation: Use a Locator for normal actions. It finds the current element each time the action runs.

useCases.title: Read an element's bounds
useCases.scenario: You need the position and size of a DOM element for mouse input.

useCases.title: Get an iframe's content frame
useCases.scenario: You need to access the frame inside an iframe element.

useCases.title: Pass a DOM handle to evaluation
useCases.scenario: You must inspect or act on a specific DOM node through page evaluation.

interview.question: How does ElementHandle differ from Locator?
interview.answer: An ElementHandle points to one particular DOM element. A Locator stores the method used to find an element and resolves it when an action runs. Therefore, a Locator is usually safer when the page can re-render.
interview.followUp: Why can a handle become stale after a React update? The update can replace the DOM node, but the handle still refers to the old node.

interview.question: What happens during ElementHandle.click()?
interview.answer: click waits for actionability, scrolls the element into view when needed, clicks it, and waits for started navigation unless configured otherwise. It can fail if the element detaches or the timeout expires.
interview.followUp: How can you check readiness without clicking? Use the action's trial option to run actionability checks while skipping the action.

interview.question: Which states can waitForElementState use?
interview.answer: waitForElementState waits for visible, hidden, stable, enabled, disabled, or editable. It returns when the state is met and throws if the timeout expires.
interview.followUp: Which state allows detachment without an error? hidden, because it also accepts an element that is no longer attached.

keyPoints: An ElementHandle represents a DOM element inside the page.
In JavaScript, page.$() can create an ElementHandle from a selector.
Navigation of the handle's original frame disposes the handle automatically.
boundingBox returns position and size, or null when the element is not visible.
contentFrame returns the Frame for an iframe handle, and null for other elements.
The stable state waits for visibility and for the element to stop moving.
gotchas: Prefer Locator objects and web-first assertions for new tests.
The selector evaluation methods can be flaky because they do not wait for actionability.
Most element-state waits fail if the element detaches; the hidden state is the exception.

expect.summary: Playwright's expect function checks values and web conditions. Web assertions retry until they pass or the assertion timeout is reached; the default timeout is 5 seconds.
expect.explanation: Playwright's expect function checks values and web elements. Locator assertions are asynchronous and retry until they pass or their timeout ends. Generic value assertions check once, unless you use expect.poll or expect.toPass for retry behavior.

parameters.name: value
parameters.description: The value or web object to check, such as a locator, page, response, or ordinary value.

parameters.name: matcher arguments
parameters.description: The expected condition selected by the matcher, such as text, visibility, equality, or a count.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Optional assertion settings, including timeout for supported assertions.

expect.returns: An assertion object used to select and run a matcher; the selected asynchronous web assertion returns a promise that must be awaited.

example.title: Retry an assertion
example.explanation: This test keeps checking the status element until its text is Submitted or the assertion timeout is reached.

useCases.title: Verify web elements
useCases.scenario: Check that a page has reached an expected state after navigation or an action.

useCases.title: Test synchronous values
useCases.scenario: Check ordinary JavaScript values such as numbers, strings, arrays, or objects.

useCases.title: Poll changing conditions
useCases.scenario: Wait for an API or other changing condition without writing a manual loop.

useCases.title: Use soft checks
useCases.scenario: Run several checks while collecting failures instead of stopping at the first one.

interview.question: What is the difference between generic and web-specific assertions?
interview.answer: Use expect(value) for a value check and choose a matcher such as toEqual or toBeTruthy. Use a locator assertion such as await expect(locator).toBeVisible() for a web element.
interview.followUp: How would you retry a custom condition? Use expect.poll for a function that returns a value, or expect.toPass for a block of code.

interview.question: How do Playwright locator assertions handle asynchronous pages?
interview.answer: A locator assertion re-fetches the element and checks it repeatedly until the condition passes or the assertion timeout is reached. The default assertion timeout is 5 seconds.
interview.followUp: How can the timeout be changed? Set it for one assertion or configure the expect timeout in the test configuration.

interview.question: What are soft assertions?
interview.answer: A soft assertion records a failure and lets the test continue. With the Playwright test runner, test.info().errors can be checked to stop later work after soft failures.
interview.followUp: Can soft assertions be used with polling? Yes, expect.soft.poll can make a polling assertion soft.

keyPoints: Call expect with a value, locator, page, or response, then select a matcher.
Web assertions retry checks against the current element instead of checking only one fetched element.
An assertion normally stops retrying after 5 seconds unless you configure another timeout.
Use expect.poll when a function must be called repeatedly until its returned value matches.
Use expect.toPass when the retry operation contains several steps or assertions.
Pass a message with expect to add useful context to test reports for both passing and failing assertions.
gotchas: Await auto-retrying assertions. Without await, the test can finish before the check completes.
Non-retrying assertions can be flaky when a page updates asynchronously.
Soft assertions let the test continue, but the test is still marked as failed.
Use Playwright's own expect because the separate expect library is not fully integrated with the Playwright test runner.

expect.configure.summary: `expect.configure` creates an expect function with reusable defaults, such as an assertion timeout or soft assertions. Use the returned function for later assertions.
expect.configure.explanation: `expect.configure` returns a separate expect function with the defaults you choose. Use that function for later assertions. The documented options include an assertion timeout and soft assertions. You can also configure polling behavior by chaining `poll` on the configured function.
expect.configure.syntax: const configuredExpect = expect.configure({ timeout?: number, soft?: boolean });

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: An options object used to set defaults such as `timeout` and `soft`.

expect.configure.returns: A new pre-configured expect function with the selected defaults.

example.title: Configure an assertion timeout
example.explanation: This creates an expect function with a 10-second assertion timeout and uses it for one locator assertion.

useCases.title: Use a longer timeout
useCases.scenario: Some UI actions need more time than the normal assertion timeout.

useCases.title: Create soft assertions
useCases.scenario: A test should collect assertion failures and continue running.

useCases.title: Reuse settings with polling
useCases.scenario: An asynchronous value must reach an expected state after repeated checks.

interview.question: What does `expect.configure` do?
interview.answer: `expect.configure` creates a separate, pre-configured expect function. For example, it can set a longer assertion timeout for operations that need more time.
interview.followUp: How would you make every assertion from that instance soft? Use `expect.configure({ soft: true })`, then call the returned function for assertions that should not stop the test immediately.

interview.question: How do you configure a custom assertion timeout?
interview.answer: Set the `timeout` option when creating the configured instance. The configured function then uses that timeout for its assertions.
interview.followUp: Can one test use different assertion timeouts? Yes. Create multiple configured expect functions, each with its own timeout, and use the appropriate one for each assertion.

interview.question: How does configured expect relate to polling?
interview.answer: A configured expect function can be chained with `poll`. This lets an asynchronous function run repeatedly until its returned value satisfies a matcher or the polling timeout is reached.
interview.followUp: How can polling report a useful failure? Pass a custom `message` in the polling options; it is used for reporting.

keyPoints: The function returned by `expect.configure` has its own defaults. These defaults can include the assertion timeout and whether assertions are soft.
Pass a configuration object to set a 10-second timeout for a configured expect function.
Set `soft: true` when you want assertions from the configured instance to be soft.
A configured expect function can be used with polling, including soft polling when needed.
gotchas: Retrying assertions need `await`; otherwise the test may continue before the assertion finishes.
For polling, a timeout of `0` disables the polling timeout.

expect.extend.summary: `expect.extend` adds custom assertions to Playwright. A matcher returns whether it passed and provides a failure message.
expect.extend.explanation: `expect.extend` adds a custom matcher to Playwright's `expect` object. The matcher checks a value, returns whether it passed, and supplies a failure message. It can use existing matchers and receive assertion options such as a timeout.
expect.extend.syntax: expect.extend({ matcherName(received, expected, options) { return { pass, message }; } })

parameters.name: matchers
parameters.description: An object whose properties are custom matcher functions.

expect.extend.returns: An extended `expect` object with the supplied custom matchers.

example.title: Retry an assertion
example.explanation: This test waits for the element with the test id `status` to contain the expected text.

useCases.title: Create domain matchers
useCases.scenario: Application-specific checks

useCases.title: Reuse custom assertions across tests
useCases.scenario: Shared test utilities

useCases.title: Combine existing matchers with custom checks
useCases.scenario: Wrapper assertions

interview.question: How do you create a custom Playwright matcher?
interview.answer: Use `expect.extend({ matcherName() { ... } })` to add a matcher. The matcher returns an object with `message` and `pass`, and can include values such as `name`, `expected`, and `actual`.
interview.followUp: How should a matcher support `not`?

interview.question: How can a custom matcher reuse Playwright assertions?
interview.answer: A custom matcher can call an existing matcher, such as `toHaveAttribute`, and catch its failure. It can then build a message with the received and expected values.
interview.followUp: Why reuse an existing matcher instead of duplicating its check?

interview.question: When do Playwright assertions retry?
interview.answer: Web-specific async assertions retry until they pass or the assertion timeout is reached. The default assertion timeout is 5 seconds, and it can be changed in the configuration or for one assertion.
interview.followUp: How is assertion timeout different from test timeout?

keyPoints: Playwright assertions use the `expect` function.
Call `expect.extend` with an object containing custom matcher functions.
After extension, the new matcher can be called through the exported `expect` object.
Return `pass` to report the result of the custom check.
Return a `message` callback to describe a failed assertion.
Custom matchers let a project add domain-specific assertions to Playwright.
gotchas: A custom matcher must return a `pass` value that shows whether the check succeeded.
`expect.toPass` has different default timeout behavior and does not use the configured expect timeout automatically.

expect.poll.summary: `expect.poll` repeatedly calls a function and checks its returned value with a matcher. It stops when the check passes or the polling timeout is reached.
expect.poll.explanation: `expect.poll` turns a synchronous expectation into a retrying asynchronous check. It repeatedly calls the supplied function, applies the chosen matcher to its return value, and stops when the matcher passes or the configured timeout is reached.

parameters.name: callback
parameters.description: Asynchronous function whose returned value is checked by the matcher.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Optional settings such as message, timeout, and intervals.

expect.poll.returns: An asynchronous expectation that can be followed by a matcher, such as `toBe(200)`.

example.title: Poll an API until it succeeds
example.explanation: The function is called again until it returns 200 or the polling timeout ends.

useCases.title: Wait for an API status
useCases.scenario: An API may return a temporary failure before it becomes ready.

useCases.title: Wait for an asynchronous value
useCases.scenario: A backend operation updates a value after an unknown delay.

useCases.title: Use soft polling
useCases.scenario: A check should report failure but allow later test steps to run.

interview.question: What does `expect.poll` do?
interview.answer: `expect.poll` repeatedly runs an asynchronous function and applies a normal matcher to its returned value. It succeeds when the matcher passes or fails when the polling timeout expires.
interview.followUp: How can polling use a different schedule? Pass an `intervals` array in the options, such as `[1000, 2000, 10000]`.

interview.question: Which options control polling?
interview.answer: The options can include `message`, `timeout`, and `intervals`. The message customizes test reporting, timeout controls how long polling continues, and intervals controls the waits between probes.
interview.followUp: What happens if intervals are omitted? Playwright uses its default polling intervals.

interview.question: Can `expect.poll` make a soft assertion?
interview.answer: Polling can be soft by using `expect.soft.poll`, or by creating an instance with `expect.configure({ soft: true })` and calling its `poll` method. A soft failure lets the test continue.
interview.followUp: When should polling be preferred over a fixed sleep? Use it when the result becomes ready at an unknown time, because it checks the condition repeatedly until success or timeout.

keyPoints: Use `expect.poll` when a value comes from an operation that may become correct later.
Set `timeout` to limit polling duration. The default is 5 seconds, and `0` disables the timeout.
Use `intervals` to control how long Playwright waits between callback calls.
Add `message` when the failure report should explain the purpose of the poll.
Use `expect.soft.poll` when a failed poll should not stop the rest of the test.
gotchas: The callback must return the value that the matcher should check. It is not enough to perform an assertion inside the callback.
The polling timeout is separate from the default assertion timeout and can be set in the options.

expect.soft.summary: Playwright's `expect` function checks values and web page state. Web assertions retry until they pass or the five-second default timeout is reached.
expect.soft.explanation: `expect.soft` creates an assertion that can fail without stopping the test. The failure still marks the test as failed, so later checks can run. You can inspect `test.info().errors` to decide whether to stop. A custom message can add context to reports.

parameters.name: value
parameters.description: Value, locator, page, or other object being checked.

parameters.name: message
parameters.description: Optional message shown in test reports.

parameters.name: expected
parameters.description: Matcher-specific expected value or condition.

expect.soft.returns: An assertion object that provides generic and web-specific matchers.

example.title: Retry an element assertion
example.explanation: This assertion keeps checking the matching element until its text is correct or the assertion timeout is reached.

useCases.title: Verify changing UI state
useCases.scenario: Check that a page element eventually displays the expected text.

useCases.title: Collect multiple failures
useCases.scenario: Run several checks while collecting all failures before ending the test.

useCases.title: Improve test failure messages
useCases.scenario: Add useful context to assertion output in reports.

interview.question: What does a soft assertion do?
interview.answer: `expect.soft` records an assertion failure and lets the test continue. The test is still marked as failed.
interview.followUp: How can you stop after soft failures? Check `test.info().errors`, then assert that its length is zero.

interview.question: How do Playwright web assertions handle changing page state?
interview.answer: Web assertions retry the locator check until it passes or the assertion timeout is reached. Playwright fetches the element again during this process.
interview.followUp: What is the default timeout? It is five seconds, and it can be changed globally or for an assertion.

interview.question: How can an assertion provide clearer failure information?
interview.answer: Pass a second argument to `expect` as a message. Reporters show that message for both passing and failing assertions.
interview.followUp: Can soft assertions have messages? Yes. Pass the message to `expect.soft` in the same way.

keyPoints: Use `expect` to express test conditions.
Generic matchers can check ordinary values, such as truthiness or equality.
Web matchers retry by locating the element again until the condition passes or times out.
Add a message as the second `expect` argument to give the assertion more context.
Use `test.info().errors` to inspect recorded soft assertion failures.
gotchas: Soft assertions continue the test, but the test still fails.
Soft assertions are available only with the Playwright test runner.
Assertions use a five-second timeout by default unless configured otherwise.

expect.toPass.summary: expect.toPass retries an asynchronous code block until its assertions pass. Configure the retry timeout and probe intervals when needed.
expect.toPass.explanation: expect.toPass retries a block of code until it completes without a failed assertion. You can set the total timeout and the delays between attempts. Its default timeout is 0, so set one when the block must be retried for a limited period.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Options object. It can contain timeout and intervals.

parameters.name: options.timeout
parameters.description: Maximum time for toPass, in milliseconds.

parameters.name: options.intervals
parameters.description: Probe delays between attempts, in milliseconds.

expect.toPass.returns: A Playwright expectation that retries the supplied asynchronous function until it passes or the timeout is reached.

example.title: Retry a code block
example.explanation: This retries the request and status check until it passes or the timeout ends.

useCases.title: Retry an API check
useCases.scenario: A request may return a temporary failure before becoming successful.

useCases.title: Retry a multi-step condition
useCases.scenario: Several operations must succeed as one condition.

useCases.title: Retry a custom check
useCases.scenario: A custom asynchronous check does not map to one locator matcher.

interview.question: What does expect.toPass do?
interview.answer: expect.toPass runs a function repeatedly until its assertions pass or its configured timeout is reached. It is useful when the operation includes several steps or a custom condition.
interview.followUp: How do you control retry timing? Pass intervals and timeout in the toPass options.

interview.question: How can retry timing be configured?
interview.answer: Use intervals to define the wait time before later attempts and timeout to limit the complete retry period. For example, intervals can be [1000, 2000].
interview.followUp: What happens if timeout is omitted? The documented default is 0, so the block is not given a normal retry period.

interview.question: When should toPass be used instead of a normal assertion?
interview.answer: Use a regular web assertion when a locator condition is enough. Use toPass when a complete function, such as a request followed by a status assertion, must be retried together.
interview.followUp: Can expect.poll be used instead? Yes. It retries a callback that returns a value, while toPass retries the whole code block.

keyPoints: Use toPass to retry a complete block rather than only one assertion.
The options let you control the overall timeout and the delays between probes.
If you do not provide intervals, Playwright uses increasing default probe delays.
gotchas: Do not assume the normal assertion timeout applies. Configure toPass with its own timeout.

FileChooser.summary: FileChooser lets you control a file input after a page action opens its file picker. Wait for the chooser during that action, then use set_files to upload or clear files.
FileChooser.explanation: A FileChooser represents the file input opened by a page action. Wait for it while performing the action that opens the chooser, then use set_files to provide a path or file data. The chooser also exposes the related input element, page, and whether multiple files are allowed.

parameters.name: files
parameters.type: str | pathlib.Path | list[str | pathlib.Path] | dict | list[dict]
parameters.description: A path, list of paths, or file data. File data can include name, mimeType, and buffer.

parameters.name: timeout
parameters.description: Maximum wait time in milliseconds. Defaults to 30000; use 0 to disable it.

parameters.name: no_wait_after
parameters.description: Deprecated. It has no effect.

FileChooser.returns: set_files returns None. element returns an ElementHandle. is_multiple returns bool. page returns Page.

example.title: Upload a file
example.code:
from playwright.sync_api import Page

def upload(page: Page) -> None:
    with page.expect_file_chooser() as chooser_info:
        page.get_by_text("Upload file").click()
    chooser = chooser_info.value
    chooser.set_files("myfile.pdf")
example.explanation: Wait for the chooser while triggering the upload control, then assign a local file to it.

useCases.title: Upload a local file
useCases.scenario: A page has a custom upload button that opens a native file picker.

useCases.title: Replace selected files
useCases.scenario: A test must replace files already selected in an input.

useCases.title: Clear file selection
useCases.scenario: A test must remove every selected file.

interview.question: How do you upload a file with FileChooser?
interview.answer: Use page.expect_file_chooser() around the action that opens the file picker. Read its value and call set_files with a path or file payload.
interview.followUp: How can you check whether several files are supported? Call is_multiple() on the chooser before assigning files.

interview.question: What can set_files accept?
interview.answer: set_files accepts a string or pathlib.Path, a list of paths, or file data containing a name, MIME type, and bytes. Relative paths are resolved from the current working directory.
interview.followUp: How do you clear the input? Pass an empty list to set_files.

interview.question: What timeout behavior does set_files have?
interview.answer: The operation waits up to 30,000 milliseconds by default. You can pass timeout=0 to disable that limit or change the default through the page or browser context.
interview.followUp: How can an operation be cancelled in the JavaScript API? Pass an AbortSignal; aborting it makes the operation fail, while the default timeout still applies.

keyPoints: A FileChooser is created when the page opens a file chooser event.
set_files assigns files to the input linked to the chooser.
element gives access to the associated input element.
is_multiple tells you whether the input accepts more than one file.
page returns the Page that produced the chooser.
gotchas: Relative file paths use the process's current working directory.
Pass an empty list to remove all selected files.
The no_wait_after option is deprecated and does nothing.

firefox.summary: Playwright installs matching Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit binaries and can run tests in several browser projects. Configure desktop, mobile, or branded-browser projects, then run all projects or select one.
firefox.explanation: Playwright Test runs end-to-end tests in supported browser engines. It can install the browser binaries that match the Playwright version, then run projects for desktop browsers, mobile device emulation, or branded browsers such as Chrome and Edge.
firefox.syntax:
npx playwright install [browser]
npx playwright test [--project=<project>]

parameters.description: Optional browser name for installation, such as `webkit` or `chromium`.

parameters.name: --project
parameters.description: Optional Playwright project name used to select one configured project.

parameters.name: install options
parameters.description: Optional browser or dependency installation flags, including `--with-deps`.

firefox.returns: The commands install, run, list, or remove Playwright browser binaries; test runs produce test results.

useCases.scenario: Use Chrome or Edge channels when testing a branded browser is required.

interview.question: Which browser engines and browser types does Playwright support?
interview.answer: Playwright supports Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit. It can also use branded Chrome and Edge channels, plus mobile device emulation.
interview.followUp: Which browsers are best for Safari-like testing? Use WebKit, preferably on macOS when platform-specific behavior such as video playback matters.

interview.question: How do you install Playwright browsers?
interview.answer: Run `npx playwright install` to install the default browser binaries. Pass a browser name, such as `webkit`, to install only that browser.
interview.followUp: How can dependencies be installed too? Use `npx playwright install --with-deps`, or run `npx playwright install-deps` separately.

interview.question: How do you run tests across several browsers?
interview.answer: Define separate projects in the Playwright configuration. Each project can select a browser, device profile, or branded browser channel, and Playwright runs all projects by default.
interview.followUp: How can one project be selected? Pass its name with `npx playwright test --project=firefox`.

keyPoints: Playwright tests Chromium, Firefox, WebKit, Google Chrome, and Microsoft Edge.
All configured projects run when you use `npx playwright test` without a project filter.
Run one configured project with `npx playwright test --project=firefox`.
Browser binaries are stored in an operating-system-specific cache unless you configure another location.
Use `npx playwright install --list` to see browsers installed by Playwright installations on the machine.
Use `npx playwright uninstall --all` to remove browsers belonging to all Playwright installations.
gotchas: Updating Playwright can require another browser installation because each Playwright version needs matching browser binaries.
Use Playwright's Firefox build instead of the branded Firefox application.
Use WebKit for Safari-like testing; Playwright cannot use the branded Safari application.
Browser features can differ by operating system, including media codec support.

Frame.summary: Playwright pages have a main frame and may contain iframe elements with additional frames. Use frameLocator to work inside an iframe, or page.frame to get a Frame by name or URL.
Frame.explanation: A page has a main frame and can also contain frames created by iframe elements. Use frameLocator to locate elements inside a frame, or use page.frame to get a Frame object by name or URL and then interact with it.

parameters.name: nameOrUrl
parameters.description: A frame name or an object with a URL pattern used to find the frame.

Frame.returns: A Frame object when using page.frame; a FrameLocator when using page.frameLocator.

useCases.scenario: A test needs a frame identified by its name.
