interview.question: What is the difference between the main frame and an embedded frame?
interview.answer: A page always has a main frame, and it may have additional frames from iframe elements. Normal page actions use the main frame unless a frame is selected.
interview.followUp: How would you target an input inside an iframe? Use page.frameLocator with a selector for the iframe, then locate and act on the element inside it.

interview.question: How do you interact with an element inside an iframe?
interview.answer: Use frameLocator when you want to locate an element inside an iframe directly. For example, call page.frameLocator('.frame-class').getByLabel('User Name').fill('John').
interview.followUp: How can you select a frame by URL instead? Get a Frame with page.frame({ url: /.*domain.*/ }) and interact with it.

interview.question: How can you obtain a Frame object?
interview.answer: The page.frame API can find a Frame by its name. It can also find one by matching its URL, after which the Frame can be used for interactions.
interview.followUp: What if the frame must be found by another selector? Locate the frame element and use its content frame to obtain the Frame object.

keyPoints: A page can contain its main frame and additional Frame objects.
The main frame is the default target for page-level interactions.
Embedded frames are created with the HTML iframe element.
You can interact with elements that belong to an embedded frame.
Use frameLocator to start locating an element inside a selected frame.
page.frame can select a frame by its name.
gotchas: Page-level actions do not automatically target an embedded frame. Use a frame locator or a Frame object for elements inside an iframe.

FrameLocator.summary: FrameLocator represents a view into an iframe. Use it to locate and interact with elements inside the frame without manually handling a Frame object.
FrameLocator.explanation: FrameLocator lets you work inside an iframe without manually obtaining a Frame object. Create one from a page or locator, then use locator methods such as getByRole, getByText, or locator to find elements inside the frame.

parameters.name: selector
parameters.description: A selector used to resolve the iframe or nested iframe.

parameters.name: index
parameters.description: The index of a matching frame; zero selects the first frame. Use it on the iframe Locator before contentFrame().

FrameLocator.returns: FrameLocator methods that find elements inside the iframe return Locator. owner() returns a Locator for the iframe element. frameLocator() returns a nested FrameLocator.

example.title: Click a button inside an iframe
example.explanation: This locates the iframe, enters its document, finds the button by its accessible role and name, and clicks it.

useCases.title: Interact with iframe content
useCases.scenario: A page embeds a form or widget in an iframe.

useCases.title: Enter nested frames
useCases.scenario: An application contains nested iframes.

useCases.title: Use role, label, text, or test ID locators
useCases.scenario: Tests need stable, user-facing element queries inside a frame.

interview.question: What is a FrameLocator?
interview.answer: A FrameLocator represents a view into an iframe. It lets you locate and act on elements in that iframe, and it can be created with page.frameLocator(), locator.contentFrame(), or locator.frameLocator().
interview.followUp: How do you convert between the two locator types? Use locator.contentFrame() to create a FrameLocator, and frameLocator.owner() to get a Locator for the iframe element.

interview.question: What does strictness mean for FrameLocator?
interview.answer: Frame locators are strict. An operation throws when the iframe selector matches more than one element, so the iframe must be narrowed before entering it.
interview.followUp: What is the current recommended way to choose one of several matching frames? Use locator.first(), locator.last(), or locator.nth(index) before contentFrame().

interview.question: What does a selector-free frame locator do?
interview.answer: The selector-free page.frameLocator() or frame.frameLocator() starts searching in any frame in the subtree. The rest of the locator is then resolved inside one frame, and multiple matching frames cause an error.
interview.followUp: Can you use owner() on that selector-free locator? No. It does not identify one particular iframe, so owner(), first(), last(), and nth() are unsupported.

keyPoints: Create a FrameLocator from an iframe Locator with contentFrame(), or from a Page or Frame with frameLocator().
getByRole() finds elements by role and accessible name, which is useful for buttons, headings, checkboxes, and other controls.
getByText() can match a text substring, an exact string, or a regular expression.
getByTestId() uses data-testid by default. The test ID attribute can be changed with selectors.setTestIdAttribute().
locator() finds an element inside the frame and supports filtering with has, hasNot, hasText, and hasNotText.
owner() converts a FrameLocator back to a Locator for the iframe element itself.
gotchas: A frame locator operation fails when its selector matches more than one iframe. Narrow the iframe locator first, for example with locator.first().contentFrame().
The has and hasNot filters use locators relative to the current match. They cannot use elements outside that locator's frame.
A frame locator created without a selector can search any frame, but it cannot use owner, first, last, or nth.

Keyboard.summary: Playwright's Keyboard API controls a virtual keyboard. Use press() for keys and shortcuts, type() for text, and down()/up() to hold and release keys.
Keyboard.explanation: Keyboard sends virtual keyboard events to the page. Use press for one key or a shortcut, type for character-by-character input, and down/up when you need to hold a key. Use insertText when only an input event is needed.
Keyboard.syntax: page.keyboard.press(key, options); page.keyboard.type(text, options); page.keyboard.down(key); page.keyboard.up(key); page.keyboard.insertText(text);

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: Key name or one character to generate or press, such as ArrowLeft or a.

parameters.name: text
parameters.description: Text to type into the focused element.

parameters.name: options.delay
parameters.description: Milliseconds between keydown and keyup for press(). Defaults to 0.

parameters.name: options.delay
parameters.description: Milliseconds between characters for type(). Defaults to 0.

example.title: Press a shortcut and type text
example.explanation: This selects all text with the platform-aware shortcut, then types text with a delay between characters.

useCases.title: Keyboard shortcuts
useCases.scenario: Trigger a keyboard shortcut such as select all or a modified key.

useCases.title: Special-key interaction
useCases.scenario: Send arrow, function, editing, or other special keys.

useCases.title: Character-by-character input
useCases.scenario: Test a page that reacts to individual key events while text is entered.

useCases.title: Held modifiers
useCases.scenario: Hold a modifier while selecting or editing text.

interview.question: What does keyboard.press() do?
interview.answer: Keyboard.press() performs a keydown and keyup as one operation. It also accepts shortcuts such as Control+Shift+T and can wait between the two events with delay.
interview.followUp: How would you hold a modifier across several actions? Call keyboard.down('Shift'), perform the actions, then call keyboard.up('Shift').

interview.question: When should type() and press() be used?
interview.answer: keyboard.type() sends keydown, keypress/input, and keyup for each character. Use keyboard.press() for special keys such as Control or ArrowDown.
interview.followUp: How can you simulate slower typing? Pass a delay option, such as { delay: 100 }, to type().

interview.question: How does insertText() differ from type()?
interview.answer: keyboard.insertText() sends only an input event. It does not send keydown, keyup, or keypress, and modifier keys do not change its text.
interview.followUp: When is this useful? Use it when the page needs text insertion but should not receive normal keyboard events.

keyPoints: The Keyboard object controls a virtual keyboard for the page.
Use ControlOrMeta for a shortcut that follows the operating system.
Calling down() again for a held key produces a repeated keydown event.
A held modifier affects keys sent through down().
type() creates the normal event sequence for every character.
Non-US keyboard characters may not receive key events.
gotchas: Prefer locator.press() when the key action targets a specific element.
Prefer locator.fill() for ordinary text input.
Holding Shift does not change the case of text sent by type().
insertText() does not create the usual keyboard event sequence.

locator.summary: Playwright .NET locators find elements and support auto-waiting and retrying. Prefer role, label, text, placeholder, alt text, title, and test ID locators before CSS or XPath.
locator.explanation: A locator describes how to find an element when an action or assertion runs. Playwright checks the page again each time, so the locator can follow DOM changes. You can chain locators and filters to narrow the result before using actions such as ClickAsync or FillAsync.
locator.syntax: var locator = Page.GetByRole(AriaRole.Button, new() { Name = "Sign in" });

parameters.name: role
parameters.description: The accessible role and optional locator options, such as Name or NameRegex.

parameters.name: value
parameters.description: The text, label, placeholder, alternative text, title, or test ID used to find an element.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Options for actions such as timeout, force, position, modifiers, and button.

locator.returns: A Locator object. Locator actions such as ClickAsync and FillAsync return no value when successful; CountAsync returns the number of matching elements.

example.title: Click a button with a locator
example.code:
var signIn = Page.GetByRole(AriaRole.Button, new() { Name = "Sign in" });
await signIn.ClickAsync();
example.explanation: This creates a role-based locator and clicks the button with the accessible name "Sign in".

useCases.title: Find interactive controls
useCases.scenario: Click or check controls in a way that matches how users and assistive technology identify them.

useCases.title: Find form fields
useCases.scenario: Fill a form using its label or placeholder.

useCases.title: Filter matching elements
useCases.scenario: Select one item from a list of similar cards.

useCases.title: Use a test ID
useCases.scenario: Use a stable selector when user-facing text or roles are not suitable.

interview.question: What is a Playwright locator?
interview.answer: A locator is a reusable description of an element. Playwright resolves it when an action or assertion runs, which supports waiting and retrying.
interview.followUp: Why can a saved locator survive a DOM update? Playwright resolves it again for each action instead of keeping one old element handle.

interview.question: Which locator should you choose first?
interview.answer: Prefer user-facing locators. Use GetByRole with an accessible name for interactive controls, GetByLabel for labeled form controls, and GetByText for non-interactive content.
interview.followUp: When is a test ID useful? Use GetByTestId when a stable explicit contract is needed or role and text do not identify the element well.

interview.question: How do you narrow a locator to one matching item?
interview.answer: Use Filter with HasText, HasTextRegex, Has, or HasNot to narrow a broader locator. The inner locator is evaluated relative to each outer match.
interview.followUp: How would you target one product card? Filter list items by the product heading, then chain GetByRole for its Add to cart button.

keyPoints: Locators are the main way Playwright finds elements while waiting and retrying actions.
The code generator can create a starting locator that you can adjust.
Add an accessible name to a role locator when several elements share the same role.
GetByText supports partial text, exact text, and regular-expression matching.
Test IDs provide a stable selector when text or roles may change.
Page.Locator accepts CSS and XPath selectors, including selectors without an explicit prefix.
gotchas: AllAsync returns immediately. It can be unreliable when the matching list changes or is still loading.
Long CSS or XPath selectors can break after ordinary page structure changes.
A locator passed to Has or HasNot is searched inside each outer match, not from the document root.

Locator.summary: A Playwright locator describes how to find elements on a page. It resolves the current element when an action runs and supports chaining, filtering, waiting, and retries.
Locator.explanation: A locator describes how to find an element on the page. Playwright resolves it again when an action runs, so the locator can follow DOM changes. You can chain locator methods to narrow the search, and actions wait for the element to be ready unless checks are bypassed.

parameters.name: selector
parameters.description: A selector or locator strategy that identifies the target element.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Options that control the locator, such as role name, text matching, or filtering.

Locator.returns: A Locator object representing the matching element or elements.

example.title: Locate and click a button
example.code:
const button = page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Sign in' });
await button.click();
example.explanation: This creates a locator for the button named Sign in, then clicks it.

useCases.title: User-facing controls
useCases.scenario: Click or fill a control using its accessible role and name.

useCases.title: Form input
useCases.scenario: Find a field through its associated label.

useCases.title: Filtered lists
useCases.scenario: Select one item from a repeated list by filtering its content.

useCases.title: Test contracts
useCases.scenario: Use a stable explicit selector when role or text is not suitable.

interview.question: What is a locator?
interview.answer: A locator is a way to find elements at the time an operation runs. Playwright resolves it again for each action, which helps it work with changing DOM content.
interview.followUp: Why is this better than storing an element handle? A locator keeps the finding rule and retries the operation against the current page state.

interview.question: Which locator should you choose?
interview.answer: Use role locators for interactive elements and include the accessible name when possible. Use label locators for form controls, text locators for non-interactive content, and test IDs when an explicit test contract is needed.
interview.followUp: When would a test ID be better than a role locator? Use it when the test needs a stable explicit contract or the element cannot be identified well by role or text.

interview.question: How does Playwright make locator actions reliable?
interview.answer: Locator actions perform actionability checks, may scroll the element into view, and can wait for navigation started by the action. The force option bypasses actionability checks.
interview.followUp: What should you do for a dynamically loaded list? Wait for the full list to finish loading before calling AllAsync, because AllAsync does not wait for matches.

keyPoints: Locators provide Playwright's main waiting and retry behavior.
Playwright finds the current matching DOM element when each action uses the locator.
Prefer role locators because they match how users and assistive technology understand the page.
Use an associated label to find a form control when a label is available.
Text locators support substring matching, exact matching, and regular expressions.
Test IDs give a stable selector when the test intentionally uses an explicit testing contract.
gotchas: Do not use AllAsync when the matching list can change. Wait until a dynamic list is complete first.
Prefer user-facing locators over long CSS or XPath selectors because implementation changes can break them.
A locator used in Has or HasNot must be relative to the locator being filtered, not rooted at the document.

locator.all.summary: `locator.all()` returns an array of locators for the elements currently matched by a locator. It does not wait for elements to appear, so use it only after a dynamic list is stable.
locator.all.explanation: Call `locator.all()` to turn a locator for several elements into an array of locators. The method returns immediately with the elements currently present. It does not wait for more elements to appear, so wait for a dynamically loaded list to finish before calling it.

example.title: Click every list item
example.explanation: This gets the current matching list items and clicks each one.

useCases.title: Act on list items
useCases.scenario: A stable list is already rendered and each item needs a separate action.

useCases.title: Process a loaded list
useCases.scenario: A list finishes loading after an explicit wait, and the test needs individual locators.

useCases.title: Loop over matches
useCases.scenario: Each matched element needs its own locator for a loop.

interview.question: What does `locator.all()` return?
interview.answer: `locator.all()` returns a promise for an array of locators. Each returned locator points to one currently matching element.
interview.followUp: What should you do for a dynamically loaded list? Wait until the complete list has loaded, then call `all()`.

interview.question: Does `locator.all()` wait for elements?
interview.answer: It returns immediately with the elements that are present at that time. It does not wait for the locator to match elements.
interview.followUp: Why can this cause flaky tests? A later-rendered element may be missing from the returned array, or the list may change during the loop.

interview.question: When is `locator.all()` appropriate?
interview.answer: Use `locator.all()` when the list is stable, including after waiting for a list that loads dynamically. Then each returned locator can be used for actions such as `click()`.
interview.followUp: How can you avoid collecting elements at all? Use a locator action or assertion that supports Playwright's waiting behavior when that fits the test.

keyPoints: It converts a multi-element locator into an array of element-specific locators.
Each item in the returned array represents one matching element.
For a list that loads over time, wait for the full list before collecting its locators.
In TypeScript, await the method and loop over the returned locators.
gotchas: The method does not wait for matching elements. Calling it while a list is changing can produce flaky results.
Do not use it while the list changes. Wait until the list is stable first.

locator.boundingBox.summary: Returns the matching element's bounding rectangle, or null when the element is not visible. Coordinates are relative to the main frame viewport.
locator.boundingBox.explanation: `boundingBox()` returns the matching element's position and size in pixels. It returns `null` when the element is not visible. The coordinates use the main frame viewport, so scrolling can make the x or y value negative.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Options object. It can include an AbortSignal and a timeout in milliseconds.

parameters.name: signal
parameters.description: Cancels the operation when aborted. Added in v1.62.

parameters.name: timeout
parameters.description: Maximum wait time in milliseconds. The default is 0 for this method; use 0 to disable timeout behavior entirely.

locator.boundingBox.returns: Promise<null | Object>. The object contains x, y, width, and height, all in pixels.

example.title: Click the center of a visible button
example.explanation: Gets the button's rectangle and clicks its center when the button is visible.

useCases.title: Use coordinates for input
useCases.scenario: You need to perform a mouse action at a precise point inside an element.

useCases.title: Read layout bounds
useCases.scenario: You need to measure an element's position or size in the viewport.

useCases.title: Work with framed content
useCases.scenario: You need coordinates for an element inside a child frame.

interview.question: What does locator.boundingBox() return?
interview.answer: It returns the matching element's bounding box, including x and y coordinates plus width and height. It returns null when the element is not visible.
interview.followUp: What coordinate system does it use? It uses the main frame viewport, and scrolling can change or make coordinates negative.

interview.question: How should code handle the method's result?
interview.answer: The method returns a promise for either an object containing x, y, width, and height, or null. In TypeScript, handle the null case before using the object.
interview.followUp: How could you safely click the center? Check the result, then pass x + width / 2 and y + height / 2 to page.mouse.click().

interview.question: How are the returned coordinates measured?
interview.answer: The coordinates are relative to the main frame viewport. This is usually the same coordinate space as the browser window.
interview.followUp: What happens inside an iframe? The child-frame element's box is still reported relative to the main frame.

keyPoints: It finds the matching element and reports its rectangular bounds.
The x and y values use the main frame viewport as their origin.
After scrolling, an element can have a negative viewport coordinate.
The result includes the element width in pixels.
The result includes the element height in pixels.
For a static page, the coordinates can be used for mouse input.
gotchas: The result can be null, so check it before reading x, y, width, or height.
Scrolling changes the returned coordinates; they are viewport-relative rather than fixed page coordinates.
For elements inside child frames, the returned coordinates use the main frame viewport.

locator.click.summary: `locator.check()` checks a checkbox or radio input. It waits until the control is ready, performs the action, and confirms the control is checked.
locator.click.explanation: `locator.check()` waits for the target to be ready, scrolls it into view when needed, clicks it, and verifies that it became checked. It works only with checkbox or radio elements. Use `force=True` to skip actionability checks, or `trial=True` to check readiness without changing the element.
locator.click.syntax: locator.check(*, force=None, no_wait_after=None, position=None, scroll=None, timeout=None, trial=None)

parameters.name: force
parameters.description: Bypass actionability checks. Defaults to `False`.

parameters.name: no_wait_after
parameters.description: Deprecated. Has no effect.

parameters.name: position
parameters.description: Point relative to the element's top-left padding box.

parameters.name: scroll
parameters.description: Scroll behavior: `"auto"` or `"none"`. Defaults to `"auto"`.

parameters.name: timeout
parameters.description: Maximum time in milliseconds. The default is 30,000; `0` disables the timeout.

parameters.name: trial
parameters.description: Run readiness checks without performing the action. Defaults to `False`.

example.title: Check a checkbox
example.code:
from playwright.sync_api import expect

checkbox = page.get_by_role("checkbox", name="Accept terms")
checkbox.check()
expect(checkbox).to_be_checked()
example.explanation: This finds a checkbox, checks it, and verifies its state.

useCases.title: Accept a form option
useCases.scenario: A form has a required checkbox for terms or consent.

useCases.title: Select a radio choice
useCases.scenario: A test must select a radio input before submitting a form.

useCases.title: Check readiness with trial
useCases.scenario: A test needs to confirm that a control is ready without changing it.

interview.question: What does `locator.check()` do?
interview.answer: It checks that the target is a checkbox or radio input, waits for actionability, scrolls it into view, clicks it, and confirms that it is checked. If it is already checked, it returns without another click.
interview.followUp: What does `trial=True` do? It performs the readiness checks but skips the check action.

interview.question: How does the force option change check behavior?
interview.answer: `force=True` bypasses the normal actionability checks. The default is `False`, so Playwright normally waits for the element to be ready.
interview.followUp: Why avoid force by default? Normal checks help detect elements that are hidden, moving, covered, or disabled.

interview.question: How does timeout handling work?
interview.answer: The default timeout is 30,000 milliseconds in the Python API. Passing `timeout=0` disables the timeout, and the default can be changed with the browser context or page timeout settings.
interview.followUp: What should replace a fixed sleep? Use Playwright's actionability waiting or an auto-retrying assertion.

keyPoints: The method supports checkbox and radio inputs.
Playwright waits for the element to pass actionability checks unless you force the action.
The element is brought into view before the click.
Playwright verifies the final checked state.
`trial=True` tests readiness without changing the control.
gotchas: The locator must resolve to a checkbox or radio input. Otherwise, the call fails.
A checked element is not clicked again.
The action fails if the element is removed while Playwright is working.
The action can time out while waiting for readiness or completion.

locator.count.summary: `locator.count()` returns the number of elements matching a locator. Use `expect(locator).to_have_count()` for count assertions to reduce flakiness.
locator.count.explanation: `locator.count()` returns how many elements currently match a locator. It is useful for reading a count, but it can be unstable when the page changes. For count assertions, use the web-first `expect(locator).toHaveCount()` assertion instead.

example.title: Count matching elements
example.explanation: This test counts elements matched by a role-based locator.

useCases.title: Inspect a count
useCases.scenario: Read how many matching elements are currently on the page.

useCases.title: Branch on a count
useCases.scenario: Use the result to control test logic, such as checking whether a result list is empty.

useCases.title: Assert a count
useCases.scenario: Verify a count with automatic waiting.

interview.question: What does `locator.count()` return?
interview.answer: `locator.count()` returns a promise that resolves to the number of elements matching the locator. In Python, the equivalent is `await locator.count()` for async code or `locator.count()` for sync code.
interview.followUp: What should you use for a count assertion? Use `expect(locator).toHaveCount()` because it waits and reduces flakiness.

interview.question: What elements does the method count?
interview.answer: The method counts every element that matches the locator at the time it is evaluated. The locator can match zero, one, or many elements.
interview.followUp: How can you count only a subset? Create a narrower locator first, such as `page.get_by_role('listitem').filter(...)`, then call `count()`.

interview.question: How is the method used in Python?
interview.answer: In Python, call `await page.get_by_role('listitem').count()` in an async test. In synchronous Playwright code, call `page.get_by_role('listitem').count()` without `await`.
interview.followUp: Why might a direct count be unreliable? A changing page can produce a transient value, so a retrying assertion is safer.

keyPoints: The method returns the number of elements that match the locator.
Use this method when you need to read a count, not when you need to make a count assertion.
For assertions, prefer the retrying `toHaveCount()` assertion.
Python supports both sync and async forms of the method.
gotchas: For assertions, prefer `expect(locator).toHaveCount()` instead of reading the count and comparing it yourself.

locator.fill.summary: locator.fill() sets the value of an input, textarea, or contenteditable element. It is Playwright's usual method for entering form text and can also clear a field with an empty string.
locator.fill.explanation: Call fill on a locator to set the value of an input, textarea, or contenteditable element. Playwright waits for actionability, focuses the element, enters the value, and sends an input event. Passing an empty string clears the field.

parameters.name: value
parameters.description: The text to set in the input, textarea, or contenteditable element.

parameters.name: force
parameters.description: Bypass actionability checks. Defaults to false.

parameters.name: signal
parameters.description: Cancel the operation with an AbortSignal.

parameters.name: timeout
parameters.description: Maximum wait time in milliseconds. The Python page uses a timeout option; the default is 0.

locator.fill.returns: None (Python sync API); the method returns after the value is filled.

example.title: Fill a text field
example.code:
from playwright.sync_api import Page

def test_fill_name(page: Page):
    page.get_by_role("textbox").fill("Peter")
    assert page.get_by_role("textbox").input_value() == "Peter"
example.explanation: This fills a textbox and checks its value.

useCases.title: Fill text fields
useCases.scenario: Enter a name, email address, or other text in a form field.

useCases.title: Fill date and time fields
useCases.scenario: Set a date, time, or local date-time input using its accepted string format.

useCases.title: Clear a field
useCases.scenario: Remove an existing value before entering new form data.

interview.question: What does locator.fill() do?
interview.answer: locator.fill(value) sets the value of an input, textarea, or contenteditable element. It waits for actionability, focuses the element, fills it, and triggers an input event.
interview.followUp: How would you clear the field? Pass an empty string, such as locator.fill("").

interview.question: How should you locate a field before filling it?
interview.answer: Use get_by_label() or get_by_role() to find the field, then call fill() with the text or supported date and time value. For example, page.get_by_label("Birth date").fill("2020-02-02").
interview.followUp: What is another useful locator? get_by_placeholder() can find an input by its placeholder text.

interview.question: When should you use press_sequentially() instead of fill()?
interview.answer: fill() is the normal choice because it sets the value directly and triggers the input event. Use press_sequentially() only when the page has special keyboard handling that needs character-by-character events.
interview.followUp: How can you add a pause between characters? Pass a delay in milliseconds to press_sequentially().

keyPoints: Use fill() as the usual way to enter form values.
The method focuses the field and sends an input event after setting the value.
It supports input elements, textareas, and contenteditable elements.
Use an empty string to clear the current value.
Playwright performs actionability checks before filling.
The value argument is a string containing the new field value.
gotchas: The target must be an input, textarea, or contenteditable element. Otherwise, the call fails.
Use press_sequentially() when the page needs individual keyboard events instead of direct filling.

locator.filter.summary: locator.filter() narrows an existing Playwright locator by text or by matching or excluding descendants. You can chain filters to identify one element without relying on position.
locator.filter.explanation: Call filter() on an existing locator to keep only elements that match extra conditions. Text filters search inside the element and its descendants. The has and hasNot options use another locator relative to each outer match, so the inner locator must belong to the same frame and must not start outside the outer element.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Filter options, including has, hasNot, hasText, and hasNotText.

example.title: Filter a locator by text
example.explanation: This finds the list item containing “Product 2”, then clicks its button.

useCases.title: Find a matching card
useCases.scenario: A list has several similar cards, and each card contains a different product name.

useCases.title: Exclude unwanted rows
useCases.scenario: Rows may contain a status such as “Out of stock”.

useCases.title: Combine filters
useCases.scenario: Several conditions identify one row, such as a person name and a button.

interview.question: What does locator.filter() do?
interview.answer: filter() narrows an existing locator. It can match text with hasText or hasNotText, or descendants with has and hasNot.
interview.followUp: How does has resolve its inner locator? It starts from each outer match, and both locators must use the same frame.

interview.question: How does hasText match text?
interview.answer: A string hasText match is case-insensitive and searches for a substring anywhere inside the element, including descendants. A regular expression can also be used.
interview.followUp: How can you exclude matching text? Use hasNotText with a string or regular expression.

interview.question: What is a common mistake when using the has option?
interview.answer: The inner locator must be relative to the outer locator. It is queried from the outer match rather than from the document root.
interview.followUp: What restriction applies to frames? The outer and inner locators must belong to the same frame, and the inner locator cannot contain a FrameLocator.

Use hasNot to exclude elements containing a matching descendant.
Use hasNotText to exclude elements containing specified text.
gotchas: The has or hasNot locator is evaluated inside each outer match, not from the page root.
Do not use all() until a dynamic list is stable.

interview.question: What does `locator.first` do?
interview.answer: `locator.first` returns a locator for the first matching element. It is useful when an operation must target one element from several matches.
interview.followUp: What is a safer alternative? Build a locator using a role, accessible name, label, text, or another unique condition so that only the intended element matches.

interview.question: Why might you use `first`?
interview.answer: It avoids a strictness error for an action that would otherwise match multiple elements. The action then uses the first match.
interview.followUp: Why can this hide a test problem? A broad locator may still select an unintended element, so the test can pass while interacting with the wrong control.

interview.question: Does `first` perform the action itself?
interview.answer: The method is available on a locator and returns another locator. The returned locator represents the first matching element; it does not immediately perform an action.
interview.followUp: How can you select another position? Use `last` for the final match or `nth(index)` for a zero-based position.

Using `first` explicitly chooses one element when several elements match an action.
A unique locator is usually safer than selecting by position.

interview.question: What does locator.getAttribute() do?

interview.followUp: What should be used for an attribute assertion? Use expect(locator).toHaveAttribute(), because the documentation recommends it to avoid flaky checks.

locator.hover.summary: Playwright locators find elements when actions or assertions run. Prefer built-in locators, especially roles with accessible names, because they match how users and assistive technology perceive the page.
locator.hover.explanation: A locator describes how to find an element when an action or assertion runs. Playwright resolves it again for each action, so a re-rendered page can provide the current matching element. Locators can also be chained through pages, frames, and other locators to narrow the match.

interview.question: What is a Playwright locator?
interview.answer: A locator is a way to find an element at the time an operation runs. Playwright resolves it again for each action, which lets it use the current element after a re-render.
interview.followUp: Why is this useful in reactive applications? It avoids keeping a stale element reference between actions, so later actions can target the newly rendered match.

interview.question: Which locator should you prefer, and why?
interview.answer: Prefer built-in locators such as get_by_role(), get_by_label(), and get_by_text(). Role locators model how users and assistive technology perceive elements, and an accessible name usually makes the match precise.
interview.followUp: When would you use get_by_label()? Use it for a form control associated with a label, such as a username or password field.

interview.question: What is the main limitation of locator.all()?
interview.answer: all() immediately returns locators for the elements currently present. It does not wait for matching elements or for a dynamic list to finish loading.
interview.followUp: How should a test handle a list loaded asynchronously? Wait until the full list is loaded and stable, then call all().

keyPoints: Locators provide Playwright's main mechanism for waiting and retrying actions.
Use get_by_role() when the element's role and accessible information describe it clearly.
Use get_by_label() to find a form control through its associated label.
Use get_by_placeholder() when an input's placeholder is the useful identifier.
Use get_by_test_id() for a test identifier when other user-facing locators are not suitable.
Locator methods can be chained on Locator and FrameLocator objects to narrow a search.
gotchas: Do not use all() while the list is still changing. It returns immediately and can produce flaky results.
Wait until a dynamic list is stable before calling all().
A role alone may match several elements. Add the accessible name to identify the intended element.
Use highlight() only while debugging. Remove it from committed test code.

interview.followUp: How would you make a text check less flaky? Use `expect(locator).toHaveText()` and enable `useInnerText` when rendered text is the intended value.

interview.question: How do you call `innerText()` in Playwright JavaScript?
interview.answer: In JavaScript, `innerText()` is asynchronous, so call it with `await`. The method returns a promise containing a string.
interview.followUp: What happens if the operation takes too long? Configure the timeout, or pass `timeout: 0` to disable the operation timeout.

interview.question: Which option controls how long `innerText()` waits?

locator.isChecked.explanation: Call `isChecked()` on a locator for a checkbox or radio input. Playwright returns a promise that resolves to `true` when the control is checked and `false` when it is not. The method throws if the located element is not a checkbox or radio input.

interview.followUp: How would you assert the state in a test? Use `expect(locator).toBeChecked()` because the documentation recommends the assertion to reduce flakiness.

interview.question: What happens when the locator points to a button?
interview.answer: The method checks the element identified by the locator and resolves to its checked state. It throws when the element is not a checkbox or radio input.
interview.followUp: What should you do if the control may not be ready yet? Use a locator assertion such as `expect(locator).toBeChecked()`, which retries until the assertion timeout.

interview.followUp: Does providing an abort signal disable the timeout? No. The timeout still applies unless `timeout: 0` is passed.

interview.answer: `locator.isEnabled()` returns whether the matched element is enabled. It resolves to a Boolean.

interview.question: What options can `isEnabled()` receive?

locator.isVisible.explanation: `locator.isVisible()` checks the current matching element and returns immediately. It does not wait for the element to become visible. For a test assertion, use `expect(locator).toBeVisible()` instead because it retries and is less prone to timing problems.

interview.question: What does `locator.isVisible()` do?
interview.answer: `isVisible()` returns a promise that resolves to a boolean describing the element's current visibility. It returns without waiting for visibility to change.
interview.followUp: How should a test wait for visibility? Use `expect(locator).toBeVisible()`, which retries until the assertion passes or its timeout expires.

interview.question: Does `isVisible()` wait or honor its timeout option?
interview.answer: The optional timeout setting is deprecated and ignored. The method does not wait for the element to become visible.
interview.followUp: Why can this cause a flaky test? A check can run before a delayed element appears, so the result may be false even though the element will soon be visible.

interview.question: When should you use `isVisible()` instead of a visibility assertion?
interview.answer: Use `isVisible()` when code needs an immediate boolean decision, such as checking whether a dialog is currently shown. Use `expect(locator).toBeVisible()` for a test assertion.
interview.followUp: How can a test handle either a button or a dialog? Combine locators with `or()`, use `first()` if both may match, and then check the dialog condition.

locator.last.explanation: `locator.last` creates a new locator for the final element matched by the current locator. The element is resolved when the locator is used, so it can work with the page's current state.

interview.followUp: How can you select an element at a specific zero-based position? Use `locator.nth(index)`.

interview.question: When might you use `locator.last`?
interview.answer: It is useful when a locator matches a list and the test needs the final item. The locator remains tied to the original matching rule.
interview.followUp: What should you consider if the list order changes? Prefer a stable role, text, or other locator that identifies the intended item rather than relying on position.

interview.question: What does `locator.press()` do?

interview.followUp: When would you avoid `fill()`? Use `press_sequentially()` when the page has special per-key keyboard handling.

interview.question: Which keys and shortcuts can `press()` accept?
