from playwright.sync_api import sync_playwright

with sync_playwright() as p:
    browser = p.chromium.launch()
    page = browser.new_page()
    page.set_content('''<button hidden>Old</button><button>Save</button>''')
    page.locator('button').visible.click()
    browser.close()
example.explanation: This creates a locator for all buttons, narrows it to visible buttons, and clicks the visible one.

useCases.title: Choose the visible match
useCases.scenario: A selector matches both hidden and visible buttons.

useCases.title: Avoid an ambiguous action
useCases.scenario: A page renders duplicate controls, but only one is displayed.

interview.question: What does `locator.visible` do?
interview.answer: `locator.visible` narrows a locator to visible elements. It is useful when the original locator also matches hidden elements, which could otherwise cause a strictness error during an action.
interview.followUp: What should you try before filtering by visibility? Use a more reliable locator that uniquely identifies the intended element, such as a role with an accessible name.

interview.question: Why can visibility filtering prevent a strictness violation?
interview.answer: If two buttons match `locator('button')` and one is hidden, clicking the original locator can fail because it is not unique. Adding `.visible` leaves only the visible button for the action.
interview.followUp: How would you select hidden elements instead? Use `locator.filter(visible=False)` on the original locator.

interview.question: Is `locator.visible` a snapshot of the element?
interview.answer: The visible locator is a narrowed locator, not an immediate element lookup. Playwright resolves locators when actions run, so the action uses the current matching DOM element.
interview.followUp: Why is this useful after a page re-render? The locator can resolve the current element rather than relying on an old element reference.

keyPoints: Playwright also supports CSS selectors with `:visible`, but the locator shortcut is the preferred form.
Calling `.visible` before `.click()` can select the visible match when the same selector also finds a hidden element.
Use `.visible` instead of writing the CSS `:visible` pseudo-class when matching visible elements.
Visibility matching is a locator technique covered by the Playwright locator documentation.
gotchas: Do not use visibility as the first choice when a stable role, name, text, or other user-facing locator can identify the element.
`locator.visible` excludes hidden elements. Use `filter(visible=False)` when you need invisible matches.

locator.waitFor.summary: Waits for a locator's element to reach a chosen state. It returns immediately if the state is already satisfied.
locator.waitFor.explanation: `locator.waitFor()` waits for the element matched by a locator to reach a chosen state. It returns at once if the state is already true. The default state is `visible`; you can also wait for `attached`, `detached`, or `hidden`.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Optional settings object. It can include an abort signal, state, and timeout.

parameters.name: signal
parameters.description: Cancels the wait when aborted. Added in v1.62.

parameters.name: state
parameters.description: The required state: `attached`, `detached`, `visible`, or `hidden`. Defaults to `visible`.

parameters.name: timeout
parameters.description: Maximum wait time in milliseconds. The method documentation lists `0` as the default.

example.title: Wait for an element
example.code:
const orderSent = page.locator('#order-sent');
await orderSent.waitFor({ state: 'visible', timeout: 5000 });
example.explanation: This waits until the matching element is visible, or until five seconds pass.

useCases.title: Wait for an element to appear
useCases.scenario: A page adds an element after an action, and the test must wait until it appears.

useCases.title: Wait for an element to detach
useCases.scenario: A loading indicator must be removed before the next assertion or action.

useCases.title: Wait for visibility
useCases.scenario: A control exists but starts hidden and becomes visible later.

interview.question: What does `locator.waitFor()` do?
interview.answer: It waits for the locator's element to reach the requested state. The supported states are `attached`, `detached`, `visible`, and `hidden`, and the default is `visible`.
interview.followUp: How would you wait for an element to be removed? Use `await locator.waitFor({ state: 'detached' })` or use `hidden` if removal or visual hiding is acceptable.

interview.question: How do you control the wait duration?
interview.answer: The default timeout is zero for this method. A timeout can be supplied in milliseconds, and Playwright settings can change the default timeout behavior.
interview.followUp: How can you wait without a limit? Pass `timeout: 0`, but use this carefully because a missing condition can make the test wait forever.

interview.question: What is the difference between `visible` and `hidden`?
interview.answer: `visible` requires a non-empty bounding box and no `visibility:hidden`. `hidden` is the opposite: the element may be detached, have an empty bounding box, or use `visibility:hidden`.
interview.followUp: Which state should you use when the element must exist in the DOM but need not be visible? Use `attached`.

keyPoints: The method resolves when the matched element satisfies the selected state.
No additional wait occurs when the condition is already true.
If no state is supplied, Playwright waits for visibility.
`attached` checks that the element is present in the DOM.
`detached` checks that the element is no longer in the DOM.
gotchas: The method can finish immediately when the requested state is already met.
An element is visible only when it has a non-empty bounding box and is not hidden with `visibility:hidden`.
A timeout of `0` disables the timeout.

locator.within.summary: locator.within() returns a locator scoped inside each element matched by a parent locator. Relative locators such as nth() are resolved separately inside every parent.
locator.within.explanation: Call within() on a locator to search inside each element matched by a parent locator. Relative locators, such as nth() and first, are evaluated separately inside every matched parent. This lets one locator describe the same position or child in multiple containers.

parameters.name: locator
parameters.description: Locator for the parent elements in which the current locator should search.

example.title: Select a relative cell inside each row
example.explanation: Selects the third cell inside every row and checks the text in those cells.

useCases.title: Scope a relative locator per parent
useCases.scenario: Select the same-position element in each repeated container, such as the third cell in every table row.

useCases.title: Search repeated containers
useCases.scenario: Build one reusable locator for matching children across multiple parent elements.

interview.question: What does locator.within() do?
interview.answer: within() returns a locator whose matches are limited to the elements inside each element matched by the parent locator. It does not immediately query or return DOM elements.
interview.followUp: What happens with nth(2).within(rows)? The third matching cell is selected separately inside every row, so the result can contain one cell per row.

interview.question: When is within() useful?
interview.answer: Use within() when the same child relationship must be applied to multiple containers, such as selecting a column cell in every table row. It keeps the locator scoped to each matched parent.
interview.followUp: How would you verify all selected cells? Use a web assertion such as toHaveText() with the expected values.

interview.question: What are within()'s argument and return value?
interview.answer: The argument is another Locator that identifies the parent elements to search within. The method returns a Locator, which can then be used for actions or assertions.
interview.followUp: Can the returned locator be used for an action? Yes, provided the resulting locator resolves to a suitable target for that action.

keyPoints: within() scopes the current locator to every element found by the supplied parent locator.
A relative position is calculated separately within each parent, not once across all matching elements.
Pass a Locator for the parent elements that should contain the search results.
gotchas: nth() does not select one item from the entire result set when used with within(). It selects that position separately inside each matched parent.

mergeExpects.summary: Playwright assertions verify values and page conditions. Web assertions retry until the condition passes or the assertion timeout is reached.
mergeExpects.explanation: Playwright web assertions check a page condition and retry the check until it passes or the assertion timeout is reached. The locator is fetched again during retries, so the assertion can observe changes made by the application.

parameters.name: value
parameters.description: The value or locator to check with expect.

mergeExpects.returns: An assertion object with generic or web-specific matchers.

example.title: Wait for text with an assertion
example.explanation: This test clicks the submit button and waits for the status element to show the expected text.

useCases.title: Verify an updated UI state
useCases.scenario: Check that a page element eventually shows text after an action.

useCases.title: Verify a value
useCases.scenario: Check a general JavaScript value with a generic matcher.

useCases.title: Use custom matchers
useCases.scenario: Combine assertion helpers from several test utility modules.

interview.question: What are Playwright web-first assertions?
interview.answer: Use Playwright's expect function with a matcher such as toHaveText. Web-specific matchers wait and retry while checking the page.
interview.followUp: What happens while the assertion retries? The locator is fetched again and checked until the condition passes or the timeout is reached.

interview.question: How does the assertion timeout work?
interview.answer: The assertion timeout controls how long a retrying assertion waits for its condition. It defaults to five seconds, and you can pass a timeout or configure it in the test configuration.
interview.followUp: How can a test use a different timeout for one assertion? Pass the timeout through the matcher options supported by that assertion.

interview.question: Which expect function should a Playwright test use?
interview.answer: Import expect from @playwright/test, or from a project fixture that exports Playwright's expect. Do not use an unrelated expect library because it is not fully integrated with the Playwright runner.
interview.followUp: How can custom matchers from several modules be used together? Combine their expect objects with mergeExpects and export the result.

keyPoints: Call expect(value), then select a matcher that describes the condition the test should verify.
Use web-specific async matchers for page checks that may become true after the test action.
A locator-based assertion fetches the element again during retries instead of checking only the first result.
Retries stop when the condition passes or when the assertion timeout expires.
Set a timeout for one assertion or configure the default assertion timeout in the test configuration.
gotchas: Use the expect exported by Playwright Test. The separate expect library is not fully integrated with the Playwright test runner.
An assertion fails after five seconds unless you set a different timeout or configure one for the test project.

Mouse.summary: Playwright's Mouse class sends mouse actions at CSS-pixel coordinates in the main-frame viewport. Use page.mouse for clicks, movement, button presses, releases, and wheel input.
Mouse.explanation: The Mouse class sends mouse actions in CSS pixels measured from the top-left of the main-frame viewport. A page exposes its Mouse object through page.mouse. Use move, down, and up for custom actions, or use click and dblclick for common actions. Wheel sends scrolling input.
Mouse.syntax:
page.mouse.click(x, y, options?)
page.mouse.dblclick(x, y, options?)
page.mouse.down(options?)
page.mouse.move(x, y, options?)
page.mouse.up(options?)
page.mouse.wheel(deltaX, deltaY)

parameters.name: x
parameters.description: Horizontal coordinate in CSS pixels relative to the main-frame viewport.

parameters.name: y
parameters.description: Vertical coordinate in CSS pixels relative to the main-frame viewport.

parameters.name: button
parameters.description: Mouse button: left, right, or middle. The default is left.

parameters.name: clickCount
parameters.description: Number of click actions. The default is 1.

parameters.name: delay
parameters.description: Milliseconds between mousedown and mouseup. The default is 0.

parameters.name: steps
parameters.description: Number of interpolated mousemove events. The default is 1.

parameters.name: deltaX
parameters.description: Horizontal scroll distance in pixels.

parameters.name: deltaY
parameters.description: Vertical scroll distance in pixels.

Mouse.returns: The documented methods return Promise<void> in the JavaScript and TypeScript API.

example.title: Draw with page.mouse
example.explanation: This test presses the left mouse button, moves through four points, and releases it to draw a square.

useCases.title: Custom mouse paths
useCases.scenario: Test drawing or drag interactions by combining move, down, and up.

useCases.title: Coordinate-based clicks
useCases.scenario: Trigger a normal or double click at exact viewport coordinates.

useCases.title: Manual scrolling
useCases.scenario: Scroll horizontally or vertically with pixel deltas.

interview.question: How are Playwright mouse coordinates defined?
interview.answer: Mouse coordinates are CSS pixels relative to the top-left of the main-frame viewport. Each page has its own Mouse object, available as page.mouse.
interview.followUp: How would you perform a drag? Call move to the start point, down to press the button, move to the destination, and up to release it.

interview.question: What does mouse.click do?
interview.answer: click is a shortcut for move, down, and up. Its options can select the button, click count, and delay between pressing and releasing.
interview.followUp: How can you create a double click without dblclick? Use two down-and-up sequences, while setting the appropriate click count if needed.

interview.question: What does the steps option change?
interview.answer: move dispatches mousemove events. By default it sends one event at the destination; steps can add interpolated events along the path.
interview.followUp: When might steps help? They can model travel through intermediate points when an application reacts to mouse movement.

keyPoints: Mouse coordinates use CSS pixels, starting at the viewport's top-left corner.
Get the mouse controller from the page.mouse property.
click moves to the point, presses the button, and releases it.
dblclick performs two press-and-release actions at the target point.
down sends a mousedown event and keeps the button pressed until up is called.
up sends a mouseup event to release the selected button.
wheel accepts horizontal and vertical pixel deltas for scrolling.
gotchas: A wheel call can start scrolling, but it returns before scrolling has finished.
With steps greater than one, move sends intermediate mousemove events between the current position and the destination.

page.summary: page.add_locator_handler() runs a callback when a matching overlay blocks an action or assertion. The callback should remove the overlay so Playwright can continue.
page.explanation: Add a handler for an unexpected visible overlay. Playwright checks for it before actions that need actionability checks and before auto-waiting assertions. The handler should remove the blocking element. After it runs, Playwright normally waits for that overlay to become hidden.

parameters.name: locator
parameters.description: Locator that identifies the overlay or other blocking element.

parameters.name: handler
parameters.description: Callback that removes the blocking element. It can receive the matching Locator.

parameters.name: no_wait_after
parameters.description: Do not wait for the matching overlay to become hidden after the callback.

parameters.name: times
parameters.description: Maximum number of callback invocations. Unlimited by default.

example.title: Close an unexpected overlay
example.code:
from playwright.sync_api import Page

def close_overlay(page: Page) -> None:
    page.get_by_role("button", name="No thanks").click()

page.add_locator_handler(
    page.get_by_text("Sign up to the newsletter"),
    close_overlay,
)
page.goto("https://example.com")
page.get_by_role("button", name="Start here").click()
example.explanation: The handler runs when the overlay is detected before an action or assertion. It closes the overlay so the action can continue.

useCases.title: Dismiss an unexpected dialog
useCases.scenario: An unpredictable newsletter or sign-up dialog blocks a test action.

useCases.title: Skip an optional prompt
useCases.scenario: A security prompt sometimes appears during a flow.

useCases.title: Run cleanup before checks
useCases.scenario: A page has recurring test-only obstructions.

interview.question: What does page.add_locator_handler() do?
interview.answer: It registers a callback for a locator that represents a blocking overlay. Before a matching action or auto-waiting assertion, Playwright runs the callback, then continues.
interview.followUp: When does it not run? It does not run merely because the overlay appears; a later action or assertion must trigger the check.

interview.question: What should the handler do?
interview.answer: The handler should remove the overlay that matched the locator. By default, Playwright then waits for that overlay to be hidden before continuing.
interview.followUp: How can that wait be disabled? Pass no_wait_after=True when the handler intentionally leaves the matching locator visible.

interview.question: How can handler calls be limited?
interview.answer: The handler receives the original Locator as an argument when defined that way. The times option limits the maximum number of calls; without it, calls are unlimited.
interview.followUp: What happens with several handlers? They may all be registered, but only one handler runs at a time.

keyPoints: The check happens before an action that needs an actionability check or before an auto-waiting assertion.
The callback runs before the blocked action or assertion proceeds.
Several handlers are allowed, but their callbacks do not run concurrently.
Set no_wait_after=True when Playwright should not wait for the matching overlay to disappear.
Use times to stop the handler after a chosen number of invocations.
gotchas: Use a normal wait and dismissal when the overlay always appears at a known point.
Registering a handler does not run it immediately when the overlay appears.
A slow handler can make the action or assertion time out.
The handler can change focus and mouse position, so prefer self-contained actions such as locator.press() and locator.click().

Page.summary: A Page represents one browser tab or popup. Use it to navigate, interact with content, and work with multiple pages in a browser context.
Page.explanation: A Page represents one browser tab or popup window. Use it to open URLs, find elements, perform actions, and read page data. A browser context can contain several pages, and pages inherit the context's settings such as viewport and locale.
Page.syntax:
const page = await context.newPage();
await page.goto(url);

parameters.name: context
parameters.description: A browser context that owns the page. The page is created with context.newPage().

parameters.name: url
parameters.description: The URL to open with page.goto().

Page.returns: Page-creation methods return a Page. Navigation and interaction methods return promises for their documented results; page.url() returns the current URL.

example.title: Open a page and read its title
example.explanation: This creates a browser page, opens a URL, reads its title, and closes the browser.

useCases.title: Navigate and interact
useCases.scenario: A test opens a normal web page and fills or clicks controls.

useCases.title: Handle a new tab
useCases.scenario: A link uses target="_blank" and opens another tab.

useCases.title: Handle a popup
useCases.scenario: A button opens a separate browser popup.

interview.question: What does a Playwright Page represent?
interview.answer: A Page is one tab or popup inside a browser context. Use it to navigate and interact with page content.
interview.followUp: How can one test use several tabs? Create more pages with context.newPage() and inspect them through context.pages().

interview.question: How do you handle a new page opened by an action?
interview.answer: Create the page-event promise before the click, then await the promise after the click. This captures a page opened by a new-tab link.
interview.followUp: How would you handle an unknown trigger? Register a context page listener and process each emitted page.

interview.question: How do you capture a popup?
interview.answer: Use page.waitForEvent('popup') before the action that opens the popup. Await the resulting promise, then use the returned Page normally.
interview.followUp: How do you handle popups whose trigger is unknown? Attach a page popup listener and wait for the popup to load before using it.

keyPoints: One browser context can contain multiple pages.
A Page models one tab or popup window.
Use a Page for navigation and page interactions.
Pages behave as active pages during automation.
Pages inherit context settings, including viewport, network routes, and locale.
Listen for the context page event to receive newly created pages.
gotchas: Pages in a browser context act as active pages without requiring a call to bringToFront().
Begin waiting for a new page before the action that creates it; otherwise the event may be missed.
For a popup, create the event wait before clicking the control that opens it.

page.addInitScript.summary: Installs JavaScript that runs in new page documents before the page's own scripts. It is useful for changing the page environment, such as making Math.random predictable.
page.addInitScript.explanation: page.addInitScript installs JavaScript that runs after a document is created but before that document's scripts. It runs again for navigations and for child frames that are attached or navigated. You can provide the script as a function, file, or raw content.

parameters.name: script
parameters.description: Function, JavaScript source string, or an object containing path or content.

parameters.name: arg
parameters.description: A value passed to the function. This is supported only when script is a function.

parameters.name: options.exposeFunctions
parameters.description: When true, functions inside arg are exposed in the page. The default is false.

page.addInitScript.returns: A Promise that resolves after the init script is installed.

example.title: Set a script before page code runs
example.explanation: The script is installed before navigation, so page code sees the replaced Math.random function.

useCases.title: Control the JavaScript environment
useCases.scenario: A test needs stable random values or another controlled browser API.

useCases.title: Repeat setup in new documents
useCases.scenario: The same setup must be present after page navigations.

useCases.title: Prepare frame environments
useCases.scenario: A child frame must receive the same early JavaScript setup.

interview.question: When does an init script run?
interview.answer: It runs after the document exists but before scripts from the page run. This lets you change the JavaScript environment before application code can observe it.
interview.followUp: What happens in a child frame? The script is evaluated in the newly attached or navigated child frame as well.

interview.question: What forms of script input does addInitScript support?
interview.answer: The method accepts a function, a JavaScript file path, or script content. An argument can be passed when the script is supplied as a function.
interview.followUp: How can functions inside the argument be handled? Set exposeFunctions to true; they are exposed to the page and calls return promises.

interview.question: Why is addInitScript useful across navigations?
interview.answer: It runs again when the page navigates and when a child frame is attached or navigated. This makes environment changes available in each new document.
interview.followUp: Can the evaluation order of page and context init scripts be used for setup dependencies? No. The documentation says that order is not defined.

keyPoints: The script runs for every page navigation.
The script also runs in child frames when they are attached or navigated.
It can prepare the JavaScript environment before site scripts execute.
A common use is making random values predictable for a test.
A relative file path is resolved from the current working directory.
You can provide JavaScript as a string instead of a file.
gotchas: Do not depend on the order when combining scripts installed on a browser context and a page.
With exposeFunctions enabled, passed functions remain available in new documents.

page.check.summary: `page.get_by_role()` locates an element by its ARIA role and accessible name. It returns a locator for actions and assertions.
page.check.explanation: `page.get_by_role()` creates a locator for an element with a required ARIA role. You can narrow the match with options such as `name`, `checked`, or `disabled`. The locator can then perform actions or work with assertions.
page.check.syntax: page.get_by_role(role, *, checked=None, description=None, disabled=None, expanded=None, include_hidden=None, level=None, name=None, pressed=None, selected=None, exact=None)

parameters.name: role
parameters.description: Required ARIA role, such as `button`, `checkbox`, or `heading`.

parameters.name: name
parameters.description: Optional accessible name filter. It accepts text or a regular expression.

parameters.name: checked
parameters.description: Optional checked-state filter.

parameters.name: description
parameters.description: Optional accessible-description filter.

parameters.name: disabled
parameters.description: Optional disabled-state filter.

example.title: Find and click a button
example.code: page.get_by_role("button", name="Submit").click()
example.explanation: This finds the button by its ARIA role and accessible name, then clicks it.

useCases.title: Locate accessible controls
useCases.scenario: A form has buttons, headings, and checkboxes with meaningful ARIA roles.

useCases.title: Disambiguate matching elements
useCases.scenario: Several elements share visible text but have different roles.

useCases.title: Filter by ARIA state
useCases.scenario: A test needs to select controls by state, such as checked or disabled.

interview.question: What does `page.get_by_role()` do?
interview.answer: It locates an element by its ARIA role and accessible name. The role is required, while options such as `name` make the locator more specific.
interview.followUp: Why prefer this over a CSS selector? It uses the interface exposed to assistive technology, so the locator also checks the element's intended user-facing role.

interview.question: How do you locate a specific button?
interview.answer: The `name` option filters by accessible name. For example, a button can be found with `page.get_by_role("button", name="Submit")`.
interview.followUp: How can you make the match case-insensitive with a pattern? Pass a Python regular expression, such as `re.compile("submit", re.IGNORECASE)`.

interview.question: What does this method return?
interview.answer: The method returns a `Locator`. You can use that locator for actions such as `click()` or checks such as visibility assertions.
interview.followUp: What happens if the role and options match more than one element? Add more locator options or refine the locator so it identifies the intended element.

keyPoints: Use the element's ARIA role and accessible name to create a locator.
The `role` argument is required.
Use `checked` to filter checkbox-like controls by their checked state.
Use `description` to filter by accessible description.
Use `disabled` to filter elements by whether they are disabled.
gotchas: For button and submit inputs, the accessible name comes from the value rather than normal text content.
Name matching is usually case-insensitive and partial. Use `exact=True` when you need a whole-string match.

page.click.summary: locator.click performs a user-like click after Playwright waits for the element to be ready. It can also use modifiers, a mouse button, a position, or forced action.
page.click.explanation: page.click clicks the element matched by a selector. Before clicking, Playwright waits for the element to be present, visible, stable, in view, and able to receive pointer events. It retries if the element is detached during these checks. Use force=True to skip nonessential actionability checks, or dispatch_event("click") to send a programmatic click.

parameters.name: selector
parameters.description: The selector used to find the element to click.

parameters.name: force
parameters.description: Skips nonessential actionability checks when true. Defaults to false.

parameters.name: timeout
parameters.description: Maximum wait time in milliseconds. Defaults to 30000; 0 disables the timeout.

parameters.name: button
parameters.description: Mouse button to use, such as left, middle, or right.

parameters.name: modifiers
parameters.description: Modifier keys to press during the click.

parameters.name: position
parameters.description: Coordinates relative to the element's padding box.

parameters.name: scroll
parameters.description: Controls whether Playwright scrolls the element into view before the action.

parameters.name: trial
parameters.description: Runs actionability checks without performing the click when true.

example.title: Click a button
example.code:
from playwright.sync_api import sync_playwright

with sync_playwright() as p:
    browser = p.chromium.launch()
    page = browser.new_page()
    page.goto("https://example.com")
    page.get_by_role("button", name="Start here").click()
    browser.close()
example.explanation: This opens a page, finds a button by its role and name, and clicks it.

useCases.title: Normal user-like click
useCases.scenario: Click a button or link after the page makes it ready.

useCases.title: Right-click or modified click
useCases.scenario: Use a secondary mouse action.

useCases.title: Force a click
useCases.scenario: Test an intentional overlay or interception.

useCases.title: Programmatic click
useCases.scenario: Trigger only the element's click event.

interview.question: What does Playwright check before a click?
interview.answer: Playwright waits for the matched element to be in the DOM, displayed, stable, scrolled into view, and able to receive pointer events. It retries when the element becomes detached during these checks.
interview.followUp: When would you use force=True? Use it when application behavior intentionally causes another element to intercept the click and you understand that normal actionability checks should be bypassed.

interview.question: How can you force a click?
interview.answer: Use force=True to bypass actionability checks. This can click an element even when normal checks would report that it is covered or otherwise not actionable.
interview.followUp: What is a more direct alternative for testing only the element's event handler? Use locator.dispatch_event("click"), which dispatches a click event without simulating a real pointer click.

interview.question: How does a programmatic click differ from a normal click?
interview.answer: locator.click performs a user-like pointer click after waiting for actionability. locator.dispatch_event("click") directly dispatches the HTMLElement click behavior and is useful when real conditions are not part of the test.
interview.followUp: Why is the direct event usually less representative? It skips pointer conditions such as visibility, stability, scrolling, and obstruction checks.

keyPoints: Playwright first waits until the selector matches an element in the document.
The target must be displayed before the click can happen.
Playwright waits for movement, such as a CSS transition, to finish.
The click action scrolls the target into view when needed.
The target must be able to receive pointer events at the chosen click point.
If the target is removed during preparation, Playwright retries the action.
gotchas: force=True skips actionability checks. Use it only when you know the page intentionally intercepts the click.
dispatch_event("click") does not simulate normal user conditions; it sends the element's click event directly.

page.content.summary: A Playwright Page represents one browser tab or popup. Use it to navigate, locate elements, perform actions, and handle page events.
page.content.explanation: A Page represents one browser tab or popup in a browser context. Use it to open URLs, find page elements, perform actions, read content, and listen for page events. Pages in the same context share that context's settings.

parameters.name: context.new_page()
parameters.description: Creates a new page in a browser context. The shown documentation does not list parameters for this operation.

page.content.returns: A Page object representing the new tab or popup.

example.title: Use a Page
example.code:
from playwright.sync_api import sync_playwright

with sync_playwright() as p:
    browser = p.chromium.launch()
    page = browser.new_page()
    page.goto("https://example.com")
    page.locator("h1").is_visible()
    browser.close()
example.explanation: Creates a page, opens a URL, checks a locator, and closes the browser.

useCases.title: Navigate and interact
useCases.scenario: Open and test a web page.

useCases.title: Manage multiple pages
useCases.scenario: Run several isolated tabs in one browser context.

useCases.title: Handle popup pages
useCases.scenario: Test links that open new tabs.

useCases.title: Share context settings
useCases.scenario: Reuse locale, viewport, or network settings across tabs.

interview.question: What does Playwright's Page object represent?
interview.answer: A Page represents one tab or popup inside a BrowserContext. Create it with context.new_page(), then use methods such as goto(), locator(), and click() to work with its content.
interview.followUp: How can you handle a tab opened by a link? Use context.expect_page() around the action that opens the tab, then read the resulting page from the event information.

interview.question: How do you work with multiple pages?
interview.answer: A browser context can contain multiple pages. Use context.pages to inspect them, or context.new_page() to create another page; each page can be used independently.
interview.followUp: Do pages need to be focused first? No. The documentation says bringing a page to the front is not required.

interview.question: How do you handle a new page opened by target="_blank"?
interview.answer: Use context.expect_page() while performing the action that opens the new tab. After the action, obtain the new Page from the captured event information and interact with it.
interview.followUp: What should be captured before the click? The page-opening expectation should be set up before the action, so the new-page event is observed reliably.

keyPoints: One browser context can contain several Page objects, such as tabs or popup windows.
A Page is the object for one tab or popup in a browser context.
Use a Page to navigate and interact with elements on the page.
Every page behaves as if it is focused and active during automation.
Pages inherit context settings, including viewport, network routing, and locale configuration.
Listen for the browser context's page event when an action creates another page.
gotchas: Pages act like active pages, so you do not need to bring one to the front before using it.
A frame locator must resolve to one frame. Matching more than one frame causes an error.

page.evaluate.summary: `page.evaluate()` runs JavaScript in the browser page and returns its result to the Playwright test. Pass test values explicitly, and use init scripts for code that must run before page loading.
page.evaluate.explanation: `page.evaluate()` runs JavaScript in the browser page, where browser globals such as `window` and `document` are available. The returned value comes back to the Playwright test. Values from the test are not visible inside the page function, so pass them as the optional argument. Playwright waits for returned promises to resolve.

parameters.name: pageFunction
parameters.description: A JavaScript function or expression evaluated in the page environment.

parameters.name: arg
parameters.description: One optional value passed into the page function. It may contain serializable values and `JSHandle` instances.

page.evaluate.returns: The value returned by the page function, with promises resolved before the result is returned.

example.title: Read a browser value
example.explanation: The function runs in the browser page and returns the document title to the test.

useCases.title: Inspect page state
useCases.scenario: Read or calculate a value that exists only in the browser, such as `document.title` or the current URL.

useCases.title: Run page-side logic
useCases.scenario: Call page APIs or application functions that are not exposed through a locator action.

useCases.title: Prepare page loading
useCases.scenario: Install a mock or seed test data before navigation starts.

interview.question: What does `page.evaluate()` do?
interview.answer: It runs a JavaScript function in the web page's browser context and returns the result to the Playwright environment. This lets the function use browser globals such as `window` and `document`.
interview.followUp: What happens if the function returns a promise? Playwright waits for the promise to resolve before returning the result.

interview.question: How do you pass data into evaluated JavaScript?
interview.answer: Test code and page code run in separate environments. A variable declared in the test is not available in the page function unless it is passed through the optional argument.
interview.followUp: How would you pass several values? Put them in one object or array and read them from the function parameter.

interview.question: When should you use an init script?
interview.answer: Use `page.add_init_script()` or `browserContext.add_init_script()` to run code before the page starts loading. This is useful for mocks or test data.
interview.followUp: When would a context-level script be useful? Use it when the setup should apply to pages in the browser context rather than only one page.

keyPoints: Use `page.evaluate()` to run JavaScript inside the loaded page.
The evaluated function can access browser objects such as `window` and `document`.
Async functions and returned promises are awaited automatically.
Send values from the test to the page through the optional argument.
A `JSHandle` passed as an argument is exposed to the page as the value it refers to.
Use an init script for code that must run before page loading begins.
gotchas: Do not reference a test variable directly inside the page function. Pass it as the second argument.
The method accepts one optional argument. It can contain serializable values, handles, or both.
When destructuring an object argument, use property names that match the passed object.
Wrap destructured arrow-function parameters in parentheses.

page.fill.summary: page.fill enters text into an input, textarea, or contenteditable element. It is discouraged for new code; use locator.fill instead.
page.fill.explanation: Use the page.fill method to put text into an input, textarea, or contenteditable element. Playwright finds the first matching element, checks that it can be used, focuses it, enters the value, and sends an input event. Prefer locator.fill for new code because the page method is discouraged.

parameters.name: selector
parameters.description: CSS or other selector used to find the element. The first match is used unless strict mode is enabled.

parameters.name: value
parameters.description: Text to enter into the input, textarea, or contenteditable element.

parameters.name: force
parameters.description: Skip actionability checks when true. Default: false.

parameters.name: strict
parameters.description: Require the selector to match exactly one element when true.

parameters.name: timeout
parameters.description: Maximum wait time in milliseconds. Default: 30000. Zero disables the timeout.

example.title: Fill a text input
example.code:
from playwright.sync_api import sync_playwright

with sync_playwright() as p:
    browser = p.chromium.launch()
    page = browser.new_page()
    page.goto("https://example.com")
    page.get_by_role("textbox").fill("Peter")
    browser.close()
example.explanation: This opens a browser, visits a page, finds a textbox by its role, and fills it.

useCases.title: Fill form fields
useCases.scenario: A form has a text, date, or time control that must receive a value.

useCases.title: Clear a field
useCases.scenario: A test must remove the current value before continuing.

interview.question: What does page.fill do?
interview.answer: It finds an element with the selector, waits for actionability, focuses it, fills the value, and triggers an input event. It supports input, textarea, and contenteditable elements.
interview.followUp: What should new code use instead? Use locator.fill, because page.fill is discouraged.

interview.question: How does selector matching work?
interview.answer: The selector is a string used to find the target element. If several elements match, the first one is used unless strict is true.
interview.followUp: What happens with strict set to true and multiple matches? The call throws an exception.

interview.question: How are clearing and actionability handled?
interview.answer: The value is the string written into the target control. An empty string clears the control.
interview.followUp: How can the normal actionability checks be skipped? Set force to true, though this should be used carefully.

keyPoints: The method waits for the element, checks that it is actionable, focuses it, and fills it.
Filling also triggers an input event.
Pass an empty string to clear the field.
A matching element inside a label can cause its associated control to be filled.
gotchas: The page method is discouraged. Use locator.fill instead.
The target must be an input, textarea, or contenteditable element.
Without strict mode, Playwright uses the first matching element.
The default timeout is 30 seconds. Use zero to disable it.

page.focus.summary: Use locator.focus() to move keyboard focus to an element. It helps test pages that change behavior when an element receives focus.
page.focus.explanation: Call locator.focus() on the element that should receive focus. Playwright waits for a matching element and then focuses it. This is useful when a page changes its behavior after focus events.

parameters.name: locator
parameters.description: A locator identifying the element to focus.

example.title: Focus a password field
example.explanation: This focuses the element matched by its accessible label.

useCases.title: Trigger focus behavior
useCases.scenario: A form shows help text or validation when a field receives focus.

useCases.title: Set the active field
useCases.scenario: A test must place focus on a named form control before another action.

useCases.title: Test dynamic forms
useCases.scenario: A page has dynamic focus handling for a password or text field.

interview.question: How do you focus an element in Playwright Python?
interview.answer: Use locator.focus() to focus a matching element. The locator identifies the element, such as a password field selected by its label.
interview.followUp: Why use a locator instead of page.focus()? The page method is discouraged in favor of the locator-based method.

interview.question: What does page.focus() do?
interview.answer: A locator focuses the element it resolves to. The page documentation says the older selector-based page.focus() method waits for a matching element to appear.
interview.followUp: What should replace page.focus(selector)? Use locator.focus() with a locator that expresses how the user finds the element.

interview.question: When is focus() useful?
interview.answer: Focus is useful for pages that handle focus events. For example, focusing a password field can trigger page behavior tied to that field receiving focus.
interview.followUp: How can you choose the element robustly? Prefer an accessible locator such as get_by_label() when the control has a label.

keyPoints: Use locator.focus() on pages that respond to focus events.
Use the locator API instead of the discouraged page.focus() API.
The older page method finds an element with a selector and focuses it.
The older page method waits when its selector has no matching element yet.
gotchas: Use focus() when the page needs to react to a focus event.
Prefer the locator method over the older page.focus() method.

page.frameLocator.summary: FrameLocator lets you locate and interact with elements inside an iframe. Create it from a page, an iframe locator, or another locator, then use normal locator methods inside the frame.
page.frameLocator.explanation: A FrameLocator lets Playwright enter an iframe and find elements inside it. Create one with Page.frameLocator(), Locator.contentFrame(), or Locator.frameLocator(), then use locator methods such as getByRole() or getByText().

parameters.name: selector
parameters.type: String (optional for Page.frameLocator; required for Locator.frameLocator)
parameters.description: Selector for the iframe element. On Page.frameLocator(), it is optional; without it, matching starts in any frame.

parameters.name: selectorOrLocator
parameters.description: A selector or Locator used to find an element in the frame locator subtree.

page.frameLocator.returns: Page.frameLocator() and Locator.frameLocator() return a FrameLocator. FrameLocator methods that locate elements return a Locator. FrameLocator.owner() returns a Locator for the iframe element.

example.title: Click inside an iframe
example.code:
const button = page.frameLocator('#my-frame').getByRole('button', { name: 'Submit' });
await button.click();
example.explanation: This finds the button named Submit inside the iframe with id my-frame, then clicks it.

useCases.title: Work inside a specific iframe
useCases.scenario: Interact with a button or form field inside a known iframe.

useCases.title: Search across frames
useCases.scenario: Find an element when the containing frame is not known in advance.

useCases.title: Convert an iframe locator
useCases.scenario: Start with an iframe Locator, then locate its contents.

interview.question: What is a FrameLocator?
interview.answer: FrameLocator represents an iframe view. It lets you locate and act on elements inside that iframe without first getting a Frame object. It can come from Page.frameLocator(), Locator.contentFrame(), or Locator.frameLocator().
interview.followUp: How do you convert between the two related types?

interview.question: What does strictness mean for frame locators?
interview.answer: Frame locators are strict. If the iframe selector matches multiple frame elements, an operation throws instead of choosing one automatically. Select one iframe first, then call contentFrame().
interview.followUp: What happens with a selector-free frame locator?

interview.question: How can a FrameLocator be created?
interview.answer: Use page.frameLocator('#my-frame') when you know the iframe selector. Use locator.contentFrame() when you already have a Locator for the iframe. Use locator.frameLocator(selector) to enter a nested iframe from a locator.
interview.followUp: How can you interact with the iframe element itself after creating a FrameLocator?

keyPoints: Create a FrameLocator from an iframe Locator with contentFrame(), directly from Page.frameLocator(), or from Locator.frameLocator().
After entering the iframe, use locator methods such as getByRole(), getByText(), getByLabel(), or locator() to find its elements.
For a selector-free frame locator, only the initial frame search spans frames. The remaining locator chain is resolved within one frame.
Call owner() to convert a FrameLocator back to a Locator for the iframe element.
gotchas: A frame locator is strict. An operation fails when its frame selector matches more than one iframe. Use Locator.first(), last(), or nth() before contentFrame() when you must choose one.
A selector-free Page.frameLocator() searches across the page and its frames. It is not tied to one iframe, so owner(), first(), last(), and nth() are not supported on it.

page.getByAltText.summary: `getByAltText` finds an element by its alternative text and returns a Locator. You can optionally require an exact, case-sensitive, whole-string match.
page.getByAltText.explanation: `getByAltText` creates a locator for an element using its `alt` text. By default, matching can include extra text. Set `exact: true` for a case-sensitive, whole-string match. Regular expressions ignore the exact option.

parameters.name: text
parameters.description: Text used to find the element. It may be a string or pattern.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Optional matching settings.

parameters.name: exact
parameters.description: Whether the string must match exactly, with case-sensitive and whole-string matching. Default: false.

example.title: Find an element by alternative text
example.code:
const image = page.getByAltText('Playwright logo');
await image.click();
example.explanation: This finds an element whose alternative text is "Playwright logo" and clicks it.

useCases.title: Locate accessible media
useCases.scenario: Find an image or other element that has useful alternative text.

useCases.title: Use semantic element text
useCases.scenario: Target an element without writing a CSS selector.

interview.question: What does `getByAltText` do?
interview.answer: It returns a Locator that matches an element by its alternative text. It is useful for elements such as images with an `alt` attribute.
interview.followUp: How would you require a whole-string match? Pass `exact: true`, unless the text is a regular expression.

interview.question: What types of text can you pass?
interview.answer: The text argument can be a string or a regular expression. A string uses the configured exactness behavior, while a regular expression performs pattern matching.
interview.followUp: What happens to `exact` when a regular expression is used? It is ignored.

interview.question: How do you use the returned locator?
interview.answer: Use `getByAltText('Playwright logo')` to create the locator, then call an action such as `click()` on it. The locator resolves the matching element when the action runs.
interview.followUp: How can you make the match case-sensitive and whole-string for a string? Use the optional `exact: true` setting.

keyPoints: Use `getByAltText` to find an element from its alternative text.
The text argument can be a string or a pattern.
The optional exact setting requests a case-sensitive, whole-string match.
Exact matching is disabled by default.
gotchas: The exact option has no effect when the text argument is a regular expression.
Even exact matching removes surrounding whitespace before comparing the text.

page.getByLabel.summary: getByLabel() returns a locator for an input using its associated label, aria-labelledby text, or aria-label. It accepts a string or regular expression.
page.getByLabel.explanation: getByLabel() creates a locator for an input by checking its associated label text, an aria-labelledby reference, or its aria-label attribute. You can pass a string or regular expression. The returned locator can be used with actions such as fill().

parameters.name: text
parameters.description: Label text to find. Accepts a string or regular expression.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Optional matching settings. exact defaults to false and is ignored for regular expressions.

parameters.name: options.exact
parameters.description: Requires a case-sensitive whole-string match. Surrounding whitespace is still trimmed.

example.title: Fill a labeled input
example.code:
const password = page.getByLabel('Password');
await password.fill('secret');
example.explanation: Finds the input associated with the Password label and enters a value.

useCases.title: Fill a labeled form field
useCases.scenario: A form input has a visible label, such as “Password”.

useCases.title: Find an accessible input
useCases.scenario: An input has aria-label but no visible label.

useCases.title: Use exact label matching
useCases.scenario: Several similar labels exist and one must match exactly.

interview.question: What does page.getByLabel() do?
interview.answer: getByLabel() returns a Locator for an input found through a label, aria-labelledby, or aria-label. The locator can then be used for actions such as fill().
interview.followUp: What can the text argument contain? It can be a string or a regular expression. The exact option changes string matching to a case-sensitive whole-string match.

interview.question: Which accessibility information can getByLabel() use?
interview.answer: The method searches for the text of an associated label or aria-labelledby element, and it can also use the aria-label attribute. It returns a Locator.
interview.followUp: How can you make matching stricter? Pass { exact: true } for a case-sensitive whole-string match, except that surrounding whitespace is still trimmed.

interview.question: What arguments does getByLabel() accept?
interview.answer: The text argument accepts either a string or a regular expression. The optional exact setting defaults to false and is ignored when the argument is a regular expression.
interview.followUp: What does exact matching mean here? It requires a case-sensitive, whole-string match while still trimming whitespace.

keyPoints: getByLabel() was added in Playwright v1.27 and locates input elements using accessible label information.
It can match the visible text of an associated label or the referenced aria-labelledby element.
It can also match an input's aria-label attribute.
The text argument can be a string or a regular expression.
Use exact matching when the text must match with case sensitivity and as a complete string.
gotchas: With exact matching, Playwright compares the whole string and ignores surrounding whitespace.

page.getByPlaceholder.summary: `getByPlaceholder()` finds an input by its placeholder text and returns a Locator. Use the Locator for actions such as filling the input.
page.getByPlaceholder.explanation: `page.getByPlaceholder()` returns a locator for an input based on its placeholder text. Use the locator to interact with the matching input, such as by calling `fill()`. By default, the text can match part of the placeholder; set `exact: true` for a case-sensitive whole-string match.

parameters.name: text
parameters.description: Placeholder text to locate. It can be a string or regular expression.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Optional matching settings.

parameters.name: options.exact
parameters.description: When true, require a case-sensitive whole-string match. This option is ignored for regular expressions.

example.title: Find an input by placeholder
example.explanation: This finds an input by its placeholder and fills it with an email address.

useCases.title: Find a form input
useCases.scenario: A form input has a useful placeholder, such as `name@example.com`, but no convenient label.

useCases.title: Require an exact match
useCases.scenario: Several inputs have similar placeholder text and only one should match exactly.

useCases.title: Match a placeholder pattern
useCases.scenario: The placeholder pattern varies and should be matched with a regular expression.

interview.question: What does `getByPlaceholder()` do?
interview.answer: `getByPlaceholder()` locates input elements using their placeholder text and returns a `Locator`. The locator can then be used for actions such as `fill()`.
interview.followUp: How do you require an exact placeholder? Pass `{ exact: true }`; this makes the match case-sensitive and whole-string, while still trimming whitespace.

interview.question: What arguments does `getByPlaceholder()` accept?
interview.answer: The first argument is a string or regular expression used to locate the placeholder text. The optional `exact` setting controls string matching.
interview.followUp: What happens with a regular expression? The `exact` option is ignored, so the regular expression controls the match.

interview.question: What does `getByPlaceholder()` return?
interview.answer: It returns a `Locator`. A locator represents a way to find elements at the time an action or assertion uses it.
interview.followUp: Why use the returned locator instead of immediately querying an element? Locator actions support Playwright's waiting and retry behavior.

keyPoints: Use it to find an input from the text shown as its placeholder.
A common use is to locate an email input and fill it with a value.
The locator text can be a plain string or a regular expression.
The method accepts an optional options object with an `exact` Boolean setting.
gotchas: The default is a partial match. Use `exact: true` when the complete placeholder must match.

page.getByRef.summary: `Page.getByRef` finds an element by an ARIA reference from the latest AI-mode accessibility snapshot. It returns a locator that can be used for actions such as clicking.
page.getByRef.explanation: `page.getByRef(String ref)` finds an element by an ARIA reference from the latest AI-mode accessibility snapshot. The reference is resolved in the element's frame, so you can use it for actions such as clicking.

parameters.name: ref
parameters.description: ARIA reference of the element, such as `e2` or `f1e3`.

example.title: Find and click a button
example.explanation: This finds a button by its role and accessible name, then clicks it.

useCases.title: Act on a snapshot reference
useCases.scenario: An AI-mode accessibility snapshot identifies a target with a ref such as `e2`.

useCases.title: Create a locator from an ARIA ref
useCases.scenario: A test needs to turn a snapshot reference into a Playwright locator.

useCases.title: Use the locator for an action
useCases.scenario: Code needs to perform an action after locating the referenced element.

interview.question: What does `Page.getByRef` do?
interview.answer: `getByRef` locates an element using an ARIA reference such as `e2`. The reference is produced by `Page.ariaSnapshot()` in AI mode.
interview.followUp: What happens if the reference is from an older snapshot? It may no longer resolve correctly because refs work against the latest snapshot.

interview.question: What are the argument and return value?
interview.answer: The method accepts a `String` ref, for example `e2`, and returns a `Locator`. The locator can then be used for actions such as `click()`.
interview.followUp: How would you make the locator less dependent on the snapshot ref? Use `Locator.normalize()` to convert it into a more resilient locator.

interview.question: Where is the reference resolved?
interview.answer: The ref is resolved against the latest accessibility snapshot taken in the element's frame. This allows code to target an element identified in an AI-mode snapshot.
interview.followUp: Can the same ref be assumed to work after the page changes? No. The documentation limits refs to the latest snapshot.

keyPoints: The method was added in Playwright 1.64.
It locates an element using its ARIA reference.
ARIA refs are reported by `Page.ariaSnapshot()`.
A ref such as `e2` can be passed to the method to locate a button.
The parameter is a string containing the element's ARIA ref.
gotchas: The reference comes from an AI-mode aria snapshot and is resolved against the latest snapshot. Do not treat it as a permanent selector.

page.getByRole.summary: Page.getByRole creates a locator using an element's ARIA role and accessible name. Use it to find user-facing controls in a way that is less dependent on CSS classes or DOM structure.
page.getByRole.explanation: getByRole creates a locator for an element with a required ARIA role. You can add options such as name to match the element's accessible name. The locator is resolved when an action or assertion uses it, so Playwright can use the current DOM element.

parameters.name: role
parameters.description: Required ARIA role, such as button, checkbox, heading, or link.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Optional matching settings. The page lists options including name, checked, disabled, expanded, level, pressed, selected, and exact.

example.title: Locate a button by role
example.explanation: This finds a button by its ARIA role and accessible name, then clicks it.

useCases.title: Locate semantic controls
useCases.scenario: Find a button, link, checkbox, heading, or another control by its semantic role.

useCases.title: Match an accessible name
useCases.scenario: Choose one control when several controls share the same role.

useCases.title: Work with dynamic pages
useCases.scenario: Use a locator in an action that should wait for the element to be ready.

interview.question: What does page.getByRole do?
interview.answer: getByRole locates elements using their ARIA role, ARIA attributes, and accessible name. It returns a Locator, which you can use for actions or assertions.
interview.followUp: Why prefer it over a CSS selector? It follows how users and assistive technology identify controls and is less tied to changing DOM structure.

interview.question: Which arguments can getByRole accept?
interview.answer: The first argument is the required role, such as button or checkbox. The options object can include name and other role-related filters, such as checked or selected.
interview.followUp: How would you distinguish two buttons with the same role? Supply a specific accessible name or add a locator filter for surrounding content.

interview.question: How does getByRole work with dynamic pages?
interview.answer: A locator is resolved when an action uses it, and Playwright performs actionability checks such as visibility and enabled state. This supports auto-waiting and helps the action use the current DOM element.
interview.followUp: What happens after a page re-render? The locator can resolve the new matching element instead of keeping an old element handle.

keyPoints: Use it to find elements through their role and accessible name.
Native HTML controls can provide roles automatically, so explicit ARIA markup is not always needed.
Prefer role locators when they describe the user-facing control clearly.
Pass name to make the match more specific.
gotchas: A role alone may match several elements. Add the accessible name when possible.
Using this method can help test accessible behavior, but it is not a complete accessibility audit.
When combining locators with or, both matches can cause a strict mode error; use first when that behavior is intended.

page.getByTestId.summary: page.getByTestId locates an element by its test ID and returns a Locator. It uses data-testid by default, but the test ID attribute can be configured.
page.getByTestId.explanation: getByTestId creates a locator for an element whose test ID matches a string or regular expression. The default attribute is data-testid. You can configure another attribute, such as data-pw, in the Playwright test configuration.

parameters.name: testId
parameters.description: The test ID value to locate. It can be a string or a regular expression.

example.title: Locate an element by test ID
example.explanation: This test creates a button with a test ID, locates it with getByTestId, and clicks it.

useCases.title: Locate a stable test target
useCases.scenario: A button or control has a stable data-testid attribute.

useCases.title: Use an explicit test contract
useCases.scenario: Visible text or an accessible role may change, but the test contract should remain stable.

useCases.title: Locate a specific list item
useCases.scenario: A list contains items with unique test IDs.

interview.question: What does page.getByTestId do?
interview.answer: getByTestId locates an element using its test ID and returns a Locator. It accepts a string or a regular expression.
interview.followUp: When should you prefer another locator? Prefer getByRole or getByText when the element's accessible role or visible text is part of the behavior being tested.

interview.question: Which attribute does getByTestId use by default?
interview.answer: The default test ID attribute is data-testid. The locator matches the supplied test ID value.
interview.followUp: How can a project use data-pw instead? Set testIdAttribute to data-pw in the Playwright test configuration.

interview.question: How do you use a custom test ID attribute?
interview.answer: Configure the testIdAttribute option in the Playwright test configuration. After that, getByTestId uses the configured attribute instead of data-testid.
interview.followUp: What should the HTML contain after this change? The target element should use the configured attribute, for example data-pw="directions".

keyPoints: Use getByTestId when an element has an explicit test ID.
The testId argument can be a string or a regular expression.
A project can replace the default test ID attribute with a custom one.
Use the method for list items when the markup provides test IDs for those items.
gotchas: The default attribute is data-testid. Configure a different test ID attribute when the application uses another attribute.
A test ID is stable, but it does not describe how a user finds the element. Prefer role or text locators when those user-facing properties matter.

page.getByText.summary: page.getByText locates elements using their text. It supports substring matching, exact matching, and regular expressions.
page.getByText.explanation: page.getByText creates a Locator for elements that contain the given text. It can use a text string or regular expression. By default, matching can use a substring; set exact to true for a case-sensitive whole-string match.

parameters.name: text
parameters.description: Text or pattern used to find the element. A string or regular expression is accepted.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Optional settings for text matching.

parameters.name: options.Exact
parameters.description: When true, require a case-sensitive whole-string match. It is ignored for regular expressions.

example.title: Find and click text
example.code:
const locator = page.getByText('Submit');
await locator.click();
example.explanation: This finds an element containing the text "Submit" and clicks it.

useCases.title: Find text content
useCases.scenario: A page has a button or message with a known label.

useCases.title: Narrow a text match
useCases.scenario: Several elements contain similar words, but one must match exactly.

useCases.title: Use a regular expression
useCases.scenario: The text changes in a predictable pattern.

interview.question: What does page.getByText do?
interview.answer: getByText returns a Locator for elements containing specified text. The text can be a string or regular expression, and the exact option can request a case-sensitive whole-string match.
interview.followUp: How does exact matching treat whitespace? It still trims and normalizes whitespace, so exact does not preserve spacing or line breaks.

interview.question: How can you request an exact text match?
interview.answer: A string normally matches text contained within an element. With exact set to true, Playwright looks for a whole-string, case-sensitive match unless the locator uses a regular expression.
interview.followUp: What happens with a regular expression? The exact option is ignored, so matching behavior comes from the expression itself.

interview.question: How are button and submit inputs matched?
interview.answer: For input elements whose type is button or submit, Playwright compares the value instead of the element's text content. This lets text lookup find controls such as an input with value "Log in".
interview.followUp: How can you narrow a text match using another property? Use Locator.filter, for example by filtering a role-based locator.

keyPoints: Use getByText to create a locator from visible element text.
A string can match a substring, exact text can be requested, or a regular expression can define the match.
The exact option requires case-sensitive matching of the whole string.
The exact option defaults to false and has no effect when the locator uses a regular expression.
gotchas: Whitespace is normalized before text matching. Line breaks and repeated spaces do not stay significant.
For button and submit inputs, matching uses the value attribute rather than text content.

page.getByTitle.summary: `page.getByTitle()` finds elements by their `title` attribute. It returns a Locator that can be used for actions and assertions.
page.getByTitle.explanation: `page.getByTitle()` returns a locator for an element with a matching `title` attribute. By default, the text may match part of the title. Set `exact: true` to require a case-sensitive, whole-string match.

parameters.name: text
parameters.description: Text or pattern used to match the element's `title` attribute.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Optional matching settings.

parameters.name: options.exact
parameters.description: Require a case-sensitive, whole-string match when using a string.

example.title: Find an element by title
example.code: await expect(page.getByTitle('Issues count')).toHaveText('25 issues');
example.explanation: This finds the element whose title attribute matches the text and checks its visible text.

useCases.title: Find an element by its title
useCases.scenario: A page uses a title attribute to identify an element, such as a count or help label.

useCases.title: Require an exact title match
useCases.scenario: Several title values contain similar text, but one complete value must be selected.

useCases.title: Match a title with a regular expression
useCases.scenario: The title value follows a pattern instead of being fixed text.

interview.question: What does `page.getByTitle()` do?
interview.answer: `getByTitle()` creates a locator for an element by its `title` attribute. It accepts a string or regular expression and returns a Locator.
interview.followUp: How do you require an exact title? Use the options object: `page.getByTitle('Issues count', { exact: true })`.

interview.question: What is the default matching behavior?
interview.answer: The default string match is not exact. It can match a title containing the requested text, without requiring the whole value to be identical.
interview.followUp: What happens with a regular expression? The `exact` option is ignored, so the regular expression controls the match.

interview.question: When is this locator useful?
interview.answer: Use `getByTitle()` when the target element has a useful `title` attribute. The returned locator can then be used for actions or assertions.
interview.followUp: How can you verify the located element? Pass the locator to an assertion such as `expect(locator).toHaveText(...)`.

keyPoints: The method locates elements through their `title` attribute.
Playwright added this method in version 1.27.
The locator text can be a string or a regular expression.
gotchas: The default is a partial match. Use `exact: true` when the complete title must match.
`exact` does not affect regular-expression matching, and exact text matching still removes surrounding whitespace.

page.goBack.summary: Moves the page to the previous browser-history entry. It returns the main navigation response, or null when no previous entry exists.
page.goBack.explanation: Call `page.goBack()` to move to the previous page in the browser history. The promise resolves to the main resource response, or `null` when there is no previous page. Options can control the timeout and when navigation is considered complete.

parameters.name: signal
parameters.description: Cancels the operation when the signal is aborted. It does not remove the default timeout.

parameters.name: timeout
parameters.description: Maximum operation time in milliseconds. Use 0 to disable it.

parameters.name: waitUntil
parameters.description: Navigation state that marks completion. Defaults to `load`.

example.title: Go back in page history
example.code:
const response = await page.goBack({ waitUntil: 'domcontentloaded' });
if (response) console.log(response.status());
example.explanation: Moves to the previous history entry and optionally returns its main resource response.

useCases.title: Check back navigation
useCases.scenario: Test a browser back action after visiting another page.

useCases.title: Restore the previous page
useCases.scenario: Return to the prior page after a workflow step.

useCases.title: Read the navigation response
useCases.scenario: Inspect the HTTP response produced by back navigation.

interview.question: What does `page.goBack()` do and what does it return?
interview.answer: It navigates to the previous entry in the page history. It returns the main resource response, or `null` if the page cannot go back.
interview.followUp: What does `waitUntil` control? It selects the event or navigation point that marks the operation as complete, such as `load`, `domcontentloaded`, or `commit`.

interview.question: Which `waitUntil` values can be used?
interview.answer: The default completion state is `load`. Other choices include `domcontentloaded`, `networkidle`, and `commit`.
interview.followUp: Which option is discouraged for tests? `networkidle`, because readiness should be checked with web assertions.

interview.question: How can you control the operation timeout?
interview.answer: The `timeout` option sets the maximum operation time in milliseconds. A value of `0` disables the timeout for this operation.
interview.followUp: Which setting takes priority for navigation methods? `page.setDefaultNavigationTimeout()` takes priority over the general default timeout settings.

keyPoints: The method changes the page to the previous browser-history entry.
The result is the response for the navigation's main resource.
If navigation redirects more than once, the returned response represents the final redirect.
The result is `null` when there is no previous history entry.
The documentation lists this method as available before Playwright version 1.9.
gotchas: Do not use this method to test a BFCache restore. It can time out and leave the Page state out of sync.
Avoid `networkidle` for test readiness. Use web assertions instead.

page.goForward.summary: Moves a page to the next entry in its browser history. It returns the navigation response, or `None` when no forward entry exists.
page.goForward.explanation: `page.go_forward()` moves the page to the next entry in its browser history. It waits for the selected navigation event and returns the main resource response when navigation occurs. It returns `None` when there is no later history entry.

parameters.name: timeout
parameters.description: Maximum operation time in milliseconds. Use 0 to disable the timeout.

parameters.name: wait_until
parameters.description: Navigation event that marks completion: `load`, `domcontentloaded`, `networkidle`, or `commit`.

page.goForward.returns: `Response | None`. It returns the main resource response, or `None` when forward navigation is not possible.

example.title: Move forward in page history
example.code:
from playwright.sync_api import sync_playwright

with sync_playwright() as p:
    browser = p.chromium.launch()
    page = browser.new_page()
    page.goto("https://example.com")
    page.go_forward()
    browser.close()
example.explanation: This opens a page, then tries to move to the next entry in that page's history.
