useCases.scenario: A test navigates back to an earlier page and must restore the next history entry.

useCases.title: Controlled navigation waiting
useCases.scenario: A test needs to wait for a chosen navigation event after moving forward.

useCases.title: Detecting missing history
useCases.scenario: A script checks whether forward history exists before continuing.

interview.question: What does `page.go_forward()` do and what does it return?
interview.answer: It navigates to the next page in the page's history. It returns the main resource response, or `None` if forward navigation is not possible.
interview.followUp: What happens after redirects? The returned response represents the final navigation after the redirects.

interview.question: Which `wait_until` values can control completion?
interview.answer: The default is `load`. Other choices are `domcontentloaded`, `networkidle`, and `commit`. The timeout is measured in milliseconds and defaults to 30 seconds.
interview.followUp: Which option is discouraged for tests? `networkidle`, because a quiet network does not reliably prove that the page is ready.

interview.question: Why is BFCache a problem with `go_forward()`?
interview.answer: The method cannot reliably test a BFCache restore. Playwright disables BFCache by default, and a restore does not produce the network navigation events that Playwright needs.
interview.followUp: What can happen if BFCache is used anyway? The call can time out and the Page object can become desynchronized.

keyPoints: A successful forward navigation returns the response for the main resource.
When the history has no later entry, the method returns `None`.
The method moves the current page to the next browser-history entry.
The operation timeout uses milliseconds and is 30 seconds by default.
Use `wait_until` to choose which navigation event marks completion; `load` is the default.
You can change the default timeout with page or browser-context timeout settings.
gotchas: Do not use this method to test a BFCache restore. Playwright may time out and its page state may become out of sync.
Avoid `networkidle` for test readiness. Use web assertions instead.

page.goto.summary: `page.goto()` navigates a Playwright page to a URL. It waits for a chosen navigation event and returns the main resource response when available.
page.goto.explanation: `page.goto()` navigates the current Playwright page to a URL. It waits until the selected navigation state is reached and returns the main resource response when one exists. It can fail for invalid URLs, SSL errors, unreachable servers, navigation timeouts, or failed main resources.

parameters.name: url
parameters.description: URL to navigate the page to. Include a scheme, such as `https://`.

parameters.name: referer
parameters.description: Optional Referer header value. It overrides the page extra header value.

parameters.name: timeout
parameters.description: Optional maximum navigation time in milliseconds. Defaults to 30 seconds; use 0 to disable it.

parameters.name: wait_until
parameters.description: Optional event that marks navigation completion: `load`, `domcontentloaded`, `networkidle`, or `commit`.

page.goto.returns: `Response | None`. Returns the main resource response, or `None` for `about:blank` and same-URL hash navigation.

example.title: Navigate to a page
example.code:
from playwright.sync_api import sync_playwright

with sync_playwright() as p:
    browser = p.chromium.launch()
    page = browser.new_page()
    page.goto("https://example.com", wait_until="domcontentloaded")
    print(page.title())
    browser.close()
example.explanation: This opens a browser page, navigates to a URL, waits for the DOM to load, and reads the page title.

useCases.title: Start page navigation
useCases.scenario: Open a website before interacting with its elements.

useCases.title: Choose a navigation wait state
useCases.scenario: Load a page and wait for the DOM before reading or testing content.

useCases.title: Inspect the response status
useCases.scenario: Check the server result after navigation.

interview.question: What does `page.goto()` return?
interview.answer: `page.goto(url)` navigates the current page and returns the main resource response. With redirects, the returned response is the first non-redirect response.
interview.followUp: What happens for a 404 response? `goto()` does not throw only because of the status code; inspect `response.status` instead.

interview.question: When does navigation finish?
interview.answer: The default `wait_until` value is `load`. Other supported values are `domcontentloaded`, `networkidle`, and `commit`.
interview.followUp: Which option is discouraged for tests? `networkidle`, because modern pages can keep background activity and assertions are a better readiness check.

interview.question: What important arguments does `goto()` accept?
interview.answer: The URL should include a scheme such as `https://`. A context `base_url` can resolve a path passed to `goto()`. The default timeout is 30 seconds, and `0` disables it.
interview.followUp: Which timeout setting has priority? The page navigation timeout takes priority over the general page and context timeouts.

keyPoints: The method returns the main resource response, using the first non-redirect response after redirects.
Navigation fails for SSL problems, invalid URLs, timeouts, unreachable servers, or a failed main resource.
`wait_until` can wait for `domcontentloaded`, `load`, `networkidle`, or `commit`.
Pass a URL with a scheme, such as `https://example.com`.
The navigation timeout defaults to 30 seconds. Pass `0` to disable the timeout.
A relative path can be resolved against the context's `base_url`.
gotchas: An HTTP error status such as 404 or 500 does not make `goto()` fail. Check the returned response status when you need to validate the server result.
Most successful navigations return a response, but `about:blank` and same-page hash changes return `None`.
Do not use headless `goto()` to open a PDF document.
Avoid `networkidle` as a test-readiness signal. Use web assertions instead.

page.hover.summary: Hovers over the first element that matches a selector. Playwright waits for it to be ready, scrolls it into view, and moves the mouse over it. Use locator.hover() for new code.
page.hover.explanation: `page.hover()` finds the first element that matches a CSS selector, waits for it to be ready, scrolls it into view, and moves the mouse over it. Use `locator.hover()` instead for new code because the page method is discouraged.

parameters.name: selector
parameters.description: A selector to search for an element. If several elements match, the first is used.

parameters.name: force
parameters.description: Skip actionability checks when true. Defaults to false.

parameters.name: modifiers
parameters.description: Modifier keys to press during the operation.

parameters.name: position
parameters.description: A point relative to the top-left of the element padding box.

parameters.name: scroll
parameters.description: Controls whether the element is scrolled into view. Defaults to "auto".

parameters.name: timeout
parameters.description: Maximum operation time in milliseconds. Defaults to 30000.

example.title: Hover over a link
example.explanation: This test opens a page and hovers over a link by using its role and accessible name.

useCases.title: Show a tooltip
useCases.scenario: A tooltip appears when the pointer rests on an element.

useCases.title: Open a hover menu
useCases.scenario: A menu opens when the pointer moves over a navigation item.

useCases.title: Test pointer interaction
useCases.scenario: A test checks that an element can be reached and hovered.

interview.question: What does `page.hover()` do?
interview.answer: It hovers over the first element matched by a selector. Playwright waits for the element to be attached, checks actionability, scrolls it into view, and moves the mouse over it.
interview.followUp: What should new code use instead? Use a locator, such as `page.getByRole('link').hover()`, because the page method is discouraged.

interview.question: How can actionability checks be controlled?
interview.answer: By default, Playwright performs actionability checks before hovering. The `force` option bypasses those checks.
interview.followUp: What happens if the element is detached during the checks? Playwright retries the whole action.

interview.question: How can the hover point and scrolling behavior be changed?
interview.answer: The `position` option gives an `x` and `y` point relative to the top-left of the element's padding box. Without it, Playwright uses a visible point.
interview.followUp: How can scrolling be prevented? Set `scroll` to `"none"`; the action then fails if the element is not already in the viewport.

keyPoints: The method finds the matching element and performs the hover action.
It waits for actionability checks unless `force` is enabled.
Playwright scrolls the element into view when needed.
The mouse moves to the element's center or to the requested position.
gotchas: Prefer `locator.hover()` for new code. The page method is discouraged.
A selector that matches several elements uses only the first match.
A timeout of `0` removes the timeout limit.

page.localStorage.summary: WebStorage provides asynchronous access to localStorage or sessionStorage for the current page origin. Use it through page.localStorage or page.sessionStorage.
page.localStorage.explanation: WebStorage gives asynchronous access to the current page origin's localStorage or sessionStorage. Use the storage object from page.localStorage or page.sessionStorage to read, write, list, remove, or clear entries.
page.localStorage.syntax:
page.localStorage.setItem(name, value)
page.localStorage.getItem(name)
page.localStorage.items()
page.localStorage.removeItem(name)
page.localStorage.clear()

parameters.name: name
parameters.description: Name of the item to retrieve.

parameters.name: name
parameters.description: Name of the item to set.

parameters.name: value
parameters.description: New value for the item.

parameters.name: name
parameters.description: Name of the item to remove.

page.localStorage.returns: The methods return Promise values in JavaScript: clear(), removeItem(), and setItem() return Promise<void>; getItem() returns Promise<null | string>; items() returns Promise<Array<Object>>.

example.title: Use page localStorage
example.explanation: This stores a token for the page origin, reads it, lists stored entries, deletes the token, and then removes all remaining entries.

useCases.title: Set page storage data
useCases.scenario: Save a value needed by later page actions, such as a test token.

useCases.title: Read or inspect storage
useCases.scenario: Check stored state during a test.

useCases.scenario: Reset browser storage between test steps.

interview.question: What does WebStorage expose?
interview.answer: WebStorage provides asynchronous access to localStorage or sessionStorage for the current origin. In JavaScript, obtain it from page.localStorage or page.sessionStorage.
interview.followUp: How can you inspect every stored entry? Call items(), which returns an array of name/value objects.

interview.question: What does setItem do when the name already exists?
interview.answer: setItem(name, value) writes a string value under a name. If that name already exists, the new value replaces the old one.
interview.followUp: What type must the value have? The documented JavaScript API requires a string.

interview.question: What does getItem return for a missing name?
interview.answer: getItem(name) returns the stored string when the name exists. If it is not present, it returns null.
interview.followUp: How do you remove all entries? Call clear(), which removes every item from the storage.

keyPoints: It can work with either localStorage or sessionStorage.
JavaScript exposes these storage objects directly on the Page instance.
Use items() to receive every entry as name/value objects.
setItem() replaces an existing value with the same name.
removeItem() deletes one named entry.
clear() empties the selected storage.
gotchas: Removing a missing item does not cause an error.

page.locator.summary: A Playwright Locator describes how to find page elements. It supports actions and queries with auto-waiting and retrying.
page.locator.explanation: `page.locator()` creates a Locator that finds matching elements when an action runs. Locators support auto-waiting and retrying. The locator is resolved again as the page changes, so actions can use the current matching element.

parameters.name: selector
parameters.description: A CSS selector used by `page.locator()` to find elements.

parameters.name: type
parameters.description: Optional event type, such as `click` or `dragstart`, for `dispatch_event()`.

parameters.name: timeout
parameters.description: Optional maximum wait time in milliseconds for locator actions. The default is 30000 in the Python API.

page.locator.returns: A Locator object for locator creation. Individual methods return values documented by the method, such as a list of Locators, a count, text arrays, or None.

example.title: Click a button with a locator
example.code:
from playwright.sync_api import sync_playwright

with sync_playwright() as p:
    browser = p.chromium.launch()
    page = browser.new_page()
    page.goto("https://example.com")
    page.get_by_role("button", name="Start").click()
    browser.close()
example.explanation: This creates a locator for a button with the accessible name Start, then clicks it.

useCases.scenario: Find and interact with a control by its semantic role and accessible name.

useCases.title: Inspect element collections
useCases.scenario: Read or assert values from several matching elements.

useCases.title: Work with dynamic pages
useCases.scenario: Handle controls that appear after page updates.

useCases.title: Dispatch browser events
useCases.scenario: Send a DOM event directly to a matching element.

interview.question: What is a Playwright Locator?
interview.answer: A Locator describes how to find an element. It is resolved when an action or query runs, and Playwright can wait and retry while the page changes.
interview.followUp: Why can `locator.all()` be flaky? It does not wait for matches, so a changing list can produce an incomplete or unstable set.

interview.question: How can you create an accessible locator?
interview.answer: `get_by_role()` finds elements by ARIA role and accessible name. It can use implicit HTML roles, such as a button element's button role.
interview.followUp: Does a role locator replace accessibility testing? No. The documentation says it provides early feedback but does not replace accessibility audits or conformance tests.

interview.question: What does Locator.click() do before clicking?
interview.answer: `click()` waits for actionability checks, scrolls the element into view, clicks it, and waits for initiated navigation unless that wait is disabled. It throws if the element detaches or the timeout is exceeded.
interview.followUp: When might `force` be used? It bypasses actionability checks, but normal checks are safer because they verify that the user can interact with the element.

keyPoints: A locator is a reusable description of one or more page elements.
`and_()` combines two locators. The result must satisfy both locator conditions.
Use `count()` to read how many elements currently match a locator.
`clear()` removes the current value from an input, textarea, or contenteditable element and sends an input event.
`check()` makes sure a checkbox or radio control is checked and verifies the final state.
`dispatch_event()` sends a DOM event even when the element is not visible.
gotchas: Do not use `all()` while a list is still changing. It returns the elements present immediately.
For text assertions, use the matching Playwright assertion instead of reading all text first.
`bounding_box()` can return no box when the element is not visible. Check the result before using its coordinates.

interview.question: What does `page.reload()` do and what does it return?
interview.answer: It refreshes the current page and returns the main resource response. If redirects occur, the response represents the last redirect.
interview.followUp: What happens after a History API URL change? `reload()` is not the method for waiting on that change; use URL waiting when an action changes the URL without a document reload.

interview.question: Which `wait_until` values can control when reload finishes?
interview.answer: The default wait state is `load`. Other choices are `domcontentloaded`, `networkidle`, and `commit`.

page.route.summary: page.route() intercepts matching network requests. A handler can modify, mock, or block each request.
page.route.explanation: page.route() adds a handler between the page and the browser network stack. Matching requests pause until the handler continues them, supplies a response, or aborts them. The handler can inspect the request and change its URL, method, headers, or body before sending it.

interview.question: What does page.route() do?
interview.answer: page.route() registers a handler for requests matching a URL pattern. The handler can continue the request, return a mock response, or abort it.
interview.followUp: How can you change a request before sending it? Use route.continue_() with options such as headers, method, post data, or URL. The new URL must use the same protocol.

interview.question: How do you mock or modify a response?
interview.answer: Use route.fulfill() to answer without contacting the network. Use route.fetch() when you need the real response first, then pass that response to fulfill() after changing it.
interview.followUp: Which response fields can you change? You can override fields such as the body, status, and headers while preserving other fields from the fetched response.

interview.question: How are multiple routes selected?
interview.answer: A page route has priority over a browser-context route when both match. If several routes match, the most recently registered route takes precedence.
interview.followUp: How can a handler let another matching handler run? Use route.fallback(). route.continue_() sends the request immediately and skips other matching handlers.

keyPoints: Use page.route() to inspect and change requests made by one page.
The handler can inspect route.request() and choose whether to continue, fulfill, or abort.
The newest matching page route runs first.
A page route wins when both a page route and a context route match.
Turning on routing disables the browser HTTP cache.
For a redirect, the handler is called only for the first URL.
gotchas: Service Workers can hide requests from page.route(). Set service_workers to "block" when using request interception.
A route handler must finish every matching request with continue_, fulfill, or abort.
Use browser_context.route() when the first request of a popup must be intercepted.

page.screenshot.summary: Playwright can capture the visible page, the full scrollable page, or one element. Save the image to a file or receive its bytes in memory.
page.screenshot.explanation: Call `page.screenshot()` to capture the current page. Pass a path to save the image, or omit it to receive image data in memory. Set `fullPage` to capture the whole scrollable page, and call `locator.screenshot()` for one element.
page.screenshot.syntax:
await page.screenshot({ path: 'screenshot.png', fullPage: true });
await page.locator('.header').screenshot({ path: 'header.png' });

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: The output file path, or screenshot options such as full-page capture, image format, clipping, and quality.

parameters.name: locator
parameters.description: A locator identifying the element to capture when using `locator.screenshot()`.

page.screenshot.returns: A screenshot buffer when no output path is supplied; otherwise, the image is saved to the specified path.

example.title: Save page and element screenshots
example.explanation: This test saves a full-page image and a separate image of the h1 element.

useCases.title: Page evidence
useCases.scenario: Save a visual record of a page during a test.

useCases.title: Full-page capture
useCases.scenario: Include content that extends below the viewport.

useCases.title: Element capture
useCases.scenario: Create a focused image for a component or visual comparison.

useCases.title: In-memory processing
useCases.scenario: Send image bytes to another processor instead of creating a file.

interview.question: How do you take a full-page screenshot?
interview.answer: Use `page.screenshot({ path: 'screenshot.png' })` to save the current page image. Add `fullPage: true` to include the entire scrollable page.
interview.followUp: How can you capture only one element? Call `locator.screenshot({ path: 'screenshot.png' })` on the target locator.

interview.question: How do you capture a screenshot in memory?
interview.answer: Call `page.screenshot()` without a path. It returns a buffer that can be processed or passed to an image comparison tool.
interview.followUp: How can the returned data be logged as text? Encode the buffer as Base64 before logging it.

interview.question: How do you screenshot one element?
interview.answer: Use a locator for the element and call its `screenshot()` method. For example, `page.locator('.header').screenshot({ path: 'screenshot.png' })` saves an image of that element.
interview.followUp: What can screenshot options control? The API also supports settings such as image format, clipping, and quality.

keyPoints: Use `page.screenshot()` with a `path` option to save a screenshot file.
Set `fullPage: true` when the image must include content across the page's complete scrollable area.
Omit the output path to receive image data in a buffer for later processing.
Use `locator.screenshot()` when the target is one element rather than the whole page.
Screenshot options include controls for image format, a clipped region, and image quality.
gotchas: Without a path, the screenshot is returned as image data instead of being written to a file.

page.selectOption.summary: selectOption selects one or more options in a <select> element. Prefer locator.selectOption() for new code.
page.selectOption.explanation: selectOption waits for the matching control and for the requested options to exist. It checks that the target is a select control, selects matching options, and then triggers input and change events. A locator is the recommended way to call it.

parameters.name: selector
parameters.description: CSS or other selector used to find the target element. The page method uses the first matching element.

parameters.name: values
parameters.type: null | string | ElementHandle | Array<string> | Object | Array<ElementHandle> | Array<Object>
parameters.description: Option text, option value, an option object, or an array of these. An object can specify value, label, or index.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Optional settings, including force to bypass actionability checks.

page.selectOption.returns: Promise<string[]> containing the values of the successfully selected options.

example.title: Select an option with a locator
example.explanation: This test opens a page and selects the option whose label is Blue.

useCases.title: Single selection
useCases.scenario: Choose one item in a standard HTML select control.

useCases.title: Multiple selection
useCases.scenario: Set several choices in a select element with the multiple attribute.

useCases.title: Label-based selection
useCases.scenario: Select by visible label when option values are not convenient.

interview.question: What does selectOption do?
interview.answer: It selects one or more options in a select element. It waits for the element, actionability checks, and the requested options before selecting them, then fires input and change events.
interview.followUp: What happens with a multiple select? Every matching requested option is selected. Without the multiple attribute, only the first matching option is selected.

interview.question: How can an option be identified?
interview.answer: The option can be identified by a string, value, label, or index. An option object may include value, label, or index, and all supplied properties must match.
interview.followUp: Can several options be selected? Yes, pass an array of strings or option objects when the select allows multiple values.

interview.question: Which API should new code use?
interview.answer: Use locator.selectOption() for new code. The page.selectOption(selector, values) method is marked discouraged in the documentation.
interview.followUp: Why prefer a locator? It provides a locator-based target and avoids relying on the older page-level selector API.

keyPoints: The operation waits for the target and for it to pass actionability checks.
It also waits until every requested option is available.
The result is an array containing the values that were selected.
After selection finishes, Playwright triggers input and change once.
A multiple select can receive all matching options from the request.
gotchas: The target must be a select element. A non-select target causes an error.
With the page method, a selector matching several elements uses only the first one.
A string can match either an option's value or its visible label.

page.setViewportSize.summary: Sets the viewport size for one Playwright page. Width and height are given in pixels.
page.setViewportSize.explanation: setViewportSize changes the viewport of one page. Set it before navigation when possible because some sites do not expect the device size to change. The method also resets the screen size; use context options when you need separate control of screen and viewport dimensions.

parameters.name: width
parameters.description: Page width in pixels.

parameters.name: height
parameters.description: Page height in pixels.

example.title: Set a page viewport
example.explanation: This test creates a context with one viewport, then changes the viewport for its page before navigation.

useCases.title: Check layouts at different viewport sizes
useCases.scenario: Responsive UI tests

useCases.title: Resize a page to a phone-like viewport
useCases.scenario: Mobile-style testing

useCases.title: Use a different viewport for one page in a shared browser
useCases.scenario: Page-specific settings

interview.question: What is the scope of page.setViewportSize()?
interview.answer: setViewportSize changes the viewport for one page. A browser context can set a viewport for all pages created in that context.
interview.followUp: How would you use different sizes in one test? Create separate pages or contexts, then call setViewportSize on each page as needed.

interview.question: What arguments does setViewportSize accept?
interview.answer: Pass the width and height as pixel values: page.setViewportSize(width, height). The method returns void.
interview.followUp: Where can you set a viewport before creating a page? Use Browser.newContext with a viewport size so the setting applies when pages are created.

interview.question: When should you call setViewportSize?
interview.answer: Set the viewport before navigation when possible. Resizing after navigation can change the device size unexpectedly for sites that do not expect it.
interview.followUp: What if screen size and viewport size need independent values? Configure both with Browser.newContext options instead of relying only on the page method.

keyPoints: Each page can have its own viewport size, even when several pages share one browser.
Use Browser.newContext to apply one viewport setting to every page in a context.
The method resizes the page viewport.
The width argument is measured in pixels.
The height argument is measured in pixels.
gotchas: Set the viewport before navigation when testing a phone-sized page, because some sites do not expect the viewport to change.
Changing the page viewport also resets the screen size. Use browser context settings if you need finer control.

page.title.summary: `page.title()` returns the current page's document title as a string. It takes no arguments.
page.title.explanation: `page.title()` reads the current document title and returns it as a string. In asynchronous Playwright code, wait for the returned promise before using the title.

example.title: Read a page title
example.explanation: This test opens a page, reads its document title, and checks the returned string.

useCases.title: Verify navigation
useCases.scenario: Check that navigation reached the expected document.

useCases.title: Capture the title
useCases.scenario: Read a page title for logging or test data.

useCases.title: Test the tab title
useCases.scenario: Assert the browser tab title in an end-to-end test.

interview.question: What does `page.title()` return?
interview.answer: It returns the current page's document title as a string. In asynchronous code, it returns a promise that must be awaited.
interview.followUp: How would you verify the title? Navigate to the page, call `await page.title()`, and compare the result with the expected string.

interview.question: What are the signature and return type?
interview.answer: The method takes no arguments. Its result is the page title, represented as `str` in Python and `Promise<string>` in JavaScript or TypeScript.
interview.followUp: What should you do if the title is generated after navigation? Wait for the page to reach the required state before reading it.

interview.question: When should you call `page.title()`?
interview.answer: Call it on a `Page` object after creating or receiving that page. The method reads the title of the document currently loaded in that page.
interview.followUp: Can one browser use several page titles? Yes. Each `Page` has its own document and its own title result.

keyPoints: The method reads the title of the document in the current page.
Call it without arguments: `page.title()`.
In JavaScript or TypeScript, await the promise before using the result.

page.type.summary: Locator.drop() tests external drag-and-drop without a real mouse drag. It can send files or clipboard-like data to an element, making it useful for upload zones.
page.type.explanation: Locator.drop() simulates an external drag-and-drop action. It sends dragenter, dragover, and drop events with synthetic DataTransfer data in the page. You can provide files or clipboard-like text data, and the API works across browsers.

parameters.name: files
parameters.type: file payload or list of file payloads
parameters.description: The files to include in the synthetic drop, with file name, MIME type, and byte buffer.

parameters.name: data
parameters.description: Clipboard-like content keyed by MIME type, such as text/plain or text/uri-list.

page.type.returns: No return value is described in the release notes.

example.title: Drop a file on an upload zone
example.explanation: This sends a synthetic file drop to the element selected by the locator.

useCases.title: Upload drop zones
useCases.scenario: Test a file upload area by dropping synthetic file content onto its target.

useCases.title: Clipboard-like drops
useCases.scenario: Test an editor or list that accepts dropped text or links.

useCases.title: Drop event handling
useCases.scenario: Verify dragenter, dragover, and drop handlers without relying on pointer movement.

interview.question: What does Locator.drop() do?
interview.answer: Locator.drop() simulates an external drag-and-drop operation on the matched element. It dispatches dragenter, dragover, and drop events using synthetic DataTransfer data.
interview.followUp: How can it test an upload area? Pass a file object with a name, MIME type, and buffer, then assert the page handled the drop.

interview.question: What kinds of data can a drop contain?
interview.answer: The files form supplies file content for the drop. The data form supplies clipboard-like values such as text/plain or text/uri-list.
interview.followUp: Why might text/uri-list be useful? An application can use it to test dropping links without creating a local file.

interview.question: Why is this useful in tests?
interview.answer: The release notes describe the API as cross-browser and useful for upload zones. A test can therefore exercise the page's drop handlers without a real mouse drag.
interview.followUp: What should be asserted after the drop? Check the application result, such as an uploaded file name, validation message, or updated list.

keyPoints: Call drop() on the locator for the drop target.
The page receives the main drag-and-drop events through a synthetic DataTransfer object.
The API is intended for cross-browser tests, including file upload drop areas.
For a file drop, provide its name, MIME type, and byte content.
For non-file drops, provide a map of MIME types to string values.
gotchas: The action targets a locator, so choose the element that receives the drop rather than the element that starts a drag.
The transferred data is synthetic page data. It does not represent a native operating-system drag operation.

page.uncheck.summary: `page.uncheck()` makes a matching checkbox or radio input unchecked. It waits for the element when needed, performs the action, and verifies the final state.
page.uncheck.explanation: `page.uncheck()` finds a checkbox or radio input, waits for it when needed, checks that it can be acted on, and clicks it if it is currently checked. It then verifies that the element is unchecked. If the operation does not finish before the timeout, it throws a timeout error.

parameters.name: selector
parameters.description: Selector used to find the element. If several elements match, the first is used.

parameters.name: force
parameters.description: Whether to bypass actionability checks. Defaults to false.

parameters.name: noWaitAfter
parameters.description: Deprecated. Has no effect.

parameters.name: position
parameters.description: Point relative to the element's top-left padding-box corner. If omitted, Playwright chooses a visible point.

parameters.name: scroll
parameters.description: Whether to scroll automatically or not before the action. Defaults to "auto".

parameters.name: strict
parameters.description: Require the selector to match one element. Added in v1.14.

parameters.name: timeout
parameters.description: Maximum time in milliseconds. JavaScript docs default to 0; zero disables the timeout.

example.title: Uncheck a checkbox
example.code: await page.uncheck('#newsletter');
example.explanation: This finds the element with the given selector and makes sure its checkbox is unchecked.

useCases.title: Clear a form option
useCases.scenario: A test must clear an optional newsletter or notification checkbox before submitting a form.

useCases.title: Set a predictable state
useCases.scenario: A test needs to set a checkbox to a known unchecked state without knowing its current state.

useCases.title: Target a selected control
useCases.scenario: A test must interact with a checkbox selected by a CSS or other Playwright selector.

interview.question: What does `page.uncheck()` do?
interview.answer: `page.uncheck(selector)` targets the first matching element, waits for it to be attached and actionable, scrolls it into view when needed, clicks it, and verifies that it is unchecked. It throws if the target is not a checkbox or radio input.
interview.followUp: How would you make the target selection safer? Use a locator and make the locator resolve to the intended element, or enable strict selector matching where supported.

interview.question: What is the purpose of the `force` option?
interview.answer: The `force` option bypasses actionability checks. The default is `false`, so Playwright normally checks that the element can be acted on before clicking it.
interview.followUp: What is the trade-off of forcing the action? It can allow an interaction that a user could not perform, so it may hide a real UI problem.

interview.question: How does timeout handling work?
interview.answer: The timeout is the maximum time for the complete operation. In the JavaScript documentation shown, it defaults to zero, which disables the timeout, and the default can be changed with page or browser-context settings.
interview.followUp: What happens when the operation exceeds a nonzero timeout? Playwright throws a `TimeoutError`.

keyPoints: Use `page.uncheck(selector)` to make a matching checkbox or radio input unchecked.
An already-unchecked element needs no click; the method returns immediately.
Playwright performs actionability checks unless `force: true` is supplied.
If the element leaves the DOM during checks, Playwright retries the complete action.
The action scrolls the target into view when necessary.
After clicking, Playwright verifies that the element is actually unchecked.
gotchas: This method is discouraged. Prefer the locator-based `locator.uncheck()` method.
The selector must match a checkbox or radio input.
If several elements match, Playwright uses only the first unless `strict` is enabled.
`no_wait_after` is deprecated and does nothing.

page.waitForLoadState.summary: Waits until the page reaches a selected load state. The default state is load, and an already-reached state resolves immediately.
page.waitForLoadState.explanation: The method waits until the selected load state has been reached for the current page. If that state was already reached, it finishes immediately. The default state is load. The navigation must already be committed when the method is called.

parameters.name: state
parameters.description: The load state to wait for: load, domcontentloaded, or networkidle. Defaults to load.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Optional settings. The signal can cancel the wait, and timeout sets the maximum wait in milliseconds.

parameters.name: options.timeout
parameters.description: Maximum wait time in milliseconds. The default is 30,000; use 0 to disable the timeout.

example.title: Wait for the DOM to load
example.explanation: This opens a page, navigates to a URL, waits for the DOMContentLoaded state, and reads the title.

useCases.title: Wait after navigation
useCases.scenario: After an action causes navigation, wait for a specific browser load event before reading page data.

useCases.title: Prepare a popup
useCases.scenario: When a popup opens, wait for its DOMContentLoaded state before using its content.

useCases.title: Coordinate page lifecycle
useCases.scenario: Use a load-state wait only when an explicit browser lifecycle state is required.

interview.question: What does waitForLoadState do?
interview.answer: It waits for a page load state. The default state is load, but you can also choose domcontentloaded or networkidle.
interview.followUp: Which state is discouraged for tests? networkidle, because a lack of connections for 500 milliseconds is not a reliable readiness check.

interview.question: What happens if the page already reached the requested state?
interview.answer: If the current document already reached the requested state, the method resolves immediately. Otherwise, it waits until that state occurs.
interview.followUp: What condition must already be true before calling it? The navigation must have been committed.

interview.question: What timeout behavior does it have?
interview.answer: The method accepts an optional state and options object. The options can include a timeout; the default operation timeout is 30 seconds, and zero disables it.
interview.followUp: How can the default timeout be changed? Use the relevant BrowserContext or Page timeout-setting method.

keyPoints: It finishes when the requested load state is reached.
It does not wait again when the document already reached that state.
The optional state defaults to load.
domcontentloaded waits for the DOMContentLoaded event.
gotchas: Usually, do not add this method before normal actions. Playwright already waits for action readiness.
Avoid networkidle for tests. Use web assertions to check that the page is ready.
Call it after navigation has started and been committed.

page.waitForRequest.explanation: Call `page.waitForRequest()` before the action that should create the request. It returns a promise, so the action can run first; awaiting the promise then gives the matching Request object. Match by URL string, regular expression, or a predicate that checks the request.

parameters.name: urlOrPredicate
parameters.description: A URL string, regular expression, or function that receives a Request and returns a boolean or a promise for a boolean.

parameters.name: options.signal
parameters.description: Optional signal used to cancel the wait.

parameters.name: options.timeout
parameters.description: Maximum wait time in milliseconds. Defaults to 30,000; use 0 to disable the timeout.

example.title: Wait for a request
example.explanation: Start waiting before the action that sends the request. Then await the saved promise to get the matching request.

useCases.title: Check a request caused by a user action
useCases.scenario: A button starts an API call.

useCases.title: Wait for a resource during navigation
useCases.scenario: A page load sends a known asset request.

useCases.title: Match by URL and HTTP method
useCases.scenario: The URL is shared by several requests.

interview.question: What does `page.waitForRequest()` return?
interview.answer: `page.waitForRequest()` waits for a request that matches a URL string, regular expression, or predicate. It resolves with the matching `Request` object.
interview.followUp: How do you avoid missing a request? Create the wait promise before the click or navigation that triggers the request.

interview.question: How should you use it with a button click?
interview.answer: Start the wait without `await`, perform the action that sends the request, and then await the saved promise. This coordinates both operations.
interview.followUp: What if the URL is not fixed? Pass a predicate that checks properties such as `request.url()` and `request.method()`.

interview.question: Which matchers can `page.waitForRequest()` accept?
interview.answer: The URL matcher can be a string, a regular expression, or a function receiving a `Request` object. The function may return a boolean or a promise for a boolean.
interview.followUp: How can the wait be cancelled? Provide an `AbortSignal`; aborting it makes the operation throw, but the normal timeout still applies.

keyPoints: The method resolves to the request that matched the supplied condition.
You can match with a URL string, a regular expression, or a predicate.
Await the returned promise after the event-triggering action to receive the Request object.
The method was added before Playwright version 1.9.
An AbortSignal can cancel the wait and cause the operation to throw.
gotchas: Create the waiting promise before the click or other action that triggers the request. Do not await it before that action.
The wait has a 30-second default timeout. Use timeout 0 to disable it, or change the page default timeout.

page.waitForResponse.explanation: `page.waitForResponse` waits for a response that matches a URL pattern, regular expression, or predicate. Start the wait before the action that causes the request, then await the returned promise after the action. The method returns the matching `Response` object.

parameters.name: urlOrPredicate
parameters.description: A glob URL pattern, regular expression, or predicate that receives a Response object.

parameters.name: action
parameters.description: An action that causes the expected network request.

page.waitForResponse.returns: A promise that resolves to the matching `Response`.

example.title: Wait for a response after an action
example.explanation: This starts waiting before the click, then captures the response caused by the click.
