useCases.scenario: An update button sends a request and the test must inspect the returned response.

useCases.title: Match a resource request
useCases.scenario: A page loads an image or other resource and the test must wait for its URL.

useCases.title: Use a response predicate
useCases.scenario: A test must wait only for a response containing a required token or successful status.

interview.question: What does `page.waitForResponse` do?
interview.answer: It waits for a network response that matches a glob, regular expression, or predicate. The result is a `Response` object.
interview.followUp: Why should the wait start before the click? The request can happen during the click, so starting the wait afterward can miss the response.

interview.question: How can you match a specific response?
interview.answer: Use a full glob such as `**/api/fetch_data`, a regular expression such as `/\.jpeg$/`, or a predicate that checks the response URL.
interview.followUp: How can you require a successful response? Use a predicate such as `response => response.url().includes('/api/items') && response.ok()`.

interview.question: What is the usual action-and-wait pattern?
interview.answer: Call `page.waitForResponse` before the action, store its promise, perform the action, and then await the promise.
interview.followUp: What can you use when URL matching is not enough? Use a predicate that receives the `Response` object and checks properties such as its URL or status.

keyPoints: Use it when an action should trigger a particular network response.
A glob pattern is a simple way to match the response URL.
A regular expression supports response URL matching when a glob is not precise enough.
A predicate lets you inspect the response and decide whether it is the one to wait for.
gotchas: Create the response promise before the action. Awaiting it before the action can make the test wait forever.
A glob must describe the full URL. Use a regular expression for more complex matching.

page.waitForSelector.summary: `page.waitForSelector` waits for an element matched by a selector to reach a state such as visible, hidden, attached, or detached. It returns immediately when the condition is already true and throws if the timeout expires.
page.waitForSelector.explanation: The method checks a selector until the element matches the selected state. It returns at once when the condition is already true. If the condition is not met before the timeout, it throws an error. The wait also works after navigation.

parameters.name: selector
parameters.description: The selector to query for.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Optional settings. Set the desired state and timeout.

page.waitForSelector.returns: ElementHandle; returns null when waiting for hidden or detached.

example.title: Wait for an image
example.code:
Page page = context.newPage();
page.waitForSelector("img");
example.explanation: This waits for an image element to be visible before continuing.

useCases.title: Wait for an element
useCases.scenario: Wait for an image or other element to appear before reading its attributes.

useCases.title: Wait for removal
useCases.scenario: Wait for an element to disappear after an operation completes.

useCases.title: Wait across navigation
useCases.scenario: Handle a selector condition while the page navigates between URLs.

interview.question: What does page.waitForSelector do?
interview.answer: It waits for a selector to reach a requested state, such as attached, detached, visible, or hidden. It returns immediately if the selector already has that state and throws when the timeout expires.
interview.followUp: How should a new test usually wait for UI readiness? Prefer locator-based actions and web-first assertions instead of this method.

interview.question: Which options control the wait?
interview.answer: The selector is the query used to find the element. The options can set the state and timeout; the default state is visible.
interview.followUp: What does visible mean here? The element must have a non-empty bounding box and must not use visibility:hidden.

interview.question: Does the wait work across navigation?
interview.answer: The method can continue to work across page navigations. It waits for the selector on the current document until the requested state is reached or the timeout expires.
interview.followUp: What happens when waiting for hidden or detached? The method may return null rather than an element handle.

keyPoints: It finishes when the selected element reaches the requested state.
An already-satisfied condition does not cause an extra wait.
The method throws when the condition remains false until the timeout.
The wait can remain useful while the page changes to another document.
gotchas: This method is discouraged for new tests. Prefer web assertions or Locator.waitFor().
The result can be null when waiting for the hidden or detached state.

page.waitForURL.summary: `page.waitForURL()` waits for the main frame to reach a matching URL. Use it after an action that causes navigation, such as clicking a link.
page.waitForURL.explanation: Call `page.waitForURL()` when an action causes navigation and you need to wait for a particular destination. It watches the main frame and accepts a string, glob, regular expression, URL pattern, or predicate. A plain string without wildcards must exactly match the URL.

parameters.name: url
parameters.description: A glob pattern, regular expression, URL pattern, or predicate that receives the URL.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Optional settings, including an AbortSignal, timeout, and waitUntil state.

example.title: Wait for a URL after a click
example.code:
await page.getByText('Click me').click();
await page.waitForURL('**/login');
example.explanation: Click the control, then wait until the main frame URL matches the glob pattern.

useCases.title: Wait after a click
useCases.scenario: A click redirects to a known route.

useCases.title: Match with a URL pattern
useCases.scenario: A flow may redirect through different paths.

interview.question: What does `page.waitForURL()` do?
interview.answer: `page.waitForURL()` waits for the main frame to reach a matching URL. It can match a glob, regular expression, URL pattern, or predicate. A string without wildcards requires an exact URL match.
interview.followUp: What happens if the click can lead to several destinations? Use a specific URL pattern that represents the expected destination, then wait for that pattern after the action.

interview.question: Which `waitUntil` values can be used?
interview.answer: The default completion state is `load`. Other choices are `domcontentloaded`, `networkidle`, and `commit`. `commit` finishes when response headers arrive and document loading starts.
interview.followUp: Which state should usually be avoided for test readiness? `networkidle`, because the documentation discourages using it for tests; assertions are preferred.

interview.question: Why is `page.waitForNavigation()` discouraged?
interview.answer: `page.waitForNavigation()` waits for the main-frame navigation and can return the main resource response. It is deprecated because it is inherently racy, so `page.waitForURL()` is the recommended replacement.
interview.followUp: How should code wait around an indirect navigation? Click the control and then wait for the expected URL with `page.waitForURL()`.

keyPoints: The method watches navigation of the page's main frame.
The URL argument can be a glob, regular expression, URL pattern, or function that receives the URL.
A string without wildcard characters must match the complete URL exactly.
The default `waitUntil` value is `load`.
The `commit` state completes after the response is received and document loading begins.
gotchas: Do not use the deprecated `page.waitForNavigation()` for new code. The documentation recommends `page.waitForURL()` because the older method can race with the navigation.
Avoid `networkidle` for test readiness. Use web assertions instead.

playwright codegen.summary: Playwright codegen records browser interactions and generates test code. It can also create assertions, locators, emulated sessions, and reusable authenticated states.
playwright codegen.explanation: Codegen opens a browser for your actions and an Inspector that shows generated code. It records actions such as clicks and fills, and it can create assertions or locators. You can also use options to emulate devices, save login state, or load a saved state.

parameters.name: URL
parameters.description: Optional website URL to open for recording.

parameters.name: --viewport-size
parameters.description: Viewport width and height.

parameters.name: --device
parameters.description: Device name to emulate.

parameters.name: --save-storage
parameters.description: File for saving browser storage state.

parameters.name: --load-storage
parameters.description: File containing browser storage state to load.

example.title: Generate a test
example.code: playwright codegen demo.playwright.dev/todomvc
example.explanation: This opens a browser and the Playwright Inspector. Interact with the page, then copy the generated test code.

useCases.title: Record browser actions
useCases.scenario: Quickly create a first test by interacting with a website.

useCases.title: Create locators
useCases.scenario: Find a robust locator for an element.

useCases.title: Use emulation
useCases.scenario: Record behavior for a mobile device or another environment.

useCases.title: Reuse authentication
useCases.scenario: Generate more tests after logging in once.

interview.question: How do you generate a Playwright test?
interview.answer: Run the codegen command with a site URL, then interact with the browser. The Inspector displays the generated code, which you can copy into the editor.
interview.followUp: How can you record from a logged-in state? Use --save-storage to save browser state, then use --load-storage with that file in another codegen session.

interview.question: What can the test generator record?
interview.answer: Codegen records actions such as clicks and fills. It can also record visibility, text, and value assertions through the Inspector toolbar.
interview.followUp: How can you choose a locator without recording actions? Stop recording, select Pick Locator, then select an element and copy or edit the generated locator.

interview.question: How do you preserve authentication during code generation?
interview.answer: Use --save-storage to store cookies, localStorage, and IndexedDB data after a session. Use --load-storage to restore that data when generating another test.
interview.followUp: What other browser behavior can codegen emulate? It can set viewport size, device, color scheme, timezone, geolocation, and language.

keyPoints: The generator chooses locators using roles, text, and test IDs first.
When a locator matches several elements, codegen refines it to identify one target.
Use the Inspector toolbar to add assertions for page elements.
Pause recording and use Pick Locator to inspect and copy a locator.
Codegen supports recording with browser and page emulation settings.
gotchas: A saved authentication file contains sensitive data. Keep it local, add it to .gitignore, or remove it after use.
Do not use a normal browser profile for automated testing. Create a separate user data directory.

playwright show-report.summary: Run Playwright tests from the command line, choose browsers and test filters, debug with UI or Inspector modes, and inspect results in the HTML report.
playwright show-report.explanation: Use the Playwright test command to run tests. By default, configured projects run in parallel and browsers run without visible windows. Add filters such as a file path or title, or use flags for a project, headed mode, debugging, or UI mode. After a run, use show-report to open the HTML report.
playwright show-report.syntax:
npx playwright test [options] [test-filter ...]
npx playwright show-report [report] [options]

parameters.name: options and test-filter
parameters.description: Optional Playwright test options and test filters, such as a file, title, project, or mode flag.

parameters.name: report
parameters.description: Optional report directory. If omitted, the latest report is shown.

parameters.name: --host, --port
parameters.description: Optional host and port for serving the report.

playwright show-report.returns: Test results appear in the terminal; show-report serves the HTML report.

example.title: Run one test in headed Chromium
example.code: npx playwright test tests/todo-page.spec.ts --project=chromium --headed
example.explanation: Runs one test file for the Chromium project and shows the browser window.

useCases.title: Continuous test runs
useCases.scenario: Run the complete configured suite in the default headless mode.

useCases.title: Local browser debugging
useCases.scenario: Select a browser project and watch the browser while a test runs.

useCases.title: Focused test development
useCases.scenario: Filter by a file, line, or title while developing one test.

useCases.title: Result investigation
useCases.scenario: Review failures, steps, and attachments after execution.

interview.question: How do you run Playwright tests?
interview.answer: Use `npx playwright test` to run the configured tests. It runs in headless mode by default, and you can select a file, title, project, or line with filters and options.
interview.followUp: How would you run only Chromium tests with the browser visible? Use `npx playwright test --project=chromium --headed`.

interview.question: How do you debug a test?
interview.answer: Use `npx playwright test --ui` for interactive UI mode. Use `npx playwright test --debug` to run with the Playwright Inspector.
interview.followUp: What is another way to inspect a previous run? Use `npx playwright show-report` to open the HTML report.

interview.question: How do you inspect test results?
interview.answer: Run `npx playwright show-report` after a test run. The HTML report lets you filter by browser and result status, then inspect errors, attachments, and test steps.
interview.followUp: How can you serve a particular report on a chosen port? Pass the report directory and use `--port`, such as `npx playwright show-report playwright-report/ --port 8080`.

keyPoints: The test command supports one test file, multiple paths, or the full configured test suite.
Use `--project=chromium` or another configured project to choose the browser setup.
Add `--ui` to open the interactive test interface and review test steps.
Add `--headed` when the browser window should be visible during execution.
Use `-g` with a title pattern to select tests by their names.
gotchas: A normal run does not open a browser window. Use --headed when you need to watch the browser.
The HTML report opens automatically after failures, but successful runs require npx playwright show-report.

playwright test --trace on.summary: Playwright Trace Viewer helps you inspect recorded test traces after a script runs. It shows actions, page states, logs, network activity, errors, console output, and DOM snapshots.
playwright test --trace on.explanation: Playwright Trace Viewer lets you inspect a recorded test after it runs. You can move through actions, compare the page state before and after each action, and inspect logs, source, network activity, errors, console output, and a DOM snapshot.

example.title: Record and open a trace
example.code:
npx playwright test --trace on
npx playwright show-report
example.explanation: This records a trace for each test, then opens the HTML report where you can select the trace.

useCases.title: Debug CI failures
useCases.scenario: A test fails on CI and the failure cannot be reproduced locally.

useCases.title: Review test behavior
useCases.scenario: A developer wants to inspect each test action and the resulting page state.

useCases.title: Keep failure traces
useCases.scenario: A team wants failure evidence without storing traces from passing tests.

interview.question: How do you open a saved Playwright trace?
interview.answer: Use `npx playwright show-trace path/to/trace.zip` to open a saved trace from the command line. You can also upload the file to trace.playwright.dev.
interview.followUp: How can you inspect a trace stored in CI? Use the CLI with its remote URL, or pass the accessible trace URL to trace.playwright.dev as the `trace` query parameter.

interview.question: How should traces usually be recorded on CI?
interview.answer: Set `trace: 'on-first-retry'` in the Playwright configuration. The trace is then created when a test is retried for the first time.
interview.followUp: What setting records traces for failed tests without requiring retries? Use `trace: 'retain-on-failure'`, which removes traces from successful runs.

interview.question: What can you inspect in Trace Viewer?
interview.answer: The Actions tab shows the locator and duration for each action. The timeline and DOM snapshot let you examine how the page changed during the test.
interview.followUp: What other diagnostic data can the viewer show? It can show logs, source, network activity, errors, console output, and an interactive DOM snapshot.

keyPoints: Trace Viewer is a graphical tool for reviewing a test after execution.
A trace can be opened with the Playwright CLI or in the browser-based viewer.
Traces are especially useful for finding why a test failed in continuous integration.
The `on-first-retry` mode records only the first retry of a test.
The `on-all-retries` mode records a trace for every retry.
The `retain-on-failure` mode keeps traces only for tests that fail.
gotchas: Using `trace: 'on'` for every test can reduce performance, so it is not recommended for regular use.
When using the tracing API directly, start tracing before you create or navigate the page.
Opening a remote trace through trace.playwright.dev can be affected by CORS rules.

playwright test --ui.summary: Playwright UI Mode lets you run and debug tests through a visual interface. It supports filters, traces, locator picking, DOM snapshots, and watch mode.
playwright test --ui.explanation: The command starts Playwright UI Mode. It shows test files and lets you run one file, a test block, or one test. You can filter tests, inspect action details and DOM snapshots, review traces, and enable watch mode to rerun tests after changes.

parameters.name: filters
parameters.description: Optional test filter or selection controls are used in the UI, including text, projects, tags, and execution status.

parameters.name: --ui-host
parameters.description: Optional host interface for exposing browser-based UI Mode, such as `0.0.0.0`.

parameters.name: --ui-port
parameters.description: Optional fixed port for browser-based UI Mode.

playwright test --ui.returns: Opens Playwright UI Mode. Test results, traces, logs, and debugging views appear in the interface.

example.title: Open UI Mode
example.code: npx playwright test --ui
example.explanation: Starts Playwright UI Mode, where you can run and inspect tests.

useCases.title: Select tests interactively
useCases.scenario: You want to run only one test or a selected group from a visible test list.

useCases.title: Debug with traces
useCases.scenario: A test fails and you need to inspect each action and its DOM state.

useCases.title: Use watch mode
useCases.scenario: You are editing a test and want it to run again after each change.

useCases.title: Pick a locator
useCases.scenario: You need to discover a reliable locator for an element.

interview.question: How do you start Playwright UI Mode, and what can it do?
interview.answer: Run `npx playwright test --ui`. UI Mode lists test files and lets you run all tests, a file, a block, or one test. It also supports filtering by text, tags, projects, and status.
interview.followUp: How can you rerun a test when its source changes? Enable watch mode with the eye icon next to the test or at the top of the sidebar.

interview.question: What debugging information does UI Mode provide?
interview.answer: UI Mode provides a timeline and action details. You can move through actions, inspect DOM snapshots before and after actions, and view related console and network logs.
interview.followUp: How can you inspect a snapshot in browser developer tools? Pop the DOM snapshot out into a separate window, then open DevTools.

interview.question: How do you find and test a locator in UI Mode?
interview.answer: Use the Pick Locator control to select an element and view the locator Playwright would use. The locator can be edited in the locator playground, and the matching element is highlighted live.
interview.followUp: How can you reuse the selected locator? Use Copy Locator, then paste the result into the test.

keyPoints: UI Mode combines test execution, debugging, trace review, and watch mode in one interface.
The sidebar shows test files and lets you expand them to reach individual tests and describe blocks.
You can filter tests by text, project, tag, or whether they passed, failed, or were skipped.
Trace navigation lets you inspect what happened at each test action.
The timeline slider limits the actions whose details, console logs, and network logs are shown.
Watch mode reruns selected tests after you edit their source.
gotchas: UI Mode does not automatically run setup tests for project dependencies. Run those setup tests manually before dependent tests.
Binding UI Mode to all network interfaces can expose traces, passwords, and secrets to other machines on the network.

Reporter.summary: A Playwright Reporter is an object with optional callbacks for test-run events. Create a custom reporter by implementing needed methods and exporting the class as the default export.
Reporter.explanation: A Reporter is an object with optional methods that Playwright calls during a test run. You can observe run, test, step, output, and error events, then finish work after the run ends.
Reporter.syntax:
class MyReporter implements Reporter { onBegin(config: FullConfig, suite: Suite): void; onTestBegin(test: TestCase, result: TestResult): void; onTestEnd(test: TestCase, result: TestResult): void; onEnd(result: FullResult): void; }
export default MyReporter;

parameters.name: config
parameters.description: Resolved Playwright configuration passed to onBegin and preprocess.

parameters.name: suite
parameters.description: Root suite containing the projects, files, and tests in the run.

parameters.name: test
parameters.description: Test case that started or finished.

parameters.name: result
parameters.description: Test result. It is populated during execution and complete in onTestEnd.

Reporter.returns: Reporter callbacks may return void; onEnd, onExit, and preprocess may return a Promise. printsToStdio returns boolean.

example.title: Configure a custom reporter
example.explanation: This configuration uses the built-in list reporter and a custom reporter with one option.

useCases.title: Build a custom report
useCases.scenario: Need custom terminal or file output for test events.

useCases.title: Observe output and errors
useCases.scenario: Need to collect worker output or global errors.

useCases.title: Preprocess tests
useCases.scenario: Need to change which tests run or their expected status before sharding.

useCases.title: Upload reports
useCases.scenario: Need to upload a completed report before the process exits.

interview.question: Are all Reporter methods required?
interview.answer: All Reporter methods are optional. A custom reporter can implement only the callbacks it needs and must be exported as the default export.
interview.followUp: How can a reporter receive configuration? Define a constructor with an options object, then pass options in the reporter tuple in testConfig.reporter.

interview.question: What does onBegin receive and when does it run?
interview.answer: onBegin runs once after test discovery and receives the resolved configuration and root suite. The root suite contains the projects, files, and tests for the run.
interview.followUp: What happens with sharding? Built-in sharding is applied after preprocess unless the reporter calls testRun.skipSharding().

interview.question: What is the difference between onTestBegin and onTestEnd?
interview.answer: onTestBegin receives a test and a still-changing TestResult. onTestEnd runs after the test finishes, when the result is complete and its status, error, and other fields can be read.
interview.followUp: Which callback observes steps? onStepBegin and onStepEnd run for each executed step while the test is still running.

keyPoints: Playwright calls reporter methods for events during test execution.
onBegin runs once and receives the root suite for the discovered run.
onTestEnd receives the completed result after a test run finishes.
Use onStdOut and onStdErr to observe worker-process output.
onError handles some global errors outside normal test execution.
preprocess can change individual tests' planned status before execution.
gotchas: Errors from custom reporter methods are swallowed. Handle them yourself if reporter failures must be detected or fail the run.
Return false from printsToStdio when the reporter does not write to the terminal, so Playwright can add a standard terminal reporter.
Use onExit for final actions such as uploading reports, after all reporters have received onEnd.

Request.summary: The Request class describes a network request made by a page. Use it to inspect request data, responses, redirects, headers, bodies, timing, and failures.
Request.explanation: A Request represents one network request made by a page. Playwright exposes its URL, method, headers, body, response, redirect links, resource type, timing, and size data. You can inspect it during request events and use different methods depending on whether you need immediate or asynchronous data.

parameters.name: name
parameters.description: The header name to look up. Matching is case-insensitive.

Request.returns: The Request API returns request data through strings, objects, buffers, booleans, nullable Response/Request/Frame/Worker values, and promises for asynchronous header, response, size, and timing operations.

example.title: Log failed requests
example.explanation: This logs the URL and error text for requests reported as failed.

useCases.title: Inspect requests
useCases.scenario: Observe network traffic during a page action.

useCases.title: Debug failures
useCases.scenario: Find why a request did not complete.

useCases.title: Inspect request bodies
useCases.scenario: Check request payloads sent by forms or APIs.

useCases.title: Analyze request performance
useCases.scenario: Measure network phases and transferred bytes.

interview.question: What is the Request event lifecycle?
interview.answer: The request event is emitted when the browser issues the request. A response event follows when status and headers arrive, and requestfinished follows after the response body is downloaded. If the request fails, requestfailed replaces requestfinished and may also replace response.
interview.followUp: How should an HTTP 404 be handled? Treat it as an HTTP response that completes normally; it is not a network failure according to the request event lifecycle.

interview.question: How do response() and existingResponse() differ?
interview.answer: response() waits for the matching response and returns null when an error prevents a response. existingResponse() checks only the current state, returning the response immediately if it has arrived or null otherwise.
interview.followUp: When should existingResponse() be preferred? Use it when polling or inspecting without delaying execution; use response() when waiting for the response is required.

interview.question: How does Playwright represent redirects?
interview.answer: A redirect finishes the original Request and causes the browser to issue a new Request. redirectedFrom() links the new request to the previous one, while redirectedTo() links the old request to the new one.
interview.followUp: How can a complete redirect chain be found? Start with the final request and repeatedly call redirectedFrom() until it returns null.

keyPoints: allHeaders() returns every request header with lower-case names.
headers() omits security-related headers such as cookies; use allHeaders() when they are needed.
headersArray() keeps original header-name casing and preserves repeated header entries.
postDataJSON() parses form data into key/value data and otherwise tries JSON.
resourceType() identifies categories such as document, script, image, fetch, or websocket.
timing() provides network timing values, including lookup, connection, request, and response phases.
gotchas: A 404 or 503 is still treated as a completed request, not a failed request.
Do not always call frame() without checking. Service Worker requests and early navigation requests may have no frame.
serviceWorker() returns null outside Chromium.

Response.summary: Response represents an HTTP response received by a page. It exposes the URL, status, headers, frame, and body, and can parse the body as text, bytes, or JSON.
Response.explanation: A Response object describes an HTTP response received by a page. Use properties for basic details such as the URL, status, and success state. Use methods to read headers or the response body as bytes, text, or JSON.
Response.syntax:
response.ok()
response.status()
await response.text()
await response.json()

parameters.name: name
parameters.description: The case-insensitive header name to inspect.

Response.returns: A Response object provides synchronous status, URL, header, frame, and success information, plus asynchronous methods for body, header, security, and network details.

example.title: Read a JSON response
example.explanation: Waits for a page response, checks for a successful status, and reads its JSON body.

useCases.title: Validate a request
useCases.scenario: Check whether a page request succeeded before using its result.

useCases.title: Read response data
useCases.scenario: Inspect an API payload returned while a page is loading.

useCases.title: Inspect network details
useCases.scenario: Debug server behavior by examining status codes and headers.

interview.question: What is Playwright's Response class?
interview.answer: Response represents a response received by a page. Its status() gives the HTTP status code, and ok() is true only for status codes from 200 through 299.
interview.followUp: How would you read a JSON error body? Use await response.json(), but handle the case where the body is not valid JSON because the method throws.

interview.question: How can you inspect response headers?
interview.answer: Use response.headers() for a synchronous object whose names are lower-cased. Use await response.allHeaders() for all headers, or await response.headersArray() when original header casing and repeated entries matter.
interview.followUp: Which method is useful for several Set-Cookie values? Use headerValues('set-cookie') to get all matching values as an array.

interview.question: How do you read a response body?
interview.answer: body() returns the body as a Buffer, text() returns it as a string, and json() parses it as JSON. Each of these body-reading methods is asynchronous.
interview.followUp: What happens if json() receives invalid JSON? It throws because parsing uses JSON.parse.

keyPoints: A Response describes an HTTP response received by a page.
ok() reports success only for status codes from 200 through 299.
text() reads the response body as a string.
body() reads the response body as a Buffer.
url() returns the response URL.
frame() identifies the frame that started the response.
gotchas: json() fails when the body is not valid JSON.
headerValue() uses a newline between multiple Set-Cookie values, not a comma.
headersArray() can contain several entries with the same header name.

Route.summary: Route lets Playwright handle a network request intercepted by page.route() or browserContext.route(). It can stop, forward, modify, inspect, fetch, or fulfill the request.
Route.explanation: A Route represents a network request intercepted by page.route() or browserContext.route(). Use request() to inspect it, abort() to stop it, continue() to send it directly to the network, fallback() to let earlier matching handlers run, fetch() to obtain a response for editing, or fulfill() to provide a response.
Route.syntax:
route.abort(errorCode?)
route.continue(options?)
route.fallback(options?)
route.fetch(options?)
route.fulfill(options?)
route.request()

parameters.name: errorCode
parameters.description: Optional network error code. The default is failed.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Optional overrides for headers, method, post data, and URL. fetch() also supports redirect, retry, and timeout settings.

Route.returns: abort(), continue(), fallback(), and fulfill() return Promise<void>; fetch() returns Promise<APIResponse>; request() returns Request.

example.title: Fulfill a routed request
example.explanation: This intercepts PNG requests and returns a supplied response instead of contacting the network.

useCases.title: Abort requests
useCases.scenario: Block unwanted requests such as tracking, media, or failing resources.

useCases.title: Modify outgoing requests
useCases.scenario: Add headers or change the method or request data before the network call.

useCases.title: Create test responses
useCases.scenario: Mock an endpoint or return a local file or JSON object.

useCases.title: Edit network responses
useCases.scenario: Change a live response before the page receives it.

interview.question: What is the difference between continue() and fallback()?
interview.answer: Use continue() to send the request to the network immediately. It can override headers, method, post data, or URL, but only the headers also apply to redirects.
interview.followUp: How would you let another matching handler process the request first? Use fallback(), which continues the chain before the request is sent.

interview.question: How do you modify a real network response?
interview.answer: Use fetch() to perform the request and receive an APIResponse without completing the route. Then change the response data and call fulfill(), optionally passing the original response.
interview.followUp: How can redirect behavior differ? fetch() applies header overrides to the fetched request and its redirects, while continue() has different rules for URL, method, and post data.

interview.question: In what order do multiple matching routes run?
interview.answer: Multiple matching routes run in reverse registration order, so the newest matching route runs first. A handler can call fallback() to pass control to the next matching handler.
interview.followUp: How can handlers be separated by request type? Inspect route.request().method(), handle the desired method, and call fallback() for other methods.

keyPoints: A Route is created when page.route() or browserContext.route() intercepts a network request.
abort() stops the intercepted request and accepts an optional network error code.
continue() sends the request directly, with optional changes to headers, method, post data, or URL.
fallback() continues the request while allowing other matching route handlers to run.
fetch() obtains the network response so the response can be changed before fulfillment.
fulfill() completes the route with a custom body, file, JSON value, status, headers, or existing response.
request() returns the Request associated with the intercepted route.
gotchas: Forbidden headers such as Cookie, Host, and Content-Length cannot be changed through request overrides.
Changing a request URL does not change which registered routes match it.
Use continue() only when later matching handlers should not run; use fallback() to continue the handler chain.
fetch() follows up to 20 redirects by default, and 0 disables redirect following.

route.fulfill.summary: A Route represents a network request intercepted by Playwright. Use it to inspect the request, block it, send it onward, fetch its real response, or return a custom response.
route.fulfill.explanation: `route.fulfill()` completes an intercepted request with a response you define. You can set its status, headers, body, content type, JSON data, file path, or base response. Use `route.request()` to inspect the request. Use `route.fetch()` when you need the real response first, then fulfill the route with changes.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Response options such as `body`, `contentType`, `headers`, `json`, `path`, `response`, and `status`.

parameters.name: errorCode
parameters.description: Optional error code used when aborting. The default is `failed`.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Request and fetch overrides such as headers, method, post data, URL, timeout, redirect limit, and retry limit.

route.fulfill.returns: The documented methods return a Promise<void>, APIResponse, or Request depending on the method.

example.title: Return a custom response
example.explanation: This intercepts matching PNG requests and returns a custom 404 response instead of sending them to the network.

useCases.title: Mock an API response
useCases.scenario: Return predictable data for an API call during a test.

useCases.title: Block network traffic
useCases.scenario: Prevent images, analytics, or unwanted resources from loading.

useCases.title: Modify live responses
useCases.scenario: Change a real server response before the page receives it.

interview.question: What does `route.fulfill()` do?
interview.answer: `route.fulfill()` ends handling for the intercepted request by returning a response. Its options can define a body, status, headers, content type, JSON value, file path, or an existing API response.
interview.followUp: How would you modify a real response? Call `route.fetch()`, read or change the returned response, then pass it to `route.fulfill()` with the needed overrides.

interview.question: When would you use `route.fetch()` instead of `route.fulfill()`?
interview.answer: `route.fetch()` sends the request and returns an `APIResponse` without completing the browser route. The response can then be inspected or changed before calling `route.fulfill()`.
interview.followUp: What happens to headers supplied to `route.fetch()`? They also apply to redirects created by that fetch; use `route.continue()` when headers should apply only to the original request.

interview.question: How can you inspect or stop a routed request?
interview.answer: `route.request()` returns the `Request` object for the request currently being routed. This lets a handler inspect request details before deciding whether to abort, continue, fulfill, or use another route action.
interview.followUp: How can a handler stop the request? Call `route.abort()` and optionally provide an error code; the default is `failed`.

keyPoints: A Route object is provided to the handler created by `page.route()` or `browserContext.route()`.
`route.fulfill()` completes the request with a response you provide.
`route.fetch()` obtains the real response but leaves route completion to your code.
`route.request()` returns the request represented by the Route object.
`route.abort()` prevents the routed request from completing normally and can accept an error code.
`route.fulfill()` can serve a local file as the response body.
gotchas: A URL override must keep the original request protocol. Changing the URL also does not change which route pattern matched.
When using a file path, Playwright determines the response content type from the file extension.
If no status is supplied, the fulfilled response uses status 200.

Setup project.explanation: A setup project is a normal Playwright test project that must finish before dependent projects start. Add its name to a dependent project's dependencies array. This lets setup tests appear in reports and use Playwright fixtures. A teardown project can run after all dependent projects finish.

interview.question: How do you make one Playwright project run before another?
interview.answer: Use a project with a testMatch pattern for the setup file, then put that project name in dependencies for projects that need it. Playwright runs the dependency first and starts the dependent projects after it passes.
interview.followUp: What happens when setup fails? Projects that depend on the failed project are not run.

interview.question: Why use project dependencies instead of globalSetup?
interview.answer: Project dependencies are the recommended approach. They integrate with the test runner, show setup in the HTML report, record traces, and support fixtures.
interview.followUp: When might globalSetup be less suitable? It does not appear as a separate report project, does not support trace recording, and cannot use Playwright fixtures.

interview.question: How does Playwright schedule dependent projects?
interview.answer: Multiple projects can depend on the same setup project. The setup runs first, and after it passes, the dependent projects can run in parallel subject to the worker limit.
interview.followUp: What if there are multiple dependency projects? Playwright runs those dependencies first and in parallel; dependent projects wait for all of them.

keyPoints: A project groups tests that share configuration.
Define projects in playwright.config.ts.
Create a setup project when shared actions must happen before other projects.
A dependency project always runs before its dependent projects.
After setup passes, dependent projects normally run in parallel within the worker limit.
Set the setup project's teardown property to name a cleanup project.

Setup and teardown actions must be written as regular tests that call the test function.
A teardown project runs only after all dependent projects finish.

test.explanation: Call test with a title and an asynchronous function. Playwright runs the function with fixtures such as page. Use expect inside it for checks. You can add details such as tags, annotations, or locks. Hooks and describe groups help share setup and organize tests.

interview.question: What does test do?
interview.answer: test declares a test with a title and a body function. The body receives fixtures and can also receive TestInfo. The runner executes the body and reports its result.
interview.followUp: How can test metadata be added? Pass a details object between the title and body. It can contain tags, annotations, and locks.

interview.question: How do Playwright test hooks differ?
interview.answer: beforeEach runs before every test in its file or describe group. afterEach runs after every test. Both can use the test's fixtures and TestInfo.
interview.followUp: When should beforeAll be used? Use it for setup that should run once per worker, and pair it with afterAll for cleanup.

interview.question: How do Playwright assertions handle asynchronous pages?
interview.answer: The Playwright expect function provides generic matchers and web matchers. Web matchers retry until the condition passes or the assertion timeout is reached.
interview.followUp: How can a check continue after failure? Use expect.soft, then inspect test.info().errors when later execution should stop after soft failures.

keyPoints: Import test to declare a test and expect to check its result.
The test body receives fixtures and may receive TestInfo as a second argument.
Add tags in test details or the title. Reports and custom reporters can use them.
Use a named lock when tests access a shared resource that cannot handle concurrent use.
Use test.describe to group tests and make the group title part of each test title.
Use test.describe.configure to set mode, retries, timeout, or locks for a scope.

Avoid serial mode when possible. A failed test skips later tests in that serial group.
Import expect from Playwright. Another expect package is not fully integrated with the Playwright test runner.

test.afterAll.summary: `test.afterAll` registers cleanup that runs once per worker after the applicable tests finish. Use it for file-level or group-level teardown.
test.afterAll.explanation: Call `test.afterAll` to register cleanup code that runs once after the applicable tests finish. The hook can use worker fixtures and an optional `TestInfo` value. If several hooks exist, Playwright runs them in registration order and continues with other applicable hooks after a failure.

interview.question: When does `test.afterAll` run?
interview.answer: `test.afterAll` registers a hook that runs once per worker after the applicable tests finish. In a test file, it applies to that file; inside a group, it applies to that group.
interview.followUp: What happens if the worker fails? The worker can restart, so the hook runs again in the new worker.

interview.question: What arguments can an `afterAll` hook use?
interview.answer: The hook receives worker fixtures and may also receive `TestInfo`. You can provide a title as the first argument to identify the hook.
interview.followUp: Why use a title? It makes the hook easier to identify in reports and test output.

interview.question: How are multiple `afterAll` hooks handled?
interview.answer: Multiple `afterAll` hooks run in the order in which they were registered. Playwright still runs other applicable hooks when one hook fails.
interview.followUp: How should cleanup code be designed? Make it safe to run after partial cleanup and after worker restarts.

keyPoints: Use `test.afterAll` for setup cleanup that should happen after the applicable tests, not after each individual test.
A hook declared at file scope runs after every test in that file.
A hook inside a `test.describe` group is limited to that group's tests.
Register hooks in dependency order when one cleanup task relies on another.

gotchas: A worker restart can cause the hook to run again. Cleanup should tolerate repeated execution.

test.afterEach.explanation: test.afterEach() registers code that Playwright runs after every test in the current file or describe group. interview.question: What does test.afterEach() do?
interview.answer: test.afterEach() registers a hook that runs after each test. A hook in a file applies to tests in that file, while a hook inside test.describe() applies to tests in that group.
interview.followUp: How can the hook inspect whether a test passed? Pass TestInfo as the second argument and compare status with expectedStatus.

interview.question: What arguments can an afterEach hook receive?
interview.answer: The hook can receive fixtures in its first argument, such as page. It can also receive TestInfo as a second argument, which provides test details such as the title and status.
interview.followUp: Can a hook use the same fixtures as the test body? Yes. The documentation says afterEach can access all the same fixtures.

interview.question: Can an afterEach hook have a title?
interview.answer: You may provide either a hook function or a title followed by the hook function. The title was added in Playwright 1.38 and can identify the hook in reports and diagnostics.
interview.followUp: What happens with multiple titled hooks? They still execute in registration order, like other afterEach hooks.

A hook inside a describe group applies to tests in that group.

Other applicable hooks still run if one hook fails.

interview.question: What does test.beforeAll do?
interview.answer: test.beforeAll registers a hook that runs once per worker process before the applicable tests. At file scope it applies to the file, and inside test.describe it applies to that group.
interview.followUp: How should resources created by the hook be cleaned up? Use test.afterAll, which runs after the applicable tests finish.

interview.question: What can a beforeAll hook receive?
interview.answer: The hook can receive worker fixtures and an optional TestInfo object. This lets setup use worker-scoped resources shared by the applicable tests.
interview.followUp: Can the hook use the page fixture? No. The documentation describes its arguments as worker fixtures, unlike test bodies and beforeEach hooks.

interview.question: How are multiple beforeAll hooks ordered?
interview.answer: Multiple beforeAll hooks run in the order in which they were registered. Playwright continues running all applicable hooks even if one has failed.
interview.followUp: What happens after a worker is restarted? The beforeAll hook runs again in the new worker, so setup must handle that lifecycle.

interview.question: How do you declare a Playwright test?
interview.answer: `test(title, body)` declares a test. The body receives fixtures and can be asynchronous, so it can use objects such as `page` for browser actions.
interview.followUp: How can one test use different setup values? Use `test.use` at file or `test.describe` scope to configure local options.

interview.question: What is the difference between declaring and conditionally skipping a test?
interview.answer: `test.skip` prevents a declared test from running. When used inside a test, Playwright starts the test and stops it at that call when the condition applies.
interview.followUp: When should `test.fixme` be used? Use it when the test is expected to need fixing, rather than when it should simply remain skipped.

interview.question: How do you change a test timeout?
interview.answer: `test.setTimeout` changes the timeout in milliseconds for the current test. A value of zero removes the timeout; a timeout set in a `beforeAll` or `afterAll` hook applies to that hook instead.
interview.followUp: How can a group share a longer timeout? Call `test.describe.configure({ timeout: 60000 })` inside the group.

Add tags through the details object or include them in the test title. Tags appear in the test report.

Call `test.setTimeout` to change the current test timeout. The value uses milliseconds.

Do not call `test.use` inside `beforeEach` or `beforeAll`; use it at file or `describe` scope.
Parallel tests cannot use shared state or global variables. Each test also runs its applicable hooks.

interview.question: What does test.describe do?
interview.answer: test.describe groups related tests under an optional title. Tests inside its callback appear under that group in the test report.
interview.followUp: How can a group share setup? Add test.beforeEach or test.beforeAll inside the group. The former runs before each test; the latter runs once per worker.

interview.question: When would you use an anonymous describe group?
interview.answer: An anonymous group omits the title and still groups the tests. It is useful when applying a shared test.use configuration without adding a group name to test titles.
interview.followUp: Can group configuration apply after test declarations? Yes. test.describe.configure applies to the whole enclosing scope, whether called before or after declarations.

interview.question: How can you configure tests inside a group?
interview.answer: test.describe.configure changes settings for the enclosing scope. Supported settings include execution mode, retries, timeout, and named locks.
interview.followUp: What happens in serial mode after a failure? Subsequent tests in that serial group are skipped, and retries start from the beginning.

interview.question: How do Playwright assertions wait?
interview.answer: A web assertion such as toHaveText re-fetches the target and checks it repeatedly until it passes or the assertion timeout is reached. The default assertion timeout is five seconds.

interview.answer: test.extend creates a new test object with custom fixtures or options. A fixture can depend on built-in fixtures, calls use with its value, and performs cleanup after use returns.

test.only.summary: A Playwright project is a named group of tests that uses one configuration. Projects let you run the same tests across browsers, devices, environments, or other settings.
test.only.explanation: A Playwright project is a named group of tests that shares a configuration. Define projects in the configuration file to run tests across browsers, devices, environments, or other settings. Playwright runs all configured projects by default, or you can select a specific project.
test.only.syntax: export default defineConfig({ projects: [{ name: 'chromium', use: { ...devices['Desktop Chrome'] } }] });

parameters.name: projects
parameters.description: A list of named project configurations. Each project can define settings such as name and use.

example.title: Run tests in multiple browsers
example.explanation: The configuration defines two projects. Playwright runs the test in each project, using a different browser.

useCases.title: Cross-browser testing
useCases.scenario: Run one test suite in Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit.

useCases.title: Responsive testing
useCases.scenario: Run tests with desktop and mobile device settings.

useCases.title: Project dependencies
useCases.scenario: Separate setup, browser, and teardown work.

interview.question: What is a Playwright project?
interview.answer: A project is a logical group of tests with the same configuration. Projects can target different browsers, devices, environments, timeouts, retries, or test groups.
interview.followUp: How do you run only one project? Use the project filter in the Playwright test command, such as selecting the project by its configured name.

interview.question: How do you configure multiple browsers?
interview.answer: Add named objects to the top-level projects array in playwright.config.ts. Each object can provide a name and use settings, such as a browser or device profile.
interview.followUp: How can you test branded browsers? Combine a device profile with a browser channel such as msedge or chrome.

interview.question: How does project filtering interact with dependencies?
interview.answer: Playwright runs all configured projects by default. Test filters can select primary tests, and dependent projects are included unless --no-deps is used.
interview.followUp: What happens when a selected project has a teardown? The teardown runs after all dependent projects have completed.

keyPoints: Use a project to give a related group of tests one shared configuration.
Projects let one test suite cover desktop browsers and emulated mobile devices.
The same tests can run with different settings, such as logged-in and logged-out state.
Device projects can represent tablet and mobile browser settings.
A teardown project runs after the projects that depend on its setup have finished.
gotchas: Every configured project runs unless you filter the command or project list.
Filtering tests can also run tests from dependent projects.
Use --no-deps when you want only the directly selected projects.

test.skip.summary: Playwright Test provides APIs to declare tests, group them, control execution, and add reusable fixtures, settings, tags, annotations, and report steps.
test.skip.explanation: Playwright's test API declares tests, groups them, controls whether they run, and adds steps, tags, annotations, fixtures, and settings. These controls can apply to one test, a group, or a whole file.
test.skip.syntax:
test(title, body)
test(title, details, body)
test.describe(title, callback)
test.skip(title, body)
test.slow()
test.step(title, body)
test.use(options)

parameters.name: title/details
parameters.description: The test or group title, or test details when the overload supports them.

parameters.name: body/callback
parameters.description: The function that contains the test or group body.

parameters.name: condition/callback
parameters.description: A condition or fixture callback used by conditional annotations.

parameters.name: timeout
parameters.description: The maximum duration, in milliseconds, for a step or configured test.

test.skip.returns: Test declarations and configuration methods return Playwright test objects or configuration results; test.step() returns a Promise for the step result.

example.title: Skip a test by browser
example.explanation: This test runs only in Chromium. In other browsers, Playwright skips it after checking the browser fixture.

useCases.title: Conditional execution
useCases.scenario: A test applies only to one browser or environment.

useCases.title: Group and configure tests
useCases.scenario: Several tests share setup, annotations, or timeout settings.

useCases.title: Create reusable fixtures
useCases.scenario: A project needs shared page objects or test options.

useCases.title: Improve test reports
useCases.scenario: A report should show meaningful action boundaries and metadata.

interview.question: How do you skip a Playwright test?
interview.answer: Use test.skip(title, body) to declare a test that never runs. Use test.skip(condition, description) or a fixture callback to skip based on configuration.
interview.followUp: How would you skip a whole group? Use test.skip(callback, description) before the tests, or use test.describe.skip() for an always-skipped group.

interview.question: What is the difference between fail and fixme?
interview.answer: test.fail() runs the test and expects it to fail. test.fixme() marks the test as needing repair and does not run its body.
interview.followUp: Which is better for a known crash or very slow test? Use fixme, because the documentation says it avoids running that test.

interview.question: How do you control test-group execution?
interview.answer: test.describe() groups tests and can scope hooks and settings. test.describe.configure() can set execution mode, retries, timeout, or locks for the enclosing scope.
interview.followUp: How can groups run concurrently while tests inside each group stay ordered? Configure the outer scope as parallel and each inner group as default mode.

keyPoints: Import test to define tests and expect to check results.
Add tags through test details or include them in the title. Tags can be selected or excluded with grep filters.
Annotations contain a type and optional description. They add context such as an issue reference.
Use test.extend() to create reusable fixtures or configurable options for tests.
Use test.step() to give a group of actions a named entry in the report.
Use test.use() to change options or fixtures for a file or group.
gotchas: Avoid serial groups when possible. Isolated tests are easier to run independently.
A runtime skip stops the test at that call. Use fixme when the test should be repaired rather than simply ignored.
test.slow() changes the timeout to three times the default. It cannot be used in beforeAll or afterAll.

test.slow.summary: test.slow() marks a Playwright test as slow and gives it three times the default timeout. Use a condition or fixture callback when only some configurations or groups need this annotation.
test.slow.explanation: Call test.slow() inside a test to mark it as slow. Playwright then gives that test three times the default timeout. You can also pass a condition and description, or pass a fixture callback to apply the annotation to tests in a file or group.

parameters.name: condition
parameters.description: When true, marks the test or tests as slow.

parameters.name: callback
parameters.description: Returns whether the test or tests should be marked slow, based on fixtures.

parameters.name: description
parameters.description: Optional text shown in the test report.

example.title: Mark a test as slow
example.explanation: This test receives three times the normal test timeout.

useCases.title: Allow a longer test timeout
useCases.scenario: A test needs more time than normal because it performs a long workflow.

useCases.title: Mark one configuration as slow
useCases.scenario: A browser-specific feature runs slowly in one browser.

useCases.title: Annotate a group of tests
useCases.scenario: All tests in a file or describe group need extra time under a fixture-based condition.

interview.question: What does test.slow() do?
interview.answer: test.slow() marks the current test as slow and triples its default timeout. It can be called inside the test body.
interview.followUp: How can slow status depend on the browser? Pass a Boolean condition, such as browserName === 'webkit', and optionally provide a description.

interview.question: How do you mark a test slow only in one configuration?
interview.answer: Use test.slow(condition, description) when one configuration needs more time. The annotation applies only when the condition is true.
interview.followUp: How can a whole group use this rule? Call test.slow() with a fixture callback outside the tests; the callback returns whether the tests are slow.

interview.question: What forms can test.slow() take?
interview.answer: The function accepts no arguments, a Boolean condition, or a fixture callback. An optional description is recorded with a conditional annotation.
interview.followUp: What is the alternative for a hook timeout? Use test.setTimeout() because test.slow() is not supported in beforeAll or afterAll.

keyPoints: A slow test gets three times the default timeout.
Call test.slow() in the test body to annotate that test.
Pass a Boolean condition and optional description for conditional slow status.
A fixture callback can mark every test in a file or describe group as slow.
gotchas: Do not call test.slow() in beforeAll or afterAll. Use test.setTimeout() for those hooks instead.

test.step.summary: test.step() groups test actions into a named report step. It supports nesting, returned values, and options for error location and report details.
test.step.explanation: Call test.step() inside a test to group actions into a named report step. Steps can be nested and can return a value. Options can add a subtitle, serializable parameters, a timeout, a custom source location, or boxed error reporting.

parameters.name: title
parameters.description: Step name shown in reports.

parameters.name: body
parameters.description: Async callback containing the step actions.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Optional settings: box, location, params, subtitle, and timeout.

test.step.returns: Promise<Object>; it resolves with the value returned by the step callback.

example.title: Add report steps
example.explanation: This test creates two named report steps. The first adds descriptive data. The second boxes failures so the report points to the step call.

useCases.title: Organize a workflow
useCases.scenario: Group several actions under one meaningful entry in a test report.

useCases.title: Add report context
useCases.scenario: Show identifiers or targets beside a step title.

useCases.title: Box helper errors
useCases.scenario: Point failures to a reusable helper call.

useCases.title: Capture step output
useCases.scenario: Return a value from a grouped operation.

interview.question: What does test.step() do?
interview.answer: Use test.step(title, body) to create a named step shown in the report. The body is an asynchronous callback, and the method returns the callback's value.
interview.followUp: How can a step expose useful data in reports? Add params for serializable data and subtitle for a short label shown with the title.

interview.question: What is a boxed test step?
interview.answer: Set box: true in the step options. If code inside the step fails, Playwright reports the error at the step call site instead of at the failing internal action.
interview.followUp: When would you avoid boxing? Keep the default when the exact failing action is more useful for debugging.

interview.question: How do step details appear in reports?
interview.answer: A step can receive params and subtitle options. Params are reported as testStep.params, while subtitle complements the title in reports and the trace viewer.
interview.followUp: What happens to very large or unbounded API arguments? Playwright omits unbounded values such as page content and request bodies from reported parameters.

keyPoints: test.step() creates a named step that appears in Playwright's test report.
Steps may contain other test.step() calls, which creates a hierarchy.
The returned promise resolves to the value produced by the step body.
The box option changes failure locations to the step call site.
Use params to attach serializable, step-specific data for reporters and the trace viewer.
Use subtitle for a short secondary label, such as a locator or order identifier.
gotchas: test.step.skip disables the step completely. The documentation recommends testStepInfo.skip() instead.
A step has no time limit unless you set the timeout option.
Reported Playwright API parameters are curated and long strings may be shortened.

test.use.summary: `test.use` overrides Playwright configuration options for a test file or a `describe` block. Use it for settings such as locale, base URL, and storage state.
test.use.explanation: `test.use` sets Playwright options for the tests in its scope. You can use it in a file or a `describe` block. A later scope can reset an option to the value from the configuration file.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Options to apply to the current test file or describe scope.

example.title: Set options for tests
example.explanation: This test overrides the locale for the file.

useCases.title: Change locale for a group
useCases.scenario: A group of tests needs a different language or region.

useCases.title: Override the base URL
useCases.scenario: One test file targets a different application address.

useCases.title: Use scoped authentication state
useCases.scenario: Tests need a prepared login state without changing all projects.

interview.question: What does `test.use` do?
interview.answer: `test.use` overrides options for a test file or a `describe` block. For example, it can set `locale` or `baseURL` for that scope.
interview.followUp: How do you restore the configuration value? Use the option again with the configuration-defined value, or use the documented reset form for that option.

interview.question: Where can you call `test.use`?
interview.answer: The setting applies to tests declared in the scope where `test.use` is called. A file-level call affects the file, while a call inside `describe` affects that group.
interview.followUp: What happens if scopes have different values? The more specific scope supplies the option for its tests.

interview.question: Why use `test.use` instead of changing the config?
interview.answer: It can override configuration options such as `locale` and `baseURL`. This lets one file or group run with different browser or context settings without changing the global configuration.
interview.followUp: Why use a scoped override instead of changing the config? It keeps special test behavior local and avoids changing unrelated tests.

keyPoints: Playwright options can be set globally, for a project, or for a test scope.
Call `test.use` inside a `describe` block to configure the tests in that group.
An option can be reset so the scope uses the value from the configuration file.
gotchas: Options set with `test.use` affect the selected scope. Reset an option explicitly when a test or group should use the configuration value again.
A `test.use` call inside a `describe` block changes options for that group, not for unrelated tests.

TestConfig.summary: TestConfig is the object exported from a Playwright configuration file. It controls test discovery, execution, retries, reporting, projects, timeouts, and other test-run settings.
TestConfig.explanation: TestConfig is the object used in the Playwright configuration file to control how tests are found and run. It can set shared options, such as time limits, retries, reporters, projects, setup files, and test output locations.

parameters.description: Directory containing test files.

parameters.name: timeout
parameters.description: Maximum duration of one test in milliseconds.

parameters.name: globalTimeout
parameters.description: Maximum duration of the complete test suite in milliseconds.

parameters.name: retries
parameters.description: Number of retry attempts for failed tests.

parameters.name: reporter
parameters.description: Test reporter configuration.

parameters.name: projects
parameters.description: Projects used to run tests in different configurations.

TestConfig.returns: A Playwright TestConfig object used as the exported configuration.
