useCases.title: Test discovery
useCases.scenario: Choose where Playwright finds test files.

useCases.title: Multiple projects
useCases.scenario: Run tests across browsers or other configurations.

useCases.title: Controlled test runs
useCases.scenario: Set retries, workers, and time limits for CI.

useCases.title: Test reporting
useCases.scenario: Select console or file-based test result output.

interview.question: What is TestConfig used for?
interview.answer: TestConfig describes the settings in the Playwright configuration file. It controls test discovery and execution, including testDir, timeout, retries, reporter, projects, and workers.
interview.followUp: How can one configuration run tests in several browsers? Define multiple entries in the projects array, with each project selecting its own browser or device settings.

interview.question: How do timeout and globalTimeout differ?
interview.answer: timeout limits an individual test. globalTimeout limits the complete test suite. The test timeout also includes the test function, fixtures, and beforeEach hooks.
interview.followUp: What happens when globalTimeout is reached? Playwright stops the run, while reporters still produce a report.

interview.question: What does fullyParallel change?
interview.answer: By default, files run in parallel, but tests in one file run in order in the same worker. fullyParallel enables parallel execution for all tests across all files.
interview.followUp: How can concurrency be limited? Set workers to a number or to a percentage of logical CPU cores, such as 50%.

keyPoints: TestConfig is the shape of the Playwright configuration file.
Use projects to run tests with multiple configurations or browsers.
retries sets how many times Playwright can retry a failed test.
workers limits the number of worker processes used for parallel test execution.
testDir selects the directory where Playwright searches for tests.
reporter chooses how test results are displayed or saved.
gotchas: Put runner settings at the top level. Do not place them inside use.
A globalTimeout of zero means that the whole-suite time limit is disabled.
Set retries explicitly if failed tests should run again.

TestInfo.summary: TestInfo gives a Playwright test access to its current test data and controls. Use it to inspect status, manage timeouts, create safe output paths, and attach files or buffers.
TestInfo.explanation: TestInfo is the information and control object for the current Playwright test. Playwright provides it to tests, hooks, and test-scoped fixtures, so you can inspect the test, manage its timeout, save files, attach data, or change its status.

parameters.name: name
parameters.description: Attachment name.

parameters.name: options
parameters.type: { body?: Buffer | string; contentType?: string; path?: string }
parameters.description: Attachment options. Use either path or body, not both.

parameters.name: ...pathSegments
parameters.description: Path segments appended under the test output directory.

parameters.name: timeout
parameters.description: New timeout in milliseconds. Zero disables the timeout.

TestInfo.returns: Methods return Promise<void> for attach(), string for outputPath(), and no value for the control methods. Properties return values such as strings, numbers, arrays, configuration objects, or test status values.

example.title: Attach test data with TestInfo
example.explanation: The test gets TestInfo as its second argument. It uses the test title and attaches a screenshot buffer to the test report.

useCases.title: Add test attachments
useCases.scenario: Save a screenshot, log, or API response so a reporter can display it with the test result.

useCases.title: Create isolated temporary files
useCases.scenario: Write downloads or debug files without collisions between parallel tests.

useCases.title: Change the test timeout
useCases.scenario: Give a setup hook more time for a slow operation.

useCases.title: Inspect test execution
useCases.scenario: Check retries, status, title, source location, or project information in hooks and fixtures.

interview.question: What is TestInfo and how does a test receive it?
interview.answer: TestInfo is the object for the currently running test. A test receives it as the second callback argument, after the fixtures object; hooks and test-scoped fixtures can also receive it.
interview.followUp: How can a test access it without a callback parameter? Use test.info(), but only while test execution is active.

interview.question: How do you attach a screenshot or file to a test?
interview.answer: Use testInfo.attach(name, options). Give options either a file path or a body, and optionally set contentType. Playwright copies attached files to a reporter-accessible location.
interview.followUp: How can you create a safe temporary file first? Call testInfo.outputPath() and write the file there before attaching it.

interview.question: What is the difference between status and expectedStatus?
interview.answer: testInfo.status is the actual result, while testInfo.expectedStatus is the result Playwright expects. In an afterEach hook, comparing them can reveal an unexpected result.
interview.followUp: What can change the expected status? For example, test.fail() makes the expected status failed, and test.skip() makes it skipped.

keyPoints: TestInfo describes the test that is running now.
You can receive TestInfo in test functions, lifecycle hooks, and test-scoped fixtures.
outputPath() creates a safe location for temporary test files.
The output path is isolated so parallel test runs do not use the same temporary location.
setTimeout() changes the timeout of the current test in milliseconds.
retry is zero on the first run and increases for each retry.
parallelIndex identifies the worker that runs the test.
gotchas: When attaching data, provide either path or body. Do not provide both.
fixme() stops the test as soon as it is called.
All path segments passed to outputPath() must remain inside that test's output directory.
Changes to testInfo.tags during the test are not shown to reporters.

toBeAttached.summary: Checks that a Locator points to an element attached to a document or shadow root. It retries until the check passes or the assertion timeout is reached.
toBeAttached.explanation: Call this async matcher with a Locator to verify that its target is connected to a document or shadow root. Playwright keeps checking until the condition passes or the assertion timeout is reached, so await the call.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Options object. Optional.

parameters.name: signal
parameters.description: An AbortSignal that can cancel the assertion.

parameters.name: timeout
parameters.description: Time to retry the assertion for, in milliseconds.

example.title: Check that an element is attached
example.explanation: This waits until the status element is connected to the document or a shadow root.

useCases.title: Confirm dynamic rendering
useCases.scenario: Wait for a component to enter the DOM before checking or using it.

useCases.title: Check UI updates
useCases.scenario: Verify that a page element has been mounted after an action.

useCases.title: Check removal
useCases.scenario: Assert that a locator is detached with the negated matcher.

interview.question: What does toBeAttached verify?
interview.answer: It checks that the Locator points to an element connected to a Document or ShadowRoot. It returns a promise and retries until the condition passes or the timeout expires.
interview.followUp: What happens if the signal is already aborted? The assertion fails without retrying.

interview.question: How do you call this matcher?
interview.answer: Use `await expect(locator).toBeAttached()` in a Playwright test. The matcher is an auto-retrying web assertion.
interview.followUp: How can you check the opposite state? Use `await expect(locator).not.toBeAttached()`.

interview.question: How does timeout control this assertion?
interview.answer: The optional `timeout` sets how long Playwright retries the assertion in milliseconds. If omitted, it uses the timeout configured for test expectations.
interview.followUp: How can a test stop the retry early? Pass an `AbortSignal` through the options object.

keyPoints: The matcher succeeds when the located element is connected to a document or shadow root.
Playwright added this matcher in version 1.33.
The `timeout` option controls the retry period in milliseconds.
Without a local timeout, Playwright uses the configured expectation timeout.
The `not` property changes the check to expect the opposite condition.
gotchas: Use await because Playwright retries this assertion asynchronously.
The assertion stops retrying when its timeout is reached.
An aborted signal makes the assertion fail and prevents more retries.

toBeChecked.summary: `toBeChecked()` verifies that a Locator points to a checked input. It retries until the expected state is reached or the assertion times out.
toBeChecked.explanation: Call `toBeChecked()` with a Locator that identifies a checkbox or radio button. Playwright waits and retries until the control has the expected state or the assertion timeout is reached. The default expectation is checked; options can instead request unchecked or indeterminate state.

parameters.name: options.checked
parameters.description: Expected checked state. Defaults to checked.

parameters.name: options.indeterminate
parameters.description: Whether to expect the control to be indeterminate. Supported for checkboxes and radio buttons.

parameters.name: options.signal
parameters.description: Signal that can cancel the assertion.

parameters.name: options.timeout
parameters.description: Maximum retry time in milliseconds. Defaults to the configured expect timeout.

example.title: Check a checkbox and assert its state
example.explanation: This checks a labeled checkbox, then waits until Playwright confirms that its checked state is true.

useCases.title: Verify a checkbox
useCases.scenario: After selecting a checkbox, verify that the control is checked.

useCases.title: Verify a radio button
useCases.scenario: After selecting a radio button, confirm that the chosen option has the checked state.

useCases.title: Verify an indeterminate control
useCases.scenario: Test a tri-state control that should show a mixed value.

interview.question: What does `toBeChecked()` verify?
interview.answer: `toBeChecked()` is a web-specific async assertion for a Locator. It waits until the matched checkbox or radio button is checked, or until the assertion timeout is reached.
interview.followUp: How would you assert the opposite state? Use `await expect(locator).not.toBeChecked()` or pass `{ checked: false }`.

interview.question: Which options change the expected state?
interview.answer: The default assertion is that the input is checked. The `checked` option lets you request a particular checked state.
interview.followUp: Can `checked` be combined with `indeterminate`? No. The documentation disallows that combination.

interview.question: Why must this assertion be awaited?
interview.answer: The assertion retries until it passes or its timeout is reached. The default timeout comes from the test configuration's expect timeout.
interview.followUp: What happens if the assertion is not awaited? The test can continue before the asynchronous assertion finishes, so the assertion must be awaited.

keyPoints: Use this matcher when a Locator should identify a checked input.
With no options, the expected state is checked.
Use the `checked` option when the expected checked state must be explicit.
Set `indeterminate: true` to test the mixed state.
The `timeout` option controls how long Playwright retries the assertion.
A signal can cancel an assertion while it is retrying.
gotchas: Do not provide both `checked` and `indeterminate`; the documentation says these options cannot be combined.
The `indeterminate` option applies only to checkbox and radio-button controls.
Await the matcher because it retries asynchronously.

toBeDisabled.summary: `toBeDisabled()` checks that a locator points to a disabled element. It retries until the check passes or the assertion timeout is reached.
toBeDisabled.explanation: `toBeDisabled()` checks that a locator points to a disabled element. It retries the check until it passes or the assertion timeout is reached. An element is disabled when it has a `disabled` attribute or is disabled with `aria-disabled`.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Optional object containing assertion options, including `timeout` and `signal`.

parameters.name: timeout
parameters.description: Maximum time to retry the assertion, in milliseconds.

parameters.name: signal
parameters.description: Signal that can cancel the assertion.

example.explanation: This test finds the Submit button and waits until Playwright confirms that it is disabled.

useCases.title: Verify that users without permission see a disabled action.
useCases.scenario: Permission-based UI

useCases.title: Confirm that a control is disabled while an operation is in progress.
useCases.scenario: Loading state

useCases.title: Check that a custom control uses `aria-disabled` when appropriate.
useCases.scenario: Accessibility behavior

interview.question: What does `toBeDisabled()` check?
interview.answer: `toBeDisabled()` is a locator assertion that verifies the matched element is disabled. It waits and retries until the condition passes or the configured assertion timeout is reached.
interview.followUp: Why use this instead of `isDisabled()`? The documentation recommends the assertion to avoid flaky tests because it waits for the expected state.

interview.question: How does Playwright determine that an element is disabled?
interview.answer: An element is considered disabled when it has a `disabled` attribute or is disabled through `aria-disabled`. The browser only applies the native `disabled` attribute to supported form controls.
interview.followUp: What happens if a `div` has a `disabled` attribute? The browser ignores that attribute for disabling the element.

interview.question: How is the assertion timeout controlled?
interview.answer: The assertion accepts an optional `timeout` value in milliseconds. If omitted, it uses the timeout configured in `TestConfig.expect`.
interview.followUp: What other option can stop a retrying assertion? An `AbortSignal` can cancel it, and the assertion then fails like a timeout.

keyPoints: Call `await expect(locator).toBeDisabled()` to verify that the locator resolves to a disabled element.
Playwright checks both the native `disabled` attribute and `aria-disabled`.
The `timeout` option sets how long Playwright retries this assertion.
Without a local timeout, the assertion uses the `TestConfig.expect` timeout.
The `toBeDisabled` locator assertion was added in Playwright v1.20.
gotchas: The `disabled` attribute works for native form controls. Adding it to another element does not disable that element in the browser.
Use `await` with this assertion because it retries asynchronously.

toBeEditable.summary: Playwright assertions use `expect` and matchers to check values and browser state. Web assertions retry until the condition passes or the assertion timeout is reached.
toBeEditable.explanation: Call `expect` with a locator, then use a locator assertion such as `toHaveText`. Playwright checks the locator again and again until the condition passes or the assertion timeout is reached. These assertions are asynchronous, so use `await`.

parameters.name: value
parameters.description: The value, locator, page, or response being checked.

parameters.name: expected
parameters.description: The expected text, URL, title, state, count, or other matcher-specific value.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Optional matcher settings, including assertion timeout.

toBeEditable.returns: Retrying assertions return `Promise<void>`; generic assertions return synchronously.

example.explanation: This test clicks Submit and waits until the status element contains the expected text.

useCases.title: Check control state
useCases.scenario: Confirm that a control is enabled, disabled, checked, or editable.

useCases.title: Check URL or title
useCases.scenario: Verify navigation after an action.

useCases.title: Check response status
useCases.scenario: Check that an API response has an OK status.

interview.question: How do you assert that a page element eventually shows text?
interview.answer: Use `expect(locator).toHaveText('Submitted')`. This is an auto-retrying web assertion, so it re-fetches the element and checks its text until it matches or the timeout is reached.
interview.followUp: How would you check that an element is absent from the page? Use `await expect(locator).toBeHidden()` when the locator should not be visible.

interview.question: How do you verify that a locator becomes visible?
interview.answer: Use `await expect(locator).toBeVisible()`. Playwright retries the check until the element is visible or the assertion timeout expires.
interview.followUp: How can the expected state be inverted? Add `.not`, for example `await expect(locator).not.toContainText('error')`.

interview.question: Why are Playwright web assertions useful?

interview.question: How do auto-retrying assertions work?

interview.followUp: How can you change the timeout for one configured expect instance? Create one with `expect.configure({ timeout: 10000 })`.

interview.question: When would you use a soft assertion?

interview.followUp: What can stop a retry before timeout? An AbortSignal can cancel the assertion, and cancellation makes it fail like a timeout.

interview.question: How do you assert an element's CSS class in Playwright?
interview.answer: Use `await expect(locator).toHaveClass(...)` to check an element's CSS class property. This locator assertion retries until it passes or the assertion timeout is reached.
interview.followUp: Why is this usually better than reading a class value first? A direct value assertion does not retry, so it can run before asynchronous page changes finish.

interview.question: How does Playwright wait while checking a locator assertion?
interview.answer: Locator assertions use Playwright's locator, which represents elements at the time the operation runs. The assertion can therefore re-fetch the element during its retry period.
interview.followUp: What can happen if the locator matches more than one element? The actionability rules require a unique match for actions such as clicking; use a more precise locator when needed.

interview.question: How is the assertion timeout controlled?
interview.answer: The default assertion timeout is five seconds. It can be changed for one assertion or configured through the test configuration's `expect` setting.
interview.followUp: What should you do for a complex condition? Use `expect.poll` or `expect.toPass` when the condition needs custom retry behavior.

interview.question: What does `toHaveCount` verify?
interview.answer: `toHaveCount(count)` checks that a locator resolves to exactly the given number of DOM nodes. It returns a promise and retries until the count matches or the assertion times out.
interview.followUp: How would you check a list's contents? Use `toHaveText` with an array of expected strings when order and text should both be verified.

interview.question: Which arguments can you pass?
interview.answer: The argument is the expected number of matching elements. Assertion options can include `timeout`, which controls how long Playwright retries the assertion.
interview.followUp: How can an assertion be cancelled? Pass an `AbortSignal` in the options; aborting makes the assertion fail like a timeout.

interview.question: Why is this matcher preferred over `locator.count()`?
interview.answer: Use `expect(locator).toHaveCount()` for an assertion instead of reading `await locator.count()` and comparing the result. The matcher is designed to retry during asynchronous page updates.
interview.followUp: Why can `locator.all()` be risky here? It does not wait for matches and may return an incomplete set while a dynamic list is still loading.

interview.question: How do you assert an element's CSS value?
interview.answer: Use `await expect(locator).toHaveCSS(property, value)` to check an element's CSS property. It retries the check until the expected value appears or the assertion timeout is reached.
interview.followUp: Why is retrying useful? A page may update after the test starts, so repeated checks reduce failures caused by timing.

interview.question: What can the locator passed to `toHaveCSS` represent?
interview.answer: The assertion uses a locator, such as `page.locator('css=button')`, and checks the named CSS property against the expected value. Locators can use CSS selectors, and Playwright extends CSS with custom pseudo-classes.
interview.followUp: When should you avoid a CSS locator? Prefer user-facing locators such as accessible roles or text when they can express the target.

interview.question: How does `toHaveCSS` differ from a non-retrying assertion?
interview.answer: The assertion is one of Playwright's auto-retrying web assertions. Playwright re-fetches the element and checks it repeatedly instead of checking only once.
interview.followUp: What should you use for a condition that is not a built-in web assertion? Use `expect.poll` or `expect.toPass` for more complex retryable checks.

interview.answer: Use `await expect(locator).toHaveId('lastname')`. The locator identifies the element, and the matcher verifies its DOM `id`. The assertion retries until it passes or times out.
interview.followUp: Can the expected ID use a pattern? Yes. Pass a JavaScript `RegExp`, such as `/^user-/`, instead of a string.

interview.question: What types of expected values does `toHaveId` accept?

interview.followUp: What happens if the element is not ready immediately? Playwright re-fetches the element and retries the assertion until it succeeds or reaches the timeout.

interview.question: What is the difference between generic and web-specific assertions?
interview.answer: Use `expect(value)` with a matcher such as `toBeTruthy()` for general values. For page state, use an async locator matcher such as `await expect(locator).toHaveText('Submitted')`, which retries until it passes or times out.

interview.question: How do Playwright's auto-retrying assertions work?
interview.answer: Auto-retrying locator assertions re-fetch the element and check it repeatedly. They stop when the condition passes or when the assertion timeout is reached.
interview.followUp: Where can the timeout be configured? Set it per assertion or configure the shared value with `testConfig.expect` in the test configuration.

interview.question: What does `pageAssertions.toHaveScreenshot` do?
interview.answer: It waits for two consecutive screenshots to match, then compares the final stable screenshot with the expected snapshot. This reduces failures caused by a page that is still changing.
interview.followUp: How can you reduce differences from dynamic content? Use options such as `mask`, `stylePath`, animation control, or pixel-difference limits, and keep the rendering environment consistent.

interview.question: How are snapshot files named and formatted?
interview.answer: The name can be a string or an array of path segments. A named snapshot must end in `.png` or `.webp`; PNG is the default when no name is supplied.
interview.followUp: Where can an array snapshot path point? It must remain inside the snapshot directory for that test file.

interview.question: How can visual comparison tolerance be configured?
interview.answer: The `threshold` option sets the allowed perceived color difference for a pixel, from 0 for strict comparison to 1 for a looser comparison. `maxDiffPixels` sets an allowed count of different pixels.
interview.followUp: What is the default threshold? The documentation gives `0.2`, while other expectation defaults can be configured in Playwright configuration.

toHaveValue.explanation: `toHaveValue` checks that a locator points to an element with the expected input value. The expected value can be a string or regular expression, and Playwright retries the check until it passes or its timeout is reached.

parameters.name: value
parameters.description: Expected input value. It can be a string or regular expression.

parameters.name: options.signal
parameters.description: Optional signal that cancels the assertion.

parameters.name: options.timeout
parameters.description: Optional retry timeout in milliseconds.

example.title: Check an input value
example.explanation: This test checks that the number input contains the string value "42". The assertion waits and retries until it passes or the assertion timeout is reached.

useCases.title: Validate a form field
useCases.scenario: Check that a text, number, or other form input contains the expected value.

useCases.title: Wait for an asynchronous update
useCases.scenario: Verify that a value eventually appears after page code updates an input.

useCases.title: Use flexible value matching
useCases.scenario: Match an input against a value pattern instead of one exact string.

interview.question: How do you assert an input value?
interview.answer: Use `await expect(locator).toHaveValue(value)`. It checks the value of the element targeted by the locator and retries until the condition passes or the assertion timeout is reached.
interview.followUp: How can the expected value be flexible? Pass a regular expression instead of a string, such as `/[0-9]/`.

interview.question: What types of expected values does `toHaveValue` support?
interview.answer: The method accepts a string or a regular expression as its expected value. The assertion returns a promise, so asynchronous tests should await it.
interview.followUp: What happens if the value does not match? The assertion keeps retrying until its timeout, then fails.

interview.question: How is the assertion timeout controlled?
interview.answer: The optional `timeout` sets how long Playwright retries the assertion in milliseconds. If omitted, it uses the timeout configured in `TestConfig.expect`.
interview.followUp: Can an assertion be cancelled? Yes. The optional `signal` can cancel a retrying assertion, causing it to fail like a timeout.

keyPoints: Use this matcher to verify the current value of an input element.
A string checks for an expected value; a regular expression supports pattern matching.
Playwright retries the value check during the assertion timeout.
Without a local timeout, the assertion uses the test configuration's expect timeout.
gotchas: The expected value may be a regular expression, not only a string.
The assertion can stop after the configured or supplied timeout.

toHaveValues.summary: Playwright assertions use `expect` with generic matchers and web-specific matchers. Web assertions retry until the condition passes or the assertion timeout is reached.
toHaveValues.explanation: Call `expect` with a value, locator, page, or response, then choose a matcher. Locator and other web-specific assertions retry by checking the target again until the condition passes or the assertion timeout is reached. Generic matchers check the value once unless you use a retrying helper.

parameters.name: value
parameters.description: The value, locator, page, or response that the assertion checks.

parameters.name: expected
parameters.description: The expected text, value, pattern, or other matcher-specific condition.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Optional assertion settings, including timeout; locator assertions also document an optional AbortSignal in current API entries.

toHaveValues.returns: Assertions return a promise for web-specific asynchronous matchers; generic matchers return an assertion result and throw when the expectation fails.

example.title: Wait for text with a locator assertion
example.explanation: The test clicks Submit, then waits for the status element to contain the expected text.

useCases.title: Check asynchronous UI text
useCases.scenario: After an action changes page content, verify the updated text without adding a fixed delay.

useCases.title: Check browser state
useCases.scenario: Verify that a selected option, title, URL, role, attribute, or screenshot matches the expected state.

useCases.title: Check an API response
useCases.scenario: Validate that an API response has an OK status.

useCases.title: Retry a custom condition
useCases.scenario: Retry a custom condition that is not covered by a built-in matcher.

interview.question: How do Playwright web-first assertions work?
interview.answer: Use `expect(locator).toHaveText('Submitted')` for page text. Locator assertions re-fetch the target and retry until the expected condition is met or the timeout is reached.
interview.followUp: How would you avoid a fixed sleep? Use an auto-retrying assertion such as `toHaveText`, or use `expect.poll` for a custom value.

interview.question: What is the difference between generic and web-specific assertions?
interview.answer: Generic matchers such as `toEqual` and `toBeTruthy` assert values. Locator, page, and response matchers provide web-specific checks and retry behavior where documented.
interview.followUp: What should you choose for asynchronously rendered UI? Prefer a locator assertion instead of a one-time generic assertion on a separately read value.

interview.question: How can assertion timeouts and retries be controlled?
interview.answer: The default assertion timeout is 5 seconds. A timeout can be passed to an assertion, or configured globally with the `testConfig.expect` setting.
interview.followUp: What can you use for a complex condition? Use `expect.poll` or `expect.toPass` when the condition needs custom retry behavior.

keyPoints: Import and call `expect` to create an assertion.
A locator text assertion checks the current element repeatedly instead of checking only one DOM snapshot.
Auto-retrying matchers stop when they pass or when their assertion timeout expires.
Use `expect.poll` or `expect.toPass` for retrying conditions that built-in matchers do not cover.
`expect(response).toBeOK()` checks that an API response has an OK status.
gotchas: Do not use a non-retrying matcher for changing page content when an auto-retrying web assertion is available.
An assertion normally waits up to 5 seconds; configure or pass a different timeout when needed.

toMatchAriaSnapshot.summary: Checks a page or locator against an accessibility-tree snapshot. The snapshot describes roles, names, attributes, and nesting.
toMatchAriaSnapshot.explanation: Use toMatchAriaSnapshot to compare a page or locator's accessibility tree with an expected template. The template can check roles, names, attributes, hierarchy, order, and dynamic text patterns.

parameters.name: expected / options
parameters.description: Expected accessibility snapshot template, or options for a stored snapshot.

parameters.name: name
parameters.description: Snapshot file name when using the options form.

parameters.name: signal
parameters.description: Signal that cancels the assertion.

parameters.name: timeout
parameters.description: Maximum time to retry the assertion.

example.title: Match a page accessibility snapshot
example.explanation: This checks the page accessibility tree against a readable YAML-like template.

useCases.title: Accessibility regression testing
useCases.scenario: Verify the accessible structure of a page or component.

useCases.title: Partial structure checks
useCases.scenario: Check stable roles and hierarchy while ignoring changing names or attributes.

useCases.title: File-based snapshots
useCases.scenario: Store a reusable accessibility baseline in an .aria.yml file.

useCases.title: Dynamic text matching
useCases.scenario: Match changing labels or counts without hard-coding one value.

interview.question: What does toMatchAriaSnapshot verify?
interview.answer: It compares the selected page or locator's accessibility tree with a predefined snapshot template. The template describes roles, names, attributes, and nesting.
interview.followUp: How can a test allow extra children? Add a /children property with the contain mode, either in the template or in expect configuration.

interview.question: What rules affect snapshot matching?
interview.answer: The template uses YAML-like indentation to express nesting. Matching is case-sensitive and order-sensitive, while whitespace in names and text is normalized.
interview.followUp: How can dynamic accessible text be matched? Use a regular expression in the accessible name or text, such as /Issues \d+/.

interview.question: How are separate snapshot files created?
interview.answer: Use toMatchAriaSnapshot with an options object and a name ending in .aria.yml. Playwright stores the snapshot in the configured snapshot directory.
interview.followUp: How can the location be changed? Configure toMatchAriaSnapshot.pathTemplate or the general snapshotPathTemplate.

keyPoints: The matcher can check the whole page or a specific locator.
Omit a name or attribute when only the role or structure matters.
Use regular expressions for changing accessible names or text.
Indentation in the template represents accessibility-tree hierarchy.
gotchas: Matching is case-sensitive. Whitespace in names and text is normalized.
Elements must appear in the same order as the template.
A single node can match at any depth, but multiple top-level nodes must share a parent.
An empty template creates a snapshot, which can help generate a baseline.

Trace viewer.summary: Playwright Trace Viewer helps you inspect a recorded test after it runs. It shows actions, page state, source code, screenshots, logs, and network activity, which is useful for debugging failures.
Trace viewer.explanation: Playwright records actions and debugging data while a test runs. The Trace Viewer lets you inspect each action with page snapshots, screenshots, source lines, logs, errors, console messages, network requests, and test metadata.
Trace viewer.syntax:
npx playwright test --trace on
npx playwright show-trace trace.zip
https://trace.playwright.dev/?trace=<trace-url>

parameters.name: trace
parameters.description: The test trace archive or remote trace URL to open.

parameters.name: --tracing
parameters.description: A tracing mode such as `on`, `off`, or `retain-on-failure` for the pytest command.

Trace viewer.returns: A trace archive that can be opened in Trace Viewer; the viewer displays recorded test actions and debugging information.

example.title: Run a test with a trace
example.explanation: Run this test with tracing enabled, then open the generated trace from the HTML report.

useCases.title: Debug a CI failure
useCases.scenario: A test fails after running in CI.

useCases.title: Inspect one action
useCases.scenario: A test has a timing or locator problem.

useCases.title: Compare DOM snapshots
useCases.scenario: You need to understand page state around an input.

useCases.title: Review network and console data
useCases.scenario: A test depends on requests or browser messages.

interview.question: What is Playwright Trace Viewer used for?
interview.answer: A trace is recorded during a test and saved as a trace archive. The Trace Viewer then shows the test actions and related debugging data, so a failed CI test can be inspected after it finishes.
interview.followUp: How can tracing be enabled for a local run? Run the test command with the trace option enabled, such as `npx playwright test --trace on`.

interview.question: What can you inspect for an individual action?
interview.answer: The Actions tab lists actions, their locators, and their durations. Selecting an action can show snapshots, the source location, and the action log; other tabs expose calls, errors, console output, and network activity.
interview.followUp: How can logs be limited to part of a test? Select a time range on the timeline; the action, console, and network views are filtered to that range.

interview.question: When does the default Playwright Test setup record traces?
interview.answer: The default configuration uses `on-first-retry`, so a trace is created on the first retry of a failed test. The HTML report links to the trace from the detailed test view.
interview.followUp: How can every local test create a trace? Use `npx playwright test --trace on` when running the tests.

keyPoints: Trace Viewer is a graphical tool for reviewing a test after it has run.
Use the timeline and action list to move through the test and inspect each step.
With screenshots enabled, the viewer provides a film strip that helps locate actions visually.
Snapshots show the page before, during, and after an action, including the input position.
Selecting an action highlights the related source line.
The Call tab includes action timing, locator details, strict-mode information, and keyboard input.
Selecting a timeline range limits network requests and other logs to that part of the test.
gotchas: The default test configuration records a trace on the first retry, not on the first run. On CI, the shown configuration retries failed tests twice.
Opening a remote trace URL in the browser can be blocked by CORS rules.
The browser viewer processes uploaded trace data locally, but remote trace URLs still need accessible storage.

Tracing.summary: Playwright tracing records browser actions and network activity for later inspection in Trace Viewer. Start it before actions, then stop it and save the trace to a file.
Tracing.explanation: Start tracing before the actions you want to inspect. Stop it afterward and provide a path to save the trace. You can create separate chunks on one browser context, group actions in the viewer, or record network traffic as a HAR file.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Options for starting tracing, such as screenshots, snapshots, sources, title, name, and live.

parameters.name: path
parameters.description: Destination file for the saved trace.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Options for starting a trace chunk, including name and title.

parameters.name: path
parameters.description: Filesystem path for the HAR output.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: HAR options such as content, mode, resourcesDir, and urlFilter.

Tracing.returns: start, startChunk, and startHar return a Disposable. stop, stopChunk, and stopHar return Promise<void>.

example.title: Record a trace
example.explanation: This records browser actions, screenshots, DOM snapshots, and network activity, then saves the trace as trace.zip.

useCases.title: Debug browser actions
useCases.scenario: Debug a failed browser flow by reviewing actions, screenshots, snapshots, and network activity.

useCases.title: Record trace chunks
useCases.scenario: Save separate trace files for different parts of one browser context.

useCases.title: Record a HAR
useCases.scenario: Capture network requests and responses for later analysis or replay.

interview.question: How do you record and save a Playwright trace?
interview.answer: Call tracing.start before the browser actions to record. Then call tracing.stop with a path such as trace.zip to save the result.
interview.followUp: How can multiple traces use one context? Start tracing once, then use startChunk and stopChunk for each trace file.

interview.question: What do screenshots and snapshots control?
interview.answer: Set screenshots to true to capture screenshots for the timeline preview. Set snapshots to true to capture DOM snapshots and record network activity on each action.
interview.followUp: Which option captures only the DOM snapshot? Use snapshots with an object such as { dom: true } rather than enabling screenshots.

interview.question: How do you record network activity as a HAR?
interview.answer: startHar begins recording network activity as a HAR file. stopHar ends the recording and saves it to the path passed to startHar.
interview.followUp: How can the HAR include only selected requests? Pass a URL glob or regular expression through urlFilter.

keyPoints: Saved traces can be opened in Trace Viewer after the script finishes.
Begin tracing before the actions that you want to inspect.
Pass path to stop to save the completed trace to a chosen file.
Use one tracing session and separate it into chunks when you need multiple trace files.
Trace groups can be nested and appear as named sections in Trace Viewer.
Set sources to true when the trace should include source files for actions.
gotchas: The context tracing API does not include test assertions. Use Playwright Test configuration when assertion details are needed.
For tests, prefer configuration-based tracing because it gives a more complete failure trace.
Do not start two HAR recordings on the same Tracing instance at once.
Use test.step for test groups when it is available instead of tracing.group.

UI Mode.summary: Playwright UI Mode is an interactive way to run and debug tests. It provides test filters, timelines, snapshots, logs, locator picking, network details, and watch mode.
UI Mode.explanation: UI Mode opens an interactive test view. It lists test files and lets you run selected tests, inspect actions, view logs and errors, examine DOM snapshots, pick locators, and watch tests rerun after changes.

example.title: Open UI Mode
example.code: npx playwright test --ui
example.explanation: Starts Playwright UI Mode, where you can choose tests and inspect their steps.

useCases.title: Debug failures
useCases.scenario: Inspect a failing test step by step with snapshots, logs, errors, and source locations.

useCases.title: Create locators
useCases.scenario: Select a page element in a DOM snapshot and copy a locator into a test.

useCases.title: Watch changes
useCases.scenario: Rerun selected tests automatically after editing test code.

useCases.title: Use remote environments
useCases.scenario: Run UI Mode from Docker or Codespaces through a browser.

interview.question: How do you open Playwright UI Mode?
interview.answer: Run `npx playwright test --ui`. UI Mode lists test files and lets you run all tests, a file, a test block, or one test.
interview.followUp: How do you rerun a test when its code changes? Enable the eye icon beside the test, which activates watch mode.

interview.question: How does UI Mode help debug a test?
interview.answer: UI Mode shows a timeline for the test. You can move across actions, inspect snapshots, and use Before and After views to compare the DOM around an action.
interview.followUp: How can you inspect an element's locator? Use Pick locator, hover over the DOM snapshot, then copy the locator from the locator playground.

interview.question: What should you know about setup projects and authentication in UI Mode?
interview.answer: UI Mode does not run setup projects automatically. Enable the setup project in the filter, run its setup test, then disable the setup project before running dependent tests.
interview.followUp: Why might authentication fail in UI Mode? The stored authentication state may have expired, so rerun the authentication setup test to create fresh state.

keyPoints: The sidebar lists test files. You can expand files and describe blocks to run, view, watch, or debug individual tests.
Use filters for test text, projects, tags such as @tag, and passed, failed, or skipped status.
The timeline lets you review test actions and see an image snapshot for each action.
Open a DOM snapshot in another window, then use browser DevTools to inspect its HTML, CSS, and console.
Pick Locator highlights elements and shows matching locators; edit the locator in the playground before copying it.
The Log tab shows internal actions such as scrolling, waiting, clicking, filling, and pressing.
Watch mode reruns selected tests when you change them, and you can enable it for one test or all tests.
gotchas: If your project uses dependencies, run setup tests manually before running dependent tests in UI Mode.
Binding UI Mode to 0.0.0.0 can expose traces, passwords, and secrets to other machines on the network.
Do not commit authentication state files to a repository because they can contain credentials that impersonate a test account.

webkit.summary: Playwright is a browser automation and end-to-end testing tool. It runs tests across Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit, with isolated contexts, waiting actions, and retrying assertions.
webkit.explanation: Playwright runs browser tests against Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit. Each test uses an isolated browser context, while locators and assertions wait for the page to reach the needed state.
webkit.syntax:
npx playwright install
npx playwright test
npx playwright test --project=firefox

example.title: A basic Playwright test
example.explanation: This test opens the site, finds a link by its accessible role and name, clicks it, and checks that the Installation heading is visible.

useCases.scenario: Run the same tests against several browser engines to find browser-specific failures.

useCases.title: Isolated test runs
useCases.scenario: Keep login and page state from leaking between tests.

useCases.title: Device emulation
useCases.scenario: Run tests on mobile-sized browser configurations using device profiles.

useCases.title: Local and CI testing
useCases.scenario: Use a headed or headless browser locally or in continuous integration.

interview.question: Which browsers can Playwright test?
interview.answer: Playwright can run tests with Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit. It also supports branded Chromium browsers such as Chrome and Edge through configured projects.
interview.followUp: How would you run only Firefox? Use the project name with the command-line option: `npx playwright test --project=firefox`.

interview.question: How are Playwright browsers installed?
interview.answer: Playwright installs browser binaries with `npx playwright install`. Running the command without a browser name installs the default browsers.
interview.followUp: How can CI install a browser and its operating-system dependencies together? Run `npx playwright install --with-deps chromium`.

interview.question: How does Playwright test multiple browser configurations?
interview.answer: Projects define browser and device configurations in the Playwright configuration file. Playwright runs all configured projects by default, or one selected project when `--project` is used.
interview.followUp: How can a test run on a mobile profile? Add a project using a device descriptor such as `devices['Mobile Chrome']`.

keyPoints: The main browser engines are Chromium, WebKit, and Firefox.
A fresh context keeps test state separate from other tests.
Actions wait until the target can safely receive the action.
Assertions retry instead of requiring fixed sleep calls.
Prefer role, label, placeholder, and test-id locators.
Configured browser projects can run in parallel by default.
gotchas: Updating Playwright can require installing matching browser binaries again.
Use Playwright's Firefox build rather than the branded Firefox browser.
Use WebKit for Safari-like testing instead of branded Safari.
A proxy or custom download host may be needed when network access is restricted.

WebSocketRoute.summary: WebSocketRoute handles a WebSocket created by a page route. It can mock the socket or connect to the real server and intercept messages.
WebSocketRoute.explanation: WebSocketRoute lets a route handler act like a WebSocket server. By default, the page-side socket is mocked and does not connect to a real server. Call connectToServer() to connect to the real server and intercept traffic. Message and close handlers disable automatic forwarding for the direction they handle, so the handler must forward or respond manually.
WebSocketRoute.syntax:
page.routeWebSocket(url, handler)
webSocketRoute.connectToServer()
webSocketRoute.onMessage(handler)
webSocketRoute.onClose(handler)
webSocketRoute.send(message)
webSocketRoute.close(options?)
webSocketRoute.protocols()
webSocketRoute.url()

parameters.name: code
parameters.description: Optional close code.

parameters.name: reason
parameters.description: Optional close reason.

parameters.name: message
parameters.description: Message to send.

parameters.name: handler
parameters.description: Function that handles messages.

parameters.name: handler
parameters.description: Function that handles closure, receiving an optional code and reason.

WebSocketRoute.returns: connectToServer() returns a server-side WebSocketRoute. protocols() returns an array of strings. url() returns the page-created WebSocket URL. close() returns a Promise<void>. Other handlers and send() do not specify a return value in the provided page text.

example.title: Mock a WebSocket
example.explanation: This creates a mocked WebSocket. It sends a response when the page sends the text "request".

useCases.title: Mock server replies
useCases.scenario: Test a page without a WebSocket backend.

useCases.title: Intercept traffic
useCases.scenario: Change or filter messages while the page uses a real WebSocket server.

useCases.title: Check protocols
useCases.scenario: Reject clients that request an unsupported WebSocket subprotocol.

interview.question: How does WebSocketRoute mock a connection?
interview.answer: A routed WebSocket is mocked by default, so it does not connect to the real server. Use onMessage() to inspect messages and send() to reply.
interview.followUp: How would you pass traffic through while changing one message? Call connectToServer(), add an onMessage() handler on the original route, and send either the changed or original message to the returned server route.

interview.question: What does connectToServer() do?
interview.answer: connectToServer() connects the routed socket to the real server and returns another WebSocketRoute for the server side. Without handlers, messages are forwarded in both directions.
interview.followUp: How can traffic be blocked in both directions? Register onMessage() on both route objects and only call send() for messages that should pass.

interview.question: Where does send() deliver a message?
interview.answer: send() sends to the page when called on the original route. When called on the route returned by connectToServer(), it sends to the server.
interview.followUp: What changes after onMessage() is registered? Automatic forwarding stops for that direction, so the handler must call send() explicitly.

keyPoints: Create a WebSocketRoute through page.routeWebSocket() or browserContext.routeWebSocket().
connectToServer() gives you a second route object for communication with the real server.
Calling onMessage() again replaces the existing message handler.
close() closes one side and accepts an optional code and reason.
protocols() returns the subprotocols requested by the page, or an empty array when none were requested.
gotchas: After registering onMessage(), forward messages yourself with send() or with the server-side route.
After registering onClose(), handle the close operation yourself; closure is no longer forwarded automatically.
A route is a mock unless the handler calls connectToServer().

Worker.summary: The Worker class represents a WebWorker. Use it to inspect a worker, run code in its context, and observe its close or console events.
Worker.explanation: A Worker represents a WebWorker attached to a page. You can inspect its URL, run JavaScript in the worker context, keep a handle to a returned value, and listen for close or console events.

worker.evaluateHandle(pageFunction[, arg])
worker.url()
worker.waitForEvent(event[, optionsOrPredicate])

parameters.description: Function or string to run in the worker context.

parameters.name: arg
parameters.description: Optional value passed to the function.

parameters.name: event
parameters.description: Event name to wait for.

parameters.name: optionsOrPredicate
parameters.description: Predicate or options object controlling the wait.

useCases.title: Run code in a worker

interview.question: What does Playwright's Worker class represent?
interview.answer: A Worker represents a WebWorker. The page emits a worker event when one is created, and the worker emits close when it is terminated.
interview.followUp: How can you observe worker creation? Register a handler on the page's worker event before the worker is created.

interview.question: How do evaluate and evaluateHandle differ?
interview.answer: worker.evaluate runs a function or expression in the worker context and returns its serializable result. It waits for a returned Promise to resolve.
interview.followUp: What should you use when the result must remain a JavaScript object handle? Use evaluateHandle, which returns a JSHandle instead of the value itself.

interview.question: How does waitForEvent work?
interview.answer: waitForEvent waits for a named worker event and can use a predicate to decide when the wait finishes. It returns the event data and throws if the page closes first.
interview.followUp: How can the wait be cancelled? Pass an AbortSignal; aborting it makes the operation throw, while the timeout still applies unless set to 0.

keyPoints: Worker is the Playwright object for interacting with a WebWorker.
Listen on the page to detect when a worker starts.
Listen for close to detect that the worker has ended.
evaluate gives back the function's result after running it in the worker.
evaluateHandle keeps the result as a JSHandle.
The console event reports calls such as console.log made inside the worker.
gotchas: evaluate returns undefined when the function produces a value that cannot be serialized.
waitForEvent has no timeout by default, but the configured timeout can change this. Set timeout to 0 to disable timeout explicitly.
